Float supports IEEE 754 equality: NaN compares unequal to every value, including itself, and positive and negative zero compare equal. Float is not Hashable.
String equality compares exact UTF-8 scalar sequences without Unicode normalization. Bytes compare byte sequences. Decimal equality compares numeric value rather than spelling or trailing zeroes. Hashing must agree with equality: equal values have equal hashes, but unequal values may collide. Hash values/algorithms are not a stable serialized format or a public source operation.
Records compare only with the same instantiated nominal type, field by field. Alternatives require the same instantiated type, tag, and equal payload fields. A record/alternative is Equal when every component is eligible for equality, and Hashable when every component is eligible for hashing. Optional and Result follow these alternative rules. Derivations respect current sharing eligibility and do not grant equality to service/resource references.
Collection Equality Hashing List[T] Same length and equal corresponding elements; requires T: Equal Unsupported Map[K, V] Same key/value associations regardless of insertion order; requires eligible keys and V: Equal Unsupported Set[T] Same members regardless of insertion order; requires eligible elements Unsupported Collections are not Hashable. A record containing a collection can be Equal but cannot automatically become a map key or set element. Function values and contract views have no implicit equality or hashing.
Manuscript let same = [1, 2] == [1, 2] let different = [1, 2] == [2, 1] # false # Rejected at type checking: Float is not Hashable. fn accepts_float_keys(values: Map[Float, Int]) -> Unit: return For guarded recursive data , eligibility is checked over the finite declaration graph. Every nonrecursive leaf must meet the bound; recursive references reuse the requirement already being checked. A cycle does not establish eligibility if a leaf fails it. Generated equality traverses finite immutable values structurally. Containers still block hashing derivation even when they guard recursive layout.
Manuscript type Tree[T: Equal]: value: T children: List[Tree[T]] This tree is Equal for eligible T; its list field prevents hashing. User-defined implementations of compiler bounds cannot override these derivations.
Compiler-defined bounds# Equal and Hashable are compiler-defined bounds. Hashing requires equality. A generic operation can require these properties using a bound , and the compiler checks whether its type arguments meet the requirement.
Use Requirements Value equality Eligible shareable data type with equality Map[K, V] key Shareable and hashable, including equality Set[T] element Shareable and hashable, including equality Equality and hash consistency# For a Hashable type, equality must be reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Equal values must hash identically under the same hash configuration. Unequal values may have the same hash; a map or set must resolve every collision by equality rather than accepting a hash match as a key match. Hashes are internal lookup aids, not stable IDs or persistence formats.
The same immutable key must retain its equality and hash behavior while stored. Neither operation depends on a resource’s open state, external authority, insertion order, or current wall-clock time. Float and records containing Float remain equality-comparable with IEEE behavior, but cannot meet Hashable’s equivalence requirement because NaN is not equal to itself.
With structural derivation, every declared field participates. A display label or cached value is not silently excluded. Model a lookup identity as its own record, then use that record as the key:
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Map from "@std/collections.ms" type CustomerKey: id: String type Customer: key: CustomerKey display_name: String test "domain identity is a value": let first = Customer(key: CustomerKey(id: "c1"), display_name: "Ada") let renamed = Customer(key: CustomerKey(id: "c1"), display_name: "Ada Lovelace") if not (first != renamed): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (first.key == renamed.key): return panic(message: "check failed") let names = Map[CustomerKey, String]().with_entry(key: first.key, value: first.display_name) let updated = names.with_entry(key: renamed.key, value: renamed.display_name) if not (updated.length() == 1): return panic(message: "check failed") A domain requiring normalized text identity should construct a canonical key value explicitly. String equality itself remains exact; adding a matching operation name to a type does not change == or key lookup.
Domain values and runtime authority# A nominal record describes domain data. Capabilities describe external authority, and a Background service controls work under a fixed lifetime. Safe concurrent sharing does not automatically grant equality to a service or resource.
The compiler generates equality and hashing operations for eligible types. The design does not introduce arbitrary user-defined operator overloading.
Previous: Collections · Next: Operation contracts

title: Operation contracts
content:
Operation contracts# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index An interface lists the operations a caller needs. This is an operation contract: a concrete implementation must supply those operations with the declared signatures. Use it when callers should depend on behavior rather than a particular data type.
The following contract refers to application-defined Money, Receipt, and PaymentError types:
Manuscript interface Payments: fn charge(amount: Money) -> Result[Receipt, PaymentError] The caller can see the amount accepted, the receipt returned on success, and the expected payment error. The contract uses the same explicit function signature rules as an ordinary declaration.
Explicit implementations# Operation contracts support explicit implementations through impl Contract for DataType; implementations bind self to the receiver. Contracts have no inheritance or default implementations.
An implementation supplies the contract’s operations for the named data type. The implementation relationship is declared explicitly rather than inferred from coincidentally similar operation names.
Manuscript interface Increment: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int type Offset: delta: Int impl Increment for Offset: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int: return value + self.delta self is an implicit receiver binding inside each implementation method, with the concrete receiver type. It is not written as a parameter, is not supplied as a call argument, and cannot be redeclared. The receiver does not add a field to the contract. Methods follow the ordinary immutable-field and reference rules.
An implementation must match the contract exactly. After substituting generic type arguments, check:
every operation appears exactly once; operation names match; parameter labels, their declaration order, and parameter types match; result types match. Missing, extra, duplicate, or mismatched operations are compile errors. A method cannot add defaults or its own generic parameters. Parameter labels and order are part of function identity .
Manuscript # Rejected: amount does not match the contract's value label. impl Increment for Offset: fn apply(amount: Int) -> Int: return amount + self.delta The rejected block is an alternative negative example, not a second block to add to the valid example.
Coherence and visibility# Declare an implementation in the module that defines its concrete type. The contract may be imported, but the concrete type must be local to that module. Each concrete type and applied contract pair has exactly one implementation; duplicates are rejected.
Importing the concrete type loads that module and its implementations. Importing an unrelated module cannot add methods to the type later. This keeps behavior independent of unrelated imports.
Concrete and generic implementation blocks obey the same defining-module rule. Orphan implementations, blanket implementations for a bare type parameter, specialization, generic operations, and implementation inheritance are unsupported. Contracts can be generic but cannot have fields, cases, default bodies, associated types, or static operations. A contract declares at least one operation. An implementation does not re-export either its type or its contract.
Exported contracts expose every operation. Types in their operation signatures obey the public surface rules .
Generic implementations# An implementation uses generic parameters from its receiver type declaration. Its receiver must be an application of a nominal data declaration in the implementation’s module. Parameter names in the receiver application come from that data declaration. Only parameters occurring in the receiver application are in scope for the interface and methods; matching the receiver determines all implementation arguments. Concrete and nested receiver applications remain supported. Interface parameter names need not match data parameter names: an application substitutes the receiver parameters positionally. An undeclared name such as U in impl ReadValue[U] for Box[U] is rejected when Box declares only T.
Manuscript interface ReadValue[T]: fn get() -> T type Box[T]: value: T impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T]: fn get() -> T: return self.value This block implements ReadValue[Int] for Box[Int], ReadValue[String] for Box[String], and every other well-formed application. Methods use the receiver declaration’s parameters but cannot declare their own. Bounds are inherited from the receiver type declaration and, for interface arguments that are receiver parameters, from the interface declaration. The compiler checks the body once under these inherited bounds, with self: Box[T], and checks exact substituted operation signatures.
Inherited bounds must prove that every nested type application and operation in the body is legal. At a use, receiver matching supplies the arguments and those arguments must satisfy the inherited bounds. When a receiver argument is specialized to a concrete type, references to that parameter in other inherited bounds use the concrete type. For example, Pair[A, B: ReadValue[A]] with receiver Pair[Int, B] gives B: ReadValue[Int].
Interface parameter bounds can restrict implementation availability without restricting the data type:
Manuscript interface SameValue[T: Equal]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool impl SameValue[T] for Box[T]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool: return self.value == other A Box[T] with no proof of T: Equal cannot use this implementation. Bounds do not make the receiver shareable beyond the ordinary derivation for its fields.
Two blocks overlap if their receiver and contract applications can simultaneously match the same pair of types. Check this by structurally unifying both pairs, with each receiver’s inherited parameters treated as distinct variables and nominal identities and invariant arguments preserved. Ignore bounds in this check: different bounds cannot select competing implementations. Reject overlap at declaration checking, even if no current call uses it. There is no most-specific selection or specialization.
Manuscript # Rejected alongside the generic block above: both apply to Box[Int]. impl ReadValue[Int] for Box[Int]: fn get() -> Int: return self.value Implementations of ReadValue[Int] and ReadValue[String] for the same receiver are distinct pairs, but their shared get name still requires an explicit view for dispatch. Generic method calls and specialized implementation dependencies obey the same finite-application rules as generic functions.
Explicit contract views# Create a contract view explicitly with Contract(value: concrete). For a generic contract, use Contract[T](value: concrete). The concrete type must have an applicable declared implementation and satisfy its bounds; a matching method name alone is not enough.
A plain view can hold a local receiver that is not shareable. The view keeps the same receiver reference. It does not copy native state, keep a resource open, or make concurrent access safe.
Manuscript fn use_increment(operation: Increment) -> Int: return operation.apply(value: 1) let offset = Offset(delta: 2) let view = Increment(value: offset) let result = use_increment(operation: view) # Rejected: conversion is not implicit at a call boundary. let wrong = use_increment(operation: offset) The plain constructor accepts an implementing concrete value or an existing plain/shared view of that exact contract application. An existing plain view is an identity conversion; a shared view loses only its static sharing guarantee. Different contracts/applications and unchecked contract-to-concrete conversions are rejected. A contract type match can recover a concrete record or alternative receiver after checking its exact nominal identity at runtime.
Write generic view arguments explicitly or supply an expected application of the same contract, plain or shared. Operation names do not infer arguments, and an expected shared type cannot refine a plain constructor.
Selecting an operation# A concrete receiver or generic parameter may call an operation directly when exactly one implemented/bounded contract supplies its name. Otherwise select a view, such as Increment(value: offset).apply(value: 1). Arguments and result types cannot resolve operation-name ambiguity. A bound method retains its receiver and has the operation’s ordinary function type.
A plain or shared contract type satisfies its own exact named generic bound without a source impl. For example, Converter[Int] satisfies T: Converter[Int], but not T: Converter[String]. Generic disambiguation can therefore construct the same plain view whether T is concrete or already a view. A behavioral bound alone does not require sharing.
Manuscript fn invoke[T: Increment](operation: T) -> Int: return Increment(value: operation).apply(value: 1) let from_concrete = invoke(operation: offset) let from_view = invoke(operation: view) Both calls satisfy the same bound; neither inserts an implicit conversion at the call boundary.
Shared contract views# Contract & Shareable, including Contract[T] & Shareable, exposes the same contract operations with a statically safe receiver. It is the only value-type intersection. General intersections, Equal/Hashable refinements, and standalone Shareable value types are rejected.
Construct a shared view explicitly with (Contract & Shareable)(value: receiver):
Manuscript let shared = (Increment & Shareable)(value: offset) let same_shared = (Increment & Shareable)(value: shared) let local = Increment(value: shared) # Explicitly discard the sharing guarantee. let operations: List[Increment & Shareable] = [shared] # Rejected: local has only the plain Increment type. let recovered = (Increment & Shareable)(value: local) # Rejected: plain contract values do not satisfy the collection element bound. let local_operations: List[Increment] = [local] Shared construction requires both an implementation proof and a sharing proof:
Receiver Shared construction Concrete shareable type implementing the exact contract Accepted Existing shared view of the exact contract application Accepted as an identity view Generic parameter bounded by the exact contract and Shareable Accepted Plain view, even with a safe hidden receiver Rejected; the sharing proof is absent Plain and shared views are distinct types. Assignments, arguments, returns, and expected types never add or discard sharing implicitly. Both explicit constructors retain the same receiver and implementation; neither adds synchronization, equality, hashing, cleanup, or lifetime extension.
Shared views can be stored in collections and captured concurrently. Bound methods use the receiver’s known sharing proof, then follow the separate callable boundary rules .
Only the receiver is guaranteed shareable. Parameters and results follow their own types: a shared service may return a nonshareable resource. Native adapters must prove receiver sharing before exposing a shared view.
Contracts and external authority# A capability is passed as an explicit input when an operation needs external authority, such as storage or a payment service. Modules and capabilities describes effects, sharing requirements, and exported boundary contracts.
Contracts can also appear as generic bounds , where they name the operations required from a type argument.
Previous: Equality and hashing · Next: Generics and bounds

title: Generics and bounds
content:
Generics and bounds# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A generic type describes a family of types using type arguments. The arguments make the element or result types visible wherever the type is used.
Generics use brackets.
Manuscript List[String] Map[String, Int] Optional[String] Result[Decimal, DiscountError] These are type expressions: a list of text, a map from text to integers, optional text, and a decimal result with an application-defined error type.
Bounds# A bound states what generic code needs from a type. Write T: Equal if the code compares values of type T, or combine requirements with &, as in T: Shareable & Hashable.
The compiler provides three property bounds: Shareable, Equal, and Hashable. Other bounds name operation contracts, such as standard Closeable. A new library facility does not add a new compiler bound. Generic declarations list their type parameters in brackets, such as [T, U].
Bound Required property Shareable Value is safe for concurrent access Equal Type supports eligible value equality Hashable Type supports hashing, which requires equality A named operation contract Type supplies the required operations through an explicit implementation A bound describes what generic code can rely on. For example, T: Shareable expresses a shareability requirement on T; it does not extend a resource lifetime or register cleanup.
Bounds are checked at every application. Hashable implies Equal, and Equal implies Shareable, both for bound satisfaction and assumptions available when checking generic bodies. Named contract bounds require an applicable explicit implementation, not merely matching method names; they do not imply Shareable for the implementing concrete type. Plain contract value types do not promise sharing. A shared Contract & Shareable value type satisfies both the named contract bound and Shareable; neither form adds equality or hashing.
Shareable, Equal, and Hashable are not standalone source value types, generic type arguments, contract-view constructors, or user implementation targets. Besides its use as a bound, Shareable may refine an operation contract application in a shared view type , such as List[ReadValue[Int] & Shareable]. Their compiler-known marker identities do not make them ordinary operation contracts. Intrinsic type and bound names cannot be redefined by module declarations, imports, or type parameters; see module name resolution .
Manuscript # Rejected: a compiler bound is not a parameter type. fn invalid_parameter(value: Shareable) -> Unit: return # Rejected: Equal is not a type argument. let invalid_argument = identity[Equal](value: 1) # Rejected: no source view constructor for a compiler bound. let invalid_view = Shareable(value: 1) impl Equal for DataType is also rejected; eligibility follows compiler derivation rather than a source implementation. A declaration such as fn invalid[Hashable](value: Hashable) -> Unit: cannot redefine Hashable as its type parameter.
Declarations and applications# Manuscript type Box[T]: value: T fn identity[T](value: T) -> T: return value fn same[T: Equal](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right let box = Box[Int](value: 1) let exact = identity[Int](value: 1) let inferred = identity(value: 1) Type parameters are ordered and their names unique. An application supplies exactly one argument per parameter. Default type arguments, higher-kinded parameters, type aliases, and variadic type parameters are unsupported. Records, alternatives, interfaces, and named functions may declare generic parameters. Implementation blocks use the receiver type declaration’s parameters and inherit applicable bounds from the type and interface declarations. Anonymous functions, contract operations, and implementation methods cannot declare their own type parameters. Methods inherit the parameters used in their implementation’s receiver; see generic implementations for receiver matching, bound checking, and overlap rejection.
Applications are invariant: Box[Int] and Box[Float] are distinct types. A generic declaration is not an unapplied type or function value. A generic function passed as a value must be explicitly specialized, for example identity[Int].
Inference from arguments# A function call may omit type arguments only when independently typed supplied argument expressions uniquely determine every parameter. The compiler matches argument types against declared parameter types, including invariant nested applications, then checks bounds and arguments after substitution. Repeated occurrences must determine the same type. No common superclass, implicit union, or numeric widening is inferred.
Manuscript fn choose[T](first: T, second: T) -> T: return first let value = choose(first: 1, second: 2) # T = Int # Rejected: conflicting evidence for T. let mixed = choose(first: 1, second: 2.0) Result annotations do not infer function type arguments. Empty lists, none, and other expressions requiring context cannot independently provide evidence. Once other arguments determine all parameters, substituted parameter types provide context to those expressions. This process does not reorder evaluation.
Manuscript fn count[T: Shareable](values: List[T]) -> Int: return 0 let known = count[Int](values: []) # Rejected: the empty list does not determine T. let unknown = count(values: []) Generic data constructors follow the same field/payload inference rule, but an expected data application may supply their type arguments before field checking. Thus let box: Box[Int] = Box(value: 1) is valid. A unique complete application must result; a constructor cannot invent an unused type parameter.
Body checking and well-formedness# A generic body is checked once against declared bounds. An unconstrained T cannot be compared with ==, used as a map key, or called through a contract operation. Bounds expose only their declared properties.
Manuscript # Rejected at declaration: missing Equal bound. fn unchecked_same[T](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right type Keys[T: Shareable & Hashable]: values: Set[T] Every nested application must satisfy its bounds under enclosing generic assumptions. Omitting the bounds from Keys is rejected even if all later uses happen to supply Int.
The same rule checks a generic implementation once under its inherited parameters and bounds. Its method bodies cannot rely on properties absent from the inherited bounds. Matching the receiver determines the implementation arguments; all implementation bounds must hold before its operations or views are available. Bounds may restrict a single implementation’s availability, but are ignored when rejecting overlapping implementations. A concrete implementation cannot specialize a pair already covered by a generic block.
Finite recursive applications# Recursive declarations follow layout rules . Separately, the compiler requires a finite regular family of recursive generic applications. Along a recursive generic cycle, arguments preserve the original parameters one-to-one in their original positions. Tree[T: Shareable] with children: List[Tree[T]] is allowed. Substituting concrete arguments, reordering them, or expanding them on a recursive cycle is rejected; Grow[T] containing List[Grow[List[T]]] would create an infinite application family. This regularity check follows recursive type references even through function signatures or contracts: an indirect runtime representation does not permit infinitely expanding static instantiations.
The same finite-application requirement covers generic function calls and specialized function values. Follow specialization dependencies through the whole module graph; on a recursive function cycle, the composed substitution must preserve the starting function’s type parameters one-to-one in their original positions. Nonrecursive calls may construct different type arguments. Reject expanding recursive specialization before Go emission, even when the recursive call is unreachable at runtime. This prevents both an infinite monomorphization worklist and generic recursion that the Go backend cannot represent.
Manuscript fn repeat[T: Shareable](value: T) -> Never: return repeat[T](value: value) # Regular specialization; allowed. fn grow[T: Shareable](value: T) -> Never: return grow[List[T]](value: [value]) # Rejected: expanding specialization. Apply the check to mutual recursion and references such as grow[List[T]] stored as function values, not only direct self-calls. Include generic implementation method calls and bound methods in specialization dependencies under their inherited receiver parameters. Generated-code compilation errors are not a substitute for a source diagnostic.
Built-in requirements# Collections require shareable contents. Map keys and set elements additionally require hashing. See equality and hashing for the relationship between these properties.
Shareable is a compiler-defined bound derived from eligible immutable components and shared contract views, or declared by audited native implementations. It is not an operation contract or a source implementation target. Function types do not satisfy it, so records with function fields cannot derive sharing. The separate callable sharing rules govern closures and generic forwarding. Sharing does not register cleanup or extend a resource’s open lifetime.
Previous: Operation contracts · Next: Type compatibility and expected types

title: Type compatibility and expected types
content:
Type compatibility and expected types# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index The type you provide must match the type required at that position. This applies to variable annotations, assignments, arguments, returns, fields, and collection elements. For example, an Int cannot silently become a Float, and two records do not become interchangeable just because their fields match.
The exception is an expression of type Never: it cannot produce a value, so it can appear where any expression value is expected. This exception does not make differently declared function types interchangeable.
Exact and nominal identity# Type form Identity and compatibility Built-in Fixed compiler or standard identity Record or alternative Defining module, declaration, and ordered type arguments; matching fields or cases do not establish compatibility Contract view Nominal contract application, plus whether it is plain or shared; conversions are explicit Generic application Exact declaration and every ordered argument; List[Int] and List[Float] are distinct Function Exact parameter labels, declaration order, parameter types, and result type; no variance or label/order adaptation Caller-written argument order affects evaluation without changing function identity. A generic bound grants properties, not subtyping. Shared/plain arguments remain distinct during inference; List[Contract] fails its element bound, while List[Contract & Shareable] may satisfy it.
Type positions use ordinary name resolution . A value shadowing a type name causes an error, not a second lookup in a hidden namespace. Unqualified cases follow alternative lookup ; expected types cannot override a lexical binding or choose an ambiguous case.
Shareable, Equal, and Hashable are compiler bounds , not standalone value types. The only value-type refinement is Contract & Shareable; other intersections and refinements are rejected.
Manuscript fn identity(value: Int) -> Int: return value let exact: fn(value: Int) -> Int = identity # Rejected: amount differs from value. let relabeled: fn(amount: Int) -> Int = identity There are no implicit numeric conversions, optional wrapping/unwrapping, result wrapping, structural record conversions, unions, or nullable references. An integer literal has type Int even under an expected Float; use the explicit conversion API . The type checker does not choose an arbitrary common type for incompatible values.
Propagating context# An expected type comes from the place a value is used: a local annotation, assignment target, return declaration, parameter after generic substitution, record field, or alternative payload.
That type can guide the expressions inside parentheses, list elements, constructor fields, and case payloads. It can supply missing type arguments for a uniquely identified constructor such as none, ok, or error.
Context does not resolve an ambiguous unqualified case name or change a type an expression already determines for itself.
Manuscript type Input: names: List[Optional[String]] let input = Input(names: [none, some(value: "Ada")]) let nested: List[List[Int]] = [[], [1]] let success: Result[Int, String] = ok(value: 1) let failure: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "unavailable") # Rejected: the result error type cannot be inferred from ok's payload. let incomplete = ok(value: 1) The compiler rejects expressions whose type cannot be determined. It does not silently assign a dynamic or unknown type.
Expression without an annotation What can be inferred none or [] Not enough information to determine the payload or element type. ok(value: 1) The success is Int, but the error type is still unknown. some(value: 1) The complete type is Optional[Int]. [none, some(value: 1)] The typed some value supplies enough context for List[Optional[Int]]. A list is rejected if its independently typed elements disagree.
Operators and try do not pass an expected result type backward into their operands. Their operands must determine their own types first. For example, knowing that the value unwrapped by try should be Int does not tell the compiler which error type an incomplete Result constructor should have.
Manuscript fn known() -> Result[Int, String]: let number: Int = try Result[Int, String].ok(value: 1) return ok(value: number) fn unknown() -> Result[Int, String]: # Rejected: the try operand's error type is undetermined. let number: Int = try ok(value: 1) return ok(value: number) Similarly, an expected Bool cannot make [] == [] well typed; neither operand determines a list element type. Explicitly qualify or annotate operands when their types would otherwise be incomplete.
Never operands use the operator candidate rules . Those rules select a required operand type locally; they do not infer it backward from an expected result.
Generic function inference uses supplied argument types only, as specified in generics . An expected return type does not infer missing function type arguments. A generic function value must be explicitly specialized before an expected function type can check it. Anonymous functions still require their own explicit parameter/result types.
Validation boundaries# Every declaration’s referenced types must resolve and every application must satisfy arity and bounds. Generic bodies are checked under declared bounds. Public signatures satisfy public type visibility , and recursive concrete layouts satisfy guarded recursion . These checks precede lowering and do not rely on Go’s structural interfaces or implicit assignments.
Runtime cancellation and resource closed-state errors do not alter static assignability. Their separate contracts remain governed by the existing runtime and reference chapters.
Previous: Generics and bounds · Next: Declarations and calls

title: Functions
content:
Functions# Core language guide · Design index Functions take named inputs and return a declared type. First learn how to declare and call them. Then learn how to pass a function as a value and what it keeps from its surrounding scope.
Concept What you will learn Declarations and calls Write explicit signatures and evaluate arguments in source order. Function values and closures Pass functions as values and understand snapshot captures and resource references.

title: Declarations and calls
content:
Declarations and calls# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A function names its inputs, declares their types, and declares the type it returns. Its body runs in source order. Use return to send a value back to the caller.
Manuscript fn decrement(value: Int) -> Int: return value - 1 let remaining = decrement(3) Function parameters and return types are explicit; local annotations are optional. The caller can infer remaining as Int from the function’s declared return type.
Declarations and resolution# Named functions are module declarations or operations inside an impl. Nested named function declarations are rejected; use an anonymous function bound to a local instead. Every parameter has a unique name and an explicit type, and every function has an explicit result type, including Unit.
The compiler collects module declaration names and signatures before checking bodies. A function can call a later declaration, and ordinary and mutual function recursion are allowed. Duplicate module names and overloaded declarations are rejected. Generic function declarations and applications follow generics .
Parameters belong to the function body’s lexical scope. A local declaration cannot reuse a parameter’s name in that same scope. Each branch, match arm, and loop body creates a nested scope; nested scopes may shadow an outer name.
Argument names# A function with exactly one declared parameter accepts either function(value) or function(name: value). The omitted label resolves to that sole parameter. Functions with more than one parameter require name: value for every supplied argument; the name identifies the declared parameter.
Manuscript fn reduce(amount: Int, deduction: Int) -> Int: return amount - deduction let remaining = reduce(amount: 10, deduction: 3) let next = decrement(3) let explicit = decrement(value: 3) The rule applies to ordinary functions, methods, function values, and library APIs. Count the callable’s declared parameters, including optional API parameters, rather than the arguments supplied at a particular call. A method’s implicit receiver does not count as a parameter. Constructors and explicit contract views still require labels, including some(value: ...), ok(value: ...), error(cause: ...), and Contract(value: receiver). A zero-parameter function uses ().
parallel receives an ordered pack of zero-argument functions through tasks: [first, second], with options such as timeout: 2.seconds supplied by name. Its heterogeneous results are specified in parallel operations .
Match payload bindings such as some(value): are patterns, rather than calls; see pattern matching .
Source declarations cannot define default or optional parameters, variadic parameters, or argument spreading. An Optional[T] source parameter is still required: callers explicitly supply none when absent. Existing trusted library API contracts may explicitly permit omitted named arguments; that permission does not follow from an Optional value type. Unknown labels, duplicate arguments, missing required arguments, and unlabeled arguments to multi-parameter functions are compile errors. Supplying both decrement(3, value: 4) arguments duplicates the sole parameter and is rejected. Supplied values must be compatible with the declared parameter types under type compatibility ; labels do not authorize numeric or contract conversions.
Collections as arguments# To accept a variable number of values, declare an ordinary list parameter:
Manuscript fn sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total let total = sum([1, 2, 3]) let empty = sum([]) The argument supplies one immutable list. An existing List[Int] can be passed as sum(existing_values) or sum(values: existing_values). The parameter is required even for an empty list. Function values use the ordinary type fn(values: List[Int]) -> Int, and functions with multiple list parameters require labels on every supplied argument.
See collections for list literals and element requirements.
Evaluation order# Execution and argument evaluation follow source order. When arguments contain calls, those calls run in the order written before the outer function receives their results. Named arguments do not reorder execution to match the parameter declaration.
Evaluate the callable expression, including a method receiver, once before its arguments. Then evaluate argument expressions from left to right in their written order. Arrange the resulting values into declaration order only after evaluation. A failed or nonreturning expression prevents all later arguments and the outer invocation from running. Constructor fields follow the same rule.
This also matters for concurrency APIs : argument preparation and closure creation happen in the caller before any operation starts.
Unit and Never# unit is the single value of Unit. A Unit function may use return, return unit, or fall through the end of its body. Other functions must return a compatible value on every reachable normal exit; bare return and reachable fallthrough are compile errors. There is no implicit return of a block’s final expression.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn check_positive(value: Int) -> Unit: if not (value > 0): return panic(message: "check failed") fn missing_value() -> Int: return panic(message: "Required value is missing") panic has type fn(message: String) -> Never. Never has no values: a Never expression cannot complete normally and is accepted where any value type is expected. This expression rule does not make List[Never] compatible with List[Int] or change function-type identity.
Return completeness uses a conservative control-flow check:
Construct Reachable normal exits return or evaluation of Never None if without else Branch exits plus a path past the statement if with else or exhaustive match The combined exits of all branches or arms for or while with a condition other than literal true A possible exit, because the body may not execute Literal while true Only a reachable break targeting that loop A nested function’s return or nested loop’s break cannot exit the enclosing function or loop. The check uses no additional constant folding.
Expression evaluation also has no normal successor when a necessarily evaluated subexpression cannot complete. This includes callable/receiver preparation, arguments, constructor fields, list elements, interpolation expressions, unary operands, and both operands of a non-short-circuit operator. A right-hand operand of and or or alone does not remove the possible exit, because it may be skipped; their left operand is always required. Creating a function value does not execute its body.
Track evaluation separately from result typing: 1 + panic(message: "stop") has type Int under the operator rules , but cannot complete normally. A failed initializer accordingly prevents the following statement from being reachable.
Manuscript fn incomplete(active: Bool) -> Int: if active: return 1 # Rejected: the false path reaches the end without returning Int. Unreachable statements remain subject to parsing, name resolution, and type checking, but do not add reachable exits. A Never function must have no reachable normal return or fallthrough. A bare call may be used as a statement and its result discarded; non-call expressions cannot be standalone statements.
Calls that suspend# A potentially blocking library call suspends the current lightweight task. It does not implicitly start another task. There are no async declarations or await annotations.
Manuscript has one function kind. Sequential code remains sequential when a library operation suspends; explicit concurrent execution is specified in concurrency .
For functions used as data and the rules for captured values, continue with function values and closures .
Previous: Type compatibility and expected types · Next: Function values and closures

title: Function values and closures
content:
Function values and closures# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index You can store a function in a local binding and pass it to another function. Write an anonymous function with fn; its type has the form fn(value: T) -> U.
A closure is a function value that keeps values from its surrounding scope. It captures snapshots of the bindings it uses. There is no separate function kind that consumes or transfers those captures.
Manuscript fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) let offset = 1 let decrement = fn(value: Int) -> Int: return value - offset let result = apply(value: 3, transform: decrement) Function types retain parameter names. Calls through values may omit the label when the function type has exactly one parameter; multi-parameter function types require labels on every supplied argument. Labels remain part of function-type identity and compatibility even when a call omits one. Calls have the same suspension and evaluation rules as declared functions.
Function type compatibility# Parameter names, declaration order, parameter types, and result type are all part of function-type identity. Compatibility is invariant: a different label, reordered signature, or different result type requires an explicit adapter function. Caller-written argument order may vary without changing the function’s declared type.
Manuscript fn subtract_one(amount: Int) -> Int: return amount - 1 fn adapt() -> Unit: # Rejected: amount and value are different function-type labels. let invalid: fn(value: Int) -> Int = subtract_one let renamed = fn(value: Int) -> Int: return subtract_one(amount: value) let result = apply(value: 3, transform: renamed) The rejected binding is a negative example; removing it leaves a valid function. Anonymous functions require explicit parameter and result types and an indented body, exactly as specified in the grammar . An annotation on the receiving variable does not omit those signatures. A generic function must be instantiated before it is stored as a value; identity[Int] is a function value, while a bare polymorphic identity is not. Bound method values have the operation’s function type with the receiver already bound and excluded from the parameter list.
An anonymous function forms its own function boundary for return, try, break, and continue. Its control-flow exits cannot exit the containing function or loop. Capture and sharing behavior remains governed by the separate contracts below.
Snapshot captures# A closure snapshots each referenced local binding when created, including a var’s current value. Later reassignment of that local does not change the snapshot. Assigning to a captured outer local is a compile error; shared mutable local cells are not implicit. Shared mutable state is accessed through synchronized services.
Immutable data is retained by value/reference as appropriate for its representation. A service or resource capture retains a reference to the same object, not a deep copy of the object’s state. Bound methods retain their receiver under the same rules. Retained environments survive through garbage collection; there is no move, borrowed capture, or automatic cleanup on closure invocation/discard.
Resource captures# Manuscript with file = try files.open(path: "data.txt"): let reader = fn() -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError]: return file.read(max_bytes: 4096) callbacks.register(handler: reader) # A later callback invocation reports IoError.Closed. The acquisition fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, IoError]; callbacks is an explicitly supplied registration service. The standard acquisition retains File & Shareable, so concurrent callback use can preserve the receiver’s sharing proof.
Capturing a resource does not extend its open lifetime or cancel its with cleanup. Resource methods detect closed state at runtime. This applies equally to resources passed through explicit parameters or retained in records.
Concurrent invocation# Concurrency APIs accept ordinary functions with a proved safe captured environment. Local copies retain that proof; storage, generic forwarding, and source function boundaries erase it. The exact boundaries are in function sharing . A safely shared resource can still be closed before invocation.
Capture request-data snapshots and application services for background work, then acquire job resources within that operation. parallel joins before returning, so an enclosing with remains active while its operations run, unless the resource is explicitly closed elsewhere.
These examples use inferred captures. An explicit capture-list syntax has not been selected and is not required by this design. See parallel , background services , and reference sharing .
Previous: Declarations and calls · Next: Conditionals

title: Control flow
content:
Control flow# Core language guide · Design index Use if for a Boolean decision, match for the cases of an alternative, and loops for repeated work. Leaving a block also runs any cleanup registered in that block.
Concept What you will learn Conditionals Branch on Bool values with if and else. Loops Iterate with for and while, and use break and continue. Pattern matching Handle alternatives exhaustively and bind their payloads.

title: Conditionals
content:
Conditionals# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use if to run a block when a Boolean condition is true. Add else to run a different block when it is false. Only the selected branch runs.
Manuscript fn status(active: Bool) -> String: if active: return "Active" else: return "Inactive" Conditions require Bool. The condition in this example is already a Boolean; numeric and text values do not acquire truth values implicitly.
if is a statement and does not produce a value. Evaluate its condition once; execute exactly one selected branch, or neither branch when the condition is false and no else is present. else aligns with the corresponding if. An additional conditional uses else if, not elif.
Each branch has its own lexical scope. Names declared in a branch are not visible after the conditional; assignments to an outer var affect that existing binding. An else if chain checks conditions in order and stops after selecting a branch.
Manuscript fn classify(value: Int) -> String: if value < 0: return "negative" else if value == 0: return "zero" else: return "positive" if 1: is rejected because its condition is Int. let result = if active: ... is rejected because if is not an expression. Use branch-local assignment to a declared var or explicit returns to select a result. The function return rules determine whether all reachable paths return.
Validating inputs# Validation uses the same ordinary control flow as any other decision:
Manuscript fn nonnegative(value: Int) -> Bool: if value < 0: return false return true The early return exits the function on the negative path. The final return runs on the remaining path. Expected failures uses this structure to reject invalid input with a domain error.
Bindings after a branch# Every binding is initialized at declaration. To select a value for use after the conditional, initialize an outer var and assign to it in the branches. Branch-local names stay inside their branch. See bindings .
Use pattern matching when the decision depends on which case of an alternative value is present.
Previous: Function values and closures · Next: Loops

title: Loops
content:
Loops# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use for / in to visit the values in a collection. Use while to repeat work while a Boolean condition is true. Inside either loop, break ends the loop and continue moves to the next iteration.
Loops are statements, not expressions. Manuscript has no labeled loops, loop-result values, integer-range syntax, or user-defined iteration protocol.
Traversing a list# Manuscript fn sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total The list contains shareable integers. Each iteration binds an element and updates the accumulator. Addition uses checked Int arithmetic, so overflow is a programming fault .
Iterable types and binding# Evaluate a for’s iterable expression once before entering the loop. The loop introduces one immutable identifier per iteration; it does not accept a binding pattern or a type annotation. The closed set of supported iterables is:
Iterable Iteration binding type Traversal order List[T] T Position order Set[T] T Insertion order Map[K, V] MapEntry[K, V] Key insertion order MapEntry[K, V] is an immutable record with fields key: K and value: V. It uses the map’s key/value eligibility requirements. Its type and named constructor MapEntry[K, V](key: key, value: value) are imported from @std/collections.ms; field access is ordinary record access. Iteration infers the entry type without requiring an import of its name. It is not a positional pair. Destructure an entry inside the body when convenient.
Manuscript fn total(values: Map[String, Int]) -> Int: var sum = 0 for entry in values: let {key, value} = entry sum = sum + value return sum for [key, value] in values: is rejected at parsing. Iterating a number, text, optional, function, or arbitrary object with a next method is rejected at type checking. Each iteration creates a new binding and lexical scope. Assigning to the iteration binding is rejected; an outer mutable accumulator can be reassigned.
Repeating while a condition holds# Manuscript fn count_down(start: Int) -> Int: var remaining = start while remaining > 0: remaining = remaining - 1 return remaining The condition is tested as a Bool. Each iteration updates remaining; the loop ends when the comparison is false.
A while reevaluates its condition before every iteration, including after continue. A for continues by selecting its next element and terminates after the last element. An empty iterable executes no body. A false initial while condition also executes no body.
Exiting an iteration# break and continue select the nearest enclosing loop within the same function body. They have no labels or arguments and are rejected outside a loop. An anonymous function inside a loop cannot break or continue that enclosing loop. return exits the current function, including when it appears in a loop body. Unreachable loop-control statements still need a valid enclosing loop.
break, continue, and return leave different control-flow paths, but each runs cleanup for the scopes it exits. Each loop iteration has its own scope. Resources registered with with in an iteration close when that iteration exits. A plain let declaration does not register cleanup. See lexical cleanup for the cleanup order and fault rules.
Cancellation# Each loop back-edge is a cancellation checkpoint, so CPU-bound loops respond promptly to cancellation without explicit calls. See propagation and checkpoints for all runtime checkpoints.
Previous: Conditionals · Next: Pattern matching

title: Pattern matching
content:
Pattern matching# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use match to handle the cases of an alternative type. Each branch can give names to the data carried by its case. For example, a payment may be paid, declined, or pending, and each outcome needs different handling.
A match accepts tagged alternative types, including Optional and Result, and operation contract views. Matching numeric or Boolean literals, guards, ranges, nested case patterns, and combined patterns is rejected. match is a statement; it cannot initialize a binding as an expression. The scrutinee evaluates once.
The following function handles the Payment type declared in alternatives :
Manuscript fn describe(payment: Payment) -> String: match payment: Paid(receipt): return "Paid: {receipt}" Declined(reason): return "Declined: {reason}" Pending(reference): return "Pending: {reference}" Payload patterns# Case payloads bind positions in the declaration’s field order. A pattern must give exactly one identifier or _ placeholder per payload field. Pattern payloads are positional even though constructors always use named fields. Nullary cases use a bare case name without ().
Manuscript type Position: case Point(x: Int, y: Int) case Unknown fn horizontal(position: Position) -> Int: match position: Position.Point(horizontal_value, _): return horizontal_value Position.Unknown: return 0 Point(x: local, y: other): is rejected at parsing. Point(x): is rejected for wrong arity. Repeated binding identifiers are rejected, while _ can occur repeatedly because it creates no name. Each arm’s payload bindings and body share a lexical scope nested inside the enclosing scope.
An unqualified case in a pattern resolves within the scrutinee’s alternative type. A qualified case must belong to that exact type. Other.Point(...) cannot match Position, even when its payload types have the same shape. Constructor-expression name lookup instead follows alternative construction .
Exhaustiveness# Match cases bind data without fallthrough; missing alternatives are compile errors. Wildcard cases must be explicit.
Every case in the example returns its own description. Running the Paid branch does not continue into Declined or Pending. The compiler checks that all alternatives are accounted for.
_: is the wildcard arm. It is permitted once, must be last, binds nothing, and covers every case not already handled. Duplicate cases, unknown cases, an arm after the wildcard, and a wildcard after all cases have been explicitly covered are rejected as invalid or unreachable arms. Qualified and unqualified spellings of the same case count as duplicates.
Manuscript fn paid(payment: Payment) -> Bool: match payment: Paid(_): return true _: return false Adding a case to an alternative invalidates exhaustive matches that lack a wildcard. A match with a wildcard remains exhaustive; its wildcard handles the new case. Return completeness is checked across all reachable arms using the function return rules .
Optional and result values# Optional and Result are also alternative types. Matching an optional distinguishes a present value from absence. Matching a result distinguishes success from an expected failure and lets the caller decide what to do with each.
Contract type patterns# A contract view keeps its concrete receiver. Match that view with ConcreteType(receiver) to handle a particular implementation, followed by _: for generic handling. This is a checked recovery of an existing receiver, not a constructor call.
Manuscript import Error from "@std/errors.ms" import JsonError from "@std/json.ms" fn describe(cause: Error) -> String: match cause: JsonError(json): match json: InvalidInput: return "Invalid JSON limits" InvalidData: return "Malformed JSON" LimitExceeded: return "JSON limit exceeded" _: return cause.message() The type must be an imported or local nominal record or alternative with an applicable explicit implementation of the scrutinee’s exact contract. Supply exactly one receiver name or _, including for a payloadless alternative. The binding has the concrete type, so its fields, cases, and implemented operations are available inside the arm. Native opaque receivers can be handled by the wildcard, but cannot be named in a concrete type pattern.
Generic patterns name the complete application, such as MyError[Int](cause); MyError[String] is a different pattern. An in-scope generic parameter may supply an argument, as in MyError[T](cause). Matching uses exact runtime nominal identities and type arguments, with the first matching arm selected. Duplicate statically identical type patterns are rejected. A pattern cannot name a different contract, a bare type parameter, or an individual alternative case.
A final wildcard is required even when every currently known implementation is listed: contracts are open to other implementations. It binds nothing; use the original contract value for generic handling. The same rules apply to plain and shared views. The scrutinee evaluates once; matching retains the same receiver reference and does not copy it, add cleanup, or catch faults and cancellation. See contract views .
Matching resource references# Matching binds ordinary payload values and references. No binding is consumed, and matching does not register resource cleanup. Destructuring bindings use brackets or braces; alternative match cases retain their Case(payload) syntax. See aggregate references .
Previous: Loops · Next: Expected failures with Result

title: Errors and validation
content:
Errors and validation# Core language guide · Design index Choose the outcome that matches the situation: Result for an expected failure with an explanation, Optional for a missing value, and a fault for a broken programming assumption. These pages show how callers respond to each one.
Concept What you will learn Expected failures with Result Return success or domain errors as ordinary values. Error propagation with try Forward compatible errors without hiding faults or cancellation. Programming faults Check invariants and understand task failure after cleanup.

title: Expected failures with Result
content:
Expected failures with Result# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use Result[T, E] when an operation can either succeed with a value of type T or fail with an expected error of type E. Import Result from @std/result.ms; import its map_error helper separately if you use it.
Return ok(value: ...) for success and error(cause: ...) for failure. Both are ordinary values. A caller can inspect the result with match or pass the error back with try. Validate runtime input with ordinary conditions before doing the work.
Returning a domain error# Manuscript type DiscountError: case InvalidPrice case InvalidPercent fn discount(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Result[Decimal, DiscountError]: if price < 0d: return error(cause: InvalidPrice) if percent < 0d or percent > 100d: return error(cause: InvalidPercent) return ok(value: price * (1d - percent / 100d)) The function checks inputs before calculating. It returns an explicit error for each invalid condition and wraps the calculated decimal in ok on success.
Handling the result# The following continues the declarations above:
Manuscript fn discount_message(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> String: let outcome = discount(price: price, percent: percent) match outcome: ok(value): return "Discounted price: {value}" error(cause): return "Discount could not be calculated." This caller chooses a response for either outcome. Another caller could inspect cause with a further match or propagate it with try .
A common error boundary# Import Error from @std/errors.ms when a boundary should accept multiple error domains. It is an ordinary interface declaring message() -> String. Standard errors implement it; user errors can declare an ordinary impl Error in their defining module.
Manuscript import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import {Error, as_error} from "@std/errors.ms" import {EncodingError, hex_decode} from "@std/encoding.ms" import {Result, map_error} from "@std/result.ms" fn decode(text: String) -> Result[Bytes, Error]: return map_error( result: hex_decode(text: text, max_bytes: 1024), transform: as_error[EncodingError], ) The conversion preserves the original EncodingError case and payload. A caller may handle any error with cause.message(), or select a specific implementation using a contract type pattern . A caller that needs only encoding errors can keep Result[Bytes, EncodingError] and match its cases directly.
Error is explicitly imported and has no special inheritance or exception machinery. Other error values remain legal in Result[T, E]. Conversion at a generic boundary is explicit, and try still requires the same error type .
Results and concurrent execution# Returning error(cause: cause) is normal function completion. In parallel, the domain Result remains the operation’s return value and does not cancel siblings. The outer API result separately reports ExecutionError; see parallel operations . A Background service reports completion-only domain errors through its configured failure observer.
Use Optional for absence without an error explanation and explicit faults for broken programming invariants.
Previous: Pattern matching · Next: Error propagation with try

title: Error propagation with try
content:
Error propagation with try# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index Use try to continue with a successful Result value or immediately return its error to your caller. This is useful when the current function cannot handle the expected failure itself.
try expression unwraps ok; on error, it returns that error from the enclosing function. The function must return a compatible Result.
The following continues the discount and DiscountError declarations in expected failures :
Manuscript fn discounted_label(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Result[String, DiscountError]: let value = try discount(price: price, percent: percent) return ok(value: "Discounted price: {value}") Success and failure paths# When discount returns ok, value contains the Decimal payload and the function builds its label. When it returns error, the enclosing function returns that error instead of executing the remaining statements.
The success types differ: the called function returns a decimal, while the enclosing function returns text. Both use DiscountError, so the error can be forwarded unchanged.
Error compatibility# Error conversion uses the standard map_error(result: outcome, transform: fn(cause: E) -> F) adapter or an explicit match; its exact signature and single-evaluation rule are in the standard API contract . A caller with a different error contract must translate the error explicitly. try does not invent a conversion or combine unrelated error types into an implicit union.
If the called operation returns Result[T, E], the function using try must return Result[U, E]. The success type may change from T to U, but the error type E must be exactly the same. Two error types are not interchangeable just because they implement the same interface. Convert explicitly before constructing the Result that try uses.
A common Error boundary follows the same rule: first use map_error(result: outcome, transform: as_error[SpecificError]) to preserve the concrete cause in an Error view, then apply try. See common error boundaries .
The expression after try is evaluated once. Try binds more tightly than arithmetic, so try operation() + 1 means (try operation()) + 1.
The compiler rejects try when:
its expression is not a Result; its error type differs from the enclosing function’s error type; the enclosing function or test returns Unit. Inside an anonymous function, try returns from that anonymous function, not from its caller or surrounding function. See expressions and type compatibility .
Cleanup and cancellation# try does not catch programming faults or parent cancellation. A propagated error is a return path and performs lexical cleanup for the scopes it leaves. A programming fault or parent cancellation follows its own unwinding rules.
Previous: Expected failures with Result · Next: Programming faults

title: Programming faults
content:
Programming faults# Core language guide · Chapter index · Design index A programming fault means an assumption the code relies on has failed. Use ordinary conditional returns to check that assumption. For ordinary invalid user input, use conditions and return a Result error so the caller can respond.
Invariant checks# Use ordinary if and return control flow to check an invariant. Import panic from @std/faults.ms when a violated invariant must produce a programming fault.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn discount_validated(price: Decimal, percent: Decimal) -> Decimal: if price <= 0d: return panic(message: "Price must be positive") if percent <= 0d or percent >= 100d: return panic(message: "Percent must be positive and below 100") return price * (1d - percent / 100d) This example expects strictly positive prices and percentages below 100 as preconditions. A violation is treated as a programming fault. Use the validating discount function in expected failures when these values come from ordinary runtime input.
Explicit faults# An explicit panic(message: message) produces a programming fault when code determines that an invariant has failed.
Its source type is fn(message: String) -> Never. It never completes normally; a call can appear where any expression result type is expected, including an Int return position. This does not create a catchable expected-error value or permit normal fallthrough in a non-Unit function. See Unit, Never, and return completeness .
Manuscript panic(message: "Required invariant was violated.") A fault aborts the current operation after cleanup. Programming faults are distinct from expected Result errors.
Cleanup and observation# Cleanup still runs after a fault. A cleanup fault can replace a pending return, domain error, or cancellation, while secondary faults are retained as diagnostics. The full selection and cleanup rules are in lexical cleanup .
An active parallel caller observes an operation fault as ExecutionError.Crashed after siblings are cancelled and joined. Background faults go to the service’s failure observer. A caller’s own fault still unwinds it; try only propagates Result errors. See execution errors .
Previous: Error propagation with try

title: Standard library
content:
Standard library guide# Design index Use this chapter to find standard types and operations. Most names need an explicit import from an @std/...ms module. Start with the type catalog, or choose a task from the sections below. The package pages list exact signatures and explain their limits.
API reference# Browse all implemented modules , including the intrinsic prelude. The reference is generated from compiler definitions; special call rules cover APIs with contextual signatures.
Reading order# 1. Standard types # Core and standard types — Find a type, its meaning, and its import path. Standard imports and API typing — Check exact import identities, callable types, and standard API rules. 2. Concurrent APIs and host lifetimes # Background services — Start work under a service that tracks it and waits during shutdown. 3. Data, state, and I/O # Minimum data operations — Look up the basic methods on collections, text, bytes, and numeric values. Readers, writers, and streams — Read and write bytes, recognize end-of-input, and close streams. Bounded queues — Connect producers and consumers with bounded storage. Synchronized state, pools, and leases — Coordinate shared state and acquire a pool lease with scoped cleanup. Local builders and immutable snapshots — Construct a value with local mutation, then freeze an immutable snapshot. 4. Application hosts # HTTP request hosts — Use HTTP clients or request hosts with bounded bodies and cleanup. CLI application hosts 5. General-purpose packages # Node.js and Go coverage — See what is implemented and what remains outside the library. Common package contracts — Review the errors, limits, and authority rules shared by packages. Expanded library conformance — Find executable checks for package behavior and limits. Runtime facilities# These are ordinary library facilities with effect, sharing, lifetime, and cancellation contracts. They add no concurrency syntax. Host-created requests, sessions, applications, and CLI runs establish fixed execution contexts. Parallel APIs join before returning; background services implement Closeable and join during shutdown.
Standard imports, immutable data, CLI streams, and concurrent APIs have concrete signatures. Queue, pool, builder, HTTP server, and buffered subprocess APIs have concrete contracts. The general-purpose package guide adds executable data, codec, filesystem, cryptographic, networking and HTTP client operations. See outstanding decisions .

title: Standard types
content:
Standard types# Guide index · Design index The catalog tells you what a type means and where to import it. The API-typing page is the detailed reference for how standard names resolve and how concurrent callables and results are checked.
Core and standard types — Find a type, its meaning, and its import path. Standard imports and API typing — Check exact import identities, callable types, and standard API rules.

title: Core and standard types
content:
Core and standard types# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use this table to find a type’s meaning and import path. “Implicit intrinsic” means the type is available without an import. Import other type names from the listed module when you use them in source.
Type Meaning Import from Bool true or false Implicit intrinsic Int Signed 64-bit integer; checked arithmetic Implicit intrinsic Float IEEE 754 binary64 Implicit intrinsic Decimal Base-10, 34 significant digits; round half to even @std/decimal.ms String Immutable, valid UTF-8 text Implicit intrinsic Bytes Immutable byte sequence @std/bytes.ms Unit One value, unit Implicit intrinsic Never No possible value Implicit intrinsic List[T], Map[K, V], Set[T] Immutable homogeneous collections with their declared sharing bounds @std/collections.ms MapEntry[K, V] Immutable standard record with key: K and value: V; map iteration yields entries @std/collections.ms Optional[T] some(value: value) or none @std/optional.ms Result[T, E] ok(value: value) or error(cause: cause) @std/result.ms ExecutionError Joined-group timeout or crash @std/tasks.ms Background Synchronized service managing work under a fixed lifetime @std/tasks.ms WorkStatus, StartError, BackgroundFailure Background status, admission failure, and failure reports @std/tasks.ms OperationId Identity of a runtime operation, used for diagnostics and Background status/cancellation @std/tasks.ms Closeable Standard close() -> Unit cleanup contract @std/cleanup.ms File, ReadStream, WriteStream Resource contracts; standard host values use shared views with synchronized lifecycle checks @std/io.ms Duration, Instant Checked nanosecond duration and monotonic clock instant @std/time.ms Process CLI authority roots @std/cli.ms Files, IoError File capability contract and expected I/O failures @std/io.ms Clock Monotonic clock capability contract @std/time.ms Functions and closures are ordinary values; runtime tasks are not exposed as source ownership types. Fixed parallel result packs preserve positional types and use bracket destructuring; they are not homogeneous lists.
References do not extend an object’s open lifetime. Use with for deterministic release and Result for expected operation failures. See parallel , background services , and Closeable .
The standard API contract defines visibility, signatures, optional arguments, and pack typing.
General-purpose types# The package guide adds opaque BigInt (@std/bigint.ms), Regex (@std/regex.ms) and wall-clock Timestamp (@std/time.ms); JsonValue/JsonLimits (@std/json.ms); structured format/filesystem/archive records; and package-specific error types (see error contracts ). New capability contracts are FileSystem, Entropy, WallClock and System, supplied by explicit CLI Process fields. TCP/TLS Connection, Listener and DatagramSocket are acquired through the existing Network authority. All names remain individually imported; no additions enter the intrinsic prelude. See coverage for implemented equivalents and remaining gaps.

title: Standard imports and API typing
content:
Standard imports and API typing# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Most standard names must be imported explicitly. Only six intrinsic types and three compiler bounds are available automatically. Native implementation or special compiler support does not make a name globally visible.
This page is the exact reference for standard exports, their identities, and API typing. A trusted manifest may implement these declarations but cannot change their source identities or typing rules.
Names and identity# Every module implicitly sees only Bool, Int, Float, String, Unit, Never, Shareable, Equal, and Hashable, as specified by module declarations . The three bounds describe compiler-verified sharing, equality, and hashing; ordinary behavior requirements use imported operation contracts. Keep new facilities in the standard library rather than expanding this list.
@std is a reserved directory supplied by the pinned compiler/runtime distribution. Each path below is a standard module, and each name is an individual export. There are no wildcard imports or automatic imports of other exports from the same module.
Module Exports @std/decimal.ms Decimal @std/bytes.ms Bytes @std/collections.ms List, Map, Set, MapEntry @std/optional.ms Optional @std/result.ms Result, map_error @std/cleanup.ms Closeable @std/tasks.ms parallel, check_cancelled, ExecutionError, OperationId, Background, BackgroundFailure, WorkStatus, StartError @std/faults.ms panic @std/time.ms Duration, Instant, Clock @std/io.ms Files, File, ReadStream, WriteStream, IoError @std/cli.ms Process Manuscript import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" Imports establish stable nominal identities independent of the application. Imported names follow ordinary collision and shadowing rules; unimported standard names are not reserved. A local declaration with the same spelling never acquires standard operators, cleanup recognition, callback checks, or native members.
The general-purpose package guide documents additional module exports and common errors . Process also exposes FileSystem, Entropy, WallClock and System roots, while its existing Network gains TCP/UDP/TLS/client/DNS operations. These additions retain explicit imports and nominal identities.
Syntax and compiler support# Some library identities need compiler support while remaining explicit exports:
Ordinary bracket literals require the canonical List import in the module. The tasks literal of the imported parallel binding is a positional pack and does not require List. A d-suffixed literal requires the canonical Decimal import. Decimal arithmetic and interpolation keep their specified behavior. Optional and Result are standard alternatives with ordinary case lookup. try recognizes the canonical Result identity; a user-defined alternative named Result does not qualify. for, collection derivation, and guarded layout recognize the standard collection identities. MapEntry is an exported record; map iteration can infer it without importing its name. with recognizes the canonical Closeable implementation, or an operation contract declaring the exact close signature. A module writing impl Closeable or a Closeable bound imports that name; using an already-typed resource does not require an otherwise unused import. Runtime API special checks attach to the resolved standard callee. A user-defined parallel is an ordinary function and never receives pack or callable-proof rules. A missing or substituted List/Decimal import rejects the corresponding literal during resolution/type checking. Inferred library values may be matched, traversed, or used through their declared members without importing every type in their public signatures. Naming such a type or using its unqualified expression constructors requires its own import. Primitive receiver members in the data API are fixed standard bindings and can likewise produce inferred library values; they add no ambient type names. Imports supply declarations, not files, clocks, or other external authority.
OperationId is the single opaque, shareable identity for runtime operations, whether started by a joined group or admitted by a Background service. It has no source constructor and no implicit equality or hashing, and it grants no scheduling, joining, or transfer authority. A Background service’s status and cancel act only on IDs it admitted. WorkStatus has nullary cases Running, Succeeded, Failed, Cancelled, Crashed, and Unknown; qualify these case names when necessary. StartError has Closed and Full. IoError has Closed, InvalidInput, Unavailable, InvalidData, LimitExceeded, and Failed(message: String). These are shareable alternatives. These errors explicitly implement the common Error contract from @std/errors.ms; see error contracts . Execution errors are defined in joining .
Manuscript fn panic(message: String) -> Never fn check_cancelled() -> Unit fn map_error[T, E, F](result: Result[T, E], transform: fn(cause: E) -> F) -> Result[T, F] These lines specify bindings rather than complete source modules. check_cancelled unwinds the current execution if it has stopped; it returns Unit otherwise. map_error returns an unchanged success payload, or invokes transform(cause: cause) exactly once for an error. It invokes no callback for success and does not catch faults or cancellation. It is sequential and imposes no additional sharing bound.
Joined concurrency# All concurrency names are explicit library exports. The call below requires the parallel import from @std/tasks.ms; no concurrency operation, error type, work identity, or service expands the intrinsic type/bound list. Every concurrency name, including check_cancelled and OperationId, is exported by @std/tasks.ms. Timeouts and scheduling are implemented by library/runtime bindings.
parallel requires tasks and permits only the optional named argument timeout: Duration. Omission means no added limit; an inherited deadline still applies. Negative timeouts fault. Zero-timeout, stop, join, and outcome rules follow joining outcomes .
tasks must be a bracket literal, optionally grouped in parentheses. Each position must independently resolve to a shareable zero-parameter function fn() -> Ri; each Ri must be shareable. The binding produces Result[Pack[R1, …, Rn], ExecutionError]. Here Pack is compiler notation, with no source type-name spelling or source constructor. Existing lists are rejected.
Standard concurrency callbacks require the argument’s callable sharing proof . Function types themselves do not satisfy Shareable; an operation cannot return another function as a shareable result. Task preparation retains callback proofs internally, while result-pack sharing follows each result type.
Direct calls only# parallel, the Background constructor, and Background.start may appear only as the resolved callee of a direct call. A plain function signature cannot retain their callback-proof requirements.
let launch = background.start and passing that binding to a helper are rejected. Other standard operations follow ordinary function-value rules. Sequential map_error may be specialized and stored as a value. Source contracts cannot express these callback-proof requirements. Restricted background submission views are therefore unsupported.
Inferred result packs# A pack can be inferred into a local, carried through an inferred generic type argument, bound in a Result match, returned through a generic T, and destructured with exact positional arity. It cannot be written in an annotation, explicit type argument, field, or named function signature. Nested inferred packs retain their exact shape. Pack identity is the ordered sequence of position types; the empty pack is distinct from Unit and List.
Packs derive Shareable position by position, but have no equality, hashing, iteration, field access, or indexing. Generic helpers such as map_error can therefore preserve a parallel pack without a new source syntax.
