Background service# Background(limit: Int) constructs a synchronized native service under the current execution context. limit must be positive. Its only optional arguments are reporter: fn(failure: BackgroundFailure) -> Unit, drain: Duration, and history_limit: Int. The defaults are the host diagnostic sink, zero drain, and 128 completed statuses. drain and history_limit must be nonnegative. A supplied reporter must be shareable; retained reporter captures must remain usable through service shutdown.
Manuscript type BackgroundFailure: case Failed(operation: OperationId, cause: String) case Crashed(operation: OperationId, message: String) # Operations of the native Background service: fn start(operation: fn() -> Result[Unit, String]) -> Result[OperationId, StartError] fn cancel(id: OperationId) -> Unit fn status(id: OperationId) -> WorkStatus fn close() -> Unit start requires a shareable callable. This is one operation signature: Operations without domain errors explicitly return ok(value: unit), and operations with domain error types explicitly translate them to String using map_error or match. There is no generic method, implicit formatting of arbitrary errors, or overload. Background explicitly implements Closeable in the standard binding.
Failure reporting# The reporter receives Failed for a returned String error and Crashed for a programming fault. Cancellation changes status rather than producing a domain error. Reporter calls are serialized, may suspend, and run outside transition locks under a shielded service context. Shutdown waits for them.
At most limit completion reports may be pending. Capacity exhaustion or a reporter fault sends both the original diagnostic and the reporting failure/overflow diagnostic to the host sink. A reporter fault never invokes the reporter recursively. The sink itself has a bounded buffer; overflow increments a retained counter and emits a host stderr diagnostic. Uncooperative reporters remain subject to host escalation.
Status eviction never reuses an ID for different work. An ID the service did not admit, including one from another service or a joined group, returns Unknown from status and is a no-op for cancellation.
Capabilities and data operations# The host’s authority roots and stream signatures are defined by CLI hosts and streams . Standard collection, byte, text, numeric, and duration members are defined in minimum data operations . Source code cannot add implementations or members to intrinsic or standard native types. Source types may implement standard contracts in their own defining module.
General user type packs, optional source parameters, generic operations, and third-party dependency package imports are unsupported. HTTP host registration follows the bounded request API .
Data services and additional host capabilities# @std/queues.ms exports Queue and QueueError; @std/state.ms exports State; @std/pools.ms exports Pool, Lease, and PoolError; @std/builders.ms exports ListBuilder, MapBuilder, SetBuilder, BytesBuilder, and StringBuilder. Their exact contracts live in queues , state and pools , and builders . None is ambient. Opaque constructor parameter names are not source fields.
@std/time.ms also exports sleep(duration: Duration) -> Unit, a sequential cancellable delay. Negative duration faults; zero performs a cancellation checkpoint.
@std/http.ms exports the bounded request host types in HTTP . Network.serve is a direct-call-only operation requiring a proved shareable handler. @std/process.ms exports Commands, CommandOutput, and CommandError in streams . CLI Process additionally has network: Network & Shareable and commands: Commands & Shareable. Imports provide types, while those fields provide actual authority.

title: Concurrent APIs and host lifetimes
content:
Concurrency services# Guide index · Design index Use parallel for a fixed set of operations and Background for work managed by a longer-lived service. Parallel calls wait for their started work before returning. A background service waits during shutdown.
Parallel operations Background services — Start work under a service that tracks it and waits during shutdown.

title: Background services
content:
Background services# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use Background for work managed by an application or component rather than by the caller’s immediate request. Import it from @std/tasks.ms. The service tracks its operations and implements Closeable so shutdown can wait for them.
You can create several services and pass them as ordinary parameters. The API reference defines which callables they accept.
Manuscript with emails = Background(limit: 32): with indexing = Background(limit: 4): serve(emails: emails, indexing: indexing) The constructing host supplies the execution parent. Construct application services under the application lifetime, session services under the session lifetime, and request services under the request lifetime. Calling a service from another context never reparents it.
Starting work# Manuscript import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import Background from "@std/tasks.ms" import StartError from "@std/tasks.ms" import OperationId from "@std/tasks.ms" type MailError: case Rejected interface Mailer: fn send(to: String) -> Result[Unit, MailError] fn enqueue(emails: Background, mailer: Mailer & Shareable, address: String) -> Result[OperationId, StartError]: let send = fn() -> Result[Unit, String]: return map_error( result: mailer.send(to: address), transform: fn(cause: MailError) -> String: return "Email delivery failed" ) return emails.start(operation: send) Start does not wait for capacity. Accepting work, reserving a slot, and checking closure happen atomically. The limit counts accepted operations whose completion has not yet been committed. Accepted work starts without an extra unbounded queue; rejected work never runs.
Completion frees the slot before failure reporting, so a slow reporter cannot hold up new admission. Start does not retry automatically.
Background operations return Result[Unit, String]: explicit ok(value: unit) on success, or a String error after domain-error adaptation. Successful operations produce status; failures reach the reporter. One operation’s failure does not cancel unrelated operations.
The returned OperationId is the same identity used in execution errors, failure reports, and traces. With this service, it supports status and cancellation without transferring shutdown responsibility. The standard API contract defines signatures, status retention, constructor defaults, bounded reporting, and fallback diagnostics.
Closures retain ordinary captured references. Capture a request-data snapshot and application services, then acquire resources inside the operation’s own with blocks. Capturing a request’s resource does not extend its lifetime; use after close returns a resource-specific error. Closure syntax is the ordinary syntax in function values and closures .
Bind the operation’s data in an ordinary closure; there is no function-plus-arguments submission form.
Lifetime and shutdown# Pass Background directly. Its start binding follows the direct-call restriction . Sharing or dropping a service reference or work ID does not change its lifetime or cancel work. Work never transfers between services.
close() -> Unit is idempotent and does not finish until admitted work and its cleanup have ended:
Close admission atomically across all aliases. Allow a configured drain period; the default is no drain delay. Request cancellation of unfinished operations. Join every admitted operation and finish bounded reporting/cleanup. Cancelling a submitting request does not cancel accepted work. Cancelling the service’s fixed parent does cancel its operations, even if a drain period was configured. A service’s close cannot join itself; host/component code outside its operations performs shutdown.
Hosts choose overall budgets, admission/reporting settings, and an escalation policy for uncooperative work. Expiry is not successful joining; the runtime cannot forcibly terminate an arbitrary goroutine safely. Closing a service before closing its application dependencies is required.
This is process-local execution, not durable delivery. Work that must survive restart needs a durable queue. If acknowledgement can be lost during request cancellation, use application idempotency keys to make resubmission safe.
Runtime and library responsibilities# The Go runtime supplies operation start, stop, join, and synchronization. Admission, reporting, and shutdown policy can be implemented over those primitives. The initial implementation may provide the service in Go behind the same imported API. These native primitives are implementation details, not source intrinsics. The compiler validates the standard binding’s callable proofs; service admission, status retention, reporting, drain, cancellation, and joining remain library/runtime behavior.

title: Data, state, and I/O
content:
Data, state, and I/O# Guide index · Design index Choose a facility based on what you need to do: work with immutable values, read or write streams, pass values through a queue, coordinate shared state, or build a value locally. I/O resources need explicit cleanup.
Minimum data operations — Look up the basic methods on collections, text, bytes, and numeric values.
Readers, writers, and streams — Read and write bytes, recognize end-of-input, and close streams.
Bounded queues — Connect producers and consumers with bounded storage.
Synchronized state, pools, and leases — Coordinate shared state and acquire a pool lease with scoped cleanup.
Local builders and immutable results — Construct a value with local mutation, then freeze an immutable snapshot.

title: Minimum data operations
content:
Minimum data operations# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index This is the reference for basic methods on standard data types. These methods belong to the canonical intrinsic or imported receiver type. They do not introduce new global names or compiler bounds.
Import standard types when naming them. Ordinary bracket list literals need List. A type inferred from a return value does not need its own import unless you name it in source. Updates produce new immutable values and leave the original unchanged. Sizes and indexes use Int; allocation failure is a host failure.
A single-parameter operation may omit its argument label. Multi-parameter operations require the exact labels below.
Collections# Receiver or constructor Signature/result List[T] length() -> Int; get(index: Int) -> Optional[T] List[T] append(value: T) -> List[T]; concat(values: List[T]) -> List[T] Map[K, V]() Empty Map[K, V] Map[K, V] length() -> Int; get(key: K) -> Optional[V]; contains(key: K) -> Bool Map[K, V] with_entry(key: K, value: V) -> Map[K, V]; without(key: K) -> Map[K, V] Set[T]() Empty Set[T] Set[T] length() -> Int; contains(value: T) -> Bool Set[T] with_value(value: T) -> Set[T]; without(value: T) -> Set[T] All existing element and key bounds apply. An empty Map/Set constructor requires explicit type arguments or a complete expected application; it supplies no inference evidence by itself. List construction uses the existing bracket literal. Negative or out-of-range list indexes return none. A size exceeding MaxInt64 faults.
Maps and sets traverse in insertion order. Replacing an equal map key retains its original key value and first insertion position; adding an existing set element retains its original value and position. Removing an absent key/element is a value-preserving operation. Removing and then adding places the new entry at the end. Equality remains independent of insertion order. A simple implementation may copy storage on update; builder APIs are specified separately once their signatures are settled.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Map from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn positives(values: List[Int]) -> List[Int]: var result: List[Int] = [] for value in values: if value > 0: result = result.append(value: value) return result test "dynamic immutable data": if not (positives(values: [3, -1, 2]) == [3, 2]): return panic(message: "check failed") let absent: Optional[Int] = none if not ([1].get(index: 5) == absent): return panic(message: "check failed") let original = Map[String, Int]().with_entry(key: "a", value: 1) let updated = original.with_entry(key: "b", value: 2).with_entry(key: "a", value: 3) if not (original.get(key: "a") == some(value: 1)): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (updated.get(key: "a") == some(value: 3)): return panic(message: "check failed") Strings and bytes# Receiver or constructor Signature/result String byte_length() -> Int; to_bytes() -> Bytes; parse_int() -> Optional[Int] Bytes(values: List[Int]) Immutable bytes; each value must be 0–255, otherwise a programming fault Bytes length() -> Int; get(index: Int) -> Optional[Int]; concat(values: Bytes) -> Bytes Bytes to_text() -> Optional[String] String.to_bytes uses UTF-8. Bytes.to_text succeeds exactly for valid UTF-8, preserving contents without normalization; invalid bytes produce none. Byte get follows list index behavior and returns the unsigned byte as Int. An empty Bytes(values: []) is valid.
parse_int accepts exactly an optional ASCII + or - followed by one or more ASCII decimal digits and an in-range mathematical value. It permits leading zeros, rejects whitespace, separators, fractions, exponents, and any unconsumed character, and returns none for invalid or out-of-range input. Runtime parsing is distinct from the stricter source literal grammar. Scalar/grapheme indexing and additional parsing/formatting APIs are unsupported.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" test "explicit byte conversion": if not ("é".byte_length() == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ("é".to_bytes().to_text() == some(value: "é")): return panic(message: "check failed") let invalid: Optional[String] = none if not (Bytes(values: [255]).to_text() == invalid): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ("-007".parse_int() == some(value: -7)): return panic(message: "check failed") Numeric and time conversion# Receiver Signature/result Int to_float() -> Float; to_decimal() -> Decimal Float truncate_to_int() -> Optional[Int] Decimal to_float() -> Float; truncate_to_int() -> Optional[Int] Int milliseconds, seconds, minutes members producing Duration Int→Decimal is exact. Int→Float and Decimal→Float round once to nearest binary64, ties to even. Decimal→Float may produce signed infinity or signed zero under the Float rules. Truncation discards the fractional part toward zero, then checks the mathematical integer against the exact signed 64-bit limits before conversion. NaN, infinities, or an out-of-range integer yield none; do not compare against a rounded Float representation of MaxInt64 and then use a Go cast.
Duration is a signed 64-bit count of nanoseconds. The three unit members work on any Int expression and multiply by 1,000,000, 1,000,000,000, or 60,000,000,000 with overflow checks. Instant is an opaque monotonic instant in the current run’s clock domain; it has no source constructor. Clock adapters and injected test clocks must preserve a single comparable domain within a run. Cross-domain comparison or subtraction faults. Duration arithmetic and Instant shifts/differences check overflow; these compiler-defined operations are enumerated in the operator table .
Boundary expectations: 1e300.truncate_to_int() is none; converting Float +2^63 to Int is none, while Float -2^63 succeeds. 2.seconds is 2,000,000,000 nanoseconds. Unsupported unit names and mixed arithmetic such as 2.seconds + 1 are type errors.

title: Readers, writers, and streams
content:
Readers, writers, and streams# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A stream reads or writes bytes over time. Its close operation releases the underlying resource. Native hosts and source fakes can both implement the contracts below.
The host supplies synchronized ReadStream & Shareable, WriteStream & Shareable, and File & Shareable views. A plain stream contract view does not itself promise concurrent safety.
Manuscript interface ReadStream: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit interface WriteStream: fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn close() -> Unit interface File: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit Read requires positive max_bytes or returns IoError.InvalidInput. ok(some(bytes)) contains 1 through max_bytes bytes; ok(none) is EOF. Empty chunks never represent EOF. The bound limits each read, not total file size. Write waits until all bytes are accepted or an error occurs; empty writes succeed without I/O. An error may follow a partial external write and supplies no rollback. Internal buffering is bounded with backpressure.
Native wrappers serialize simultaneous reads/writes without holding a lifecycle lock during blocking I/O. Close marks admission closed, interrupts active I/O where supported, waits for admitted I/O to end, and releases the handle once. Later calls return IoError.Closed. Concurrent close callers wait for the same release/fault. A flag check followed by unsynchronized handle use is insufficient. Uncancellable I/O can delay release and requires host escalation; expected completion errors belong to read/write, and unexpected release failures are cleanup faults.
Plain and shared contract values declaring these exact close operations are eligible for with under Closeable ; cleanup does not require concurrent sharing. Source fakes implement the selected stream contract and explicitly construct shared views when substituting for standard host roots or acquisitions; no native File constructor or contract inheritance is needed. Adapters honor cancellation and undelivered acquisition . The bounded subprocess facility is exported by @std/process.ms. The CLI host supplies process.commands: Commands & Shareable:
Manuscript # Commands fn run(program: String, arguments: List[String], input: Bytes, max_output_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[CommandOutput, CommandError] type CommandOutput: exit_code: Int stdout: Bytes stderr: Bytes CommandError has InvalidInput, Unavailable, TimedOut, OutputLimit, and Failed(message: String). Empty/NUL program names, NUL arguments, negative bounds, and negative timeout return InvalidInput. The total stdout plus stderr bound is nonnegative. Nonzero ordinary exit is an ok output with that code. Timeout or output overflow stops and joins the process before returning its error; caller cancellation unwinds after joining. POSIX process groups include descendants in termination.
On platforms without process-group support the wrapper controls the direct process, with bounded pipe completion; descendant supervision needs a platform host contract. Interactive subprocess streams remain separate future contracts; network sockets , streaming HTTP and WebSockets are implemented.

title: Bounded queues
content:
Bounded queues# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use a queue to pass values from producers to consumers. Queue[T] has synchronized, bounded storage and requires shareable elements. Send and receive can wait and respond to cancellation. Closing the queue is explicit.
Facility Contract Queue[T] Shareable elements; synchronized bounded queue; cancellable send/receive; explicit close Using the contract# Sending and receiving must respond to cancellation. Explicit close is part of the contract, so shutdown needs a deliberate end to admission and communication. A queue is a library facility and does not introduce another concurrency syntax.
API# Queue[T: Shareable](capacity: Int) creates synchronized storage with positive capacity. The queue is opaque, shareable, and neither equal nor hashable. A nonpositive capacity is a programming fault.
Manuscript fn send(value: T) -> Result[Unit, QueueError] fn receive() -> Optional[T] fn close() -> Unit Import Queue and QueueError from @std/queues.ms; QueueError has the nullary case Closed. Send waits for space, receive waits for a value, and both respond to caller cancellation. Close atomically stops send admission and wakes all waiters. Already buffered values drain in FIFO order; once drained, receive returns none, including repeated receives. Blocked and later senders return error(cause: QueueError.Closed). Close is idempotent and is eligible for with. A committed send or receive may precede cancellation; cancellation does not roll back queue effects.
See shareable collection elements and cooperative cancellation .
Previous: Readers, writers, and streams · Next: Synchronized state, pools, and leases

title: Synchronized state, pools, and leases
content:
Synchronized state, pools, and leases# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use synchronized services for application state shared by requests and background work. A pool supplies leases: acquire a lease in a with block, then return it to the pool through close. Keeping a reference to the lease does not extend its lifetime.
Pool references can be shared by requests and background work. A job acquires its own lease under its own scope. Retaining a lease reference does not prolong its lease lifetime.
Access and closure must be coordinated: close waits for or cancels outstanding operations before allowing reuse, and stale aliases report closed state rather than using a connection assigned to another caller. Supported simultaneous use is explicit in the adapter/service contract.
State# Import State from @std/state.ms. State[T: Shareable](value: T) is an opaque synchronized reference. get() -> T, set(value: T) -> Unit, and swap(value: T) -> T each execute atomically. Swap returns the previous value. A read followed by a write is not an atomic update. State is shareable but has no equality, hashing, or cleanup operation. Each operation checks caller cancellation before and after its transition; committed changes are not rolled back.
Pools and leases# Import Pool, Lease, and PoolError from @std/pools.ms. Pool[T](resources: List[T]) owns a nonempty fixed collection of distinct resource receivers. T must be a concrete shared operation-contract view declaring close() -> Unit. Construct views explicitly before pooling; a type variable’s implementation bound does not establish this representation at construction. The supplied resources must remain under the pool’s exclusive lifecycle management.
Manuscript # Pool[T] fn acquire() -> Result[Lease[T], PoolError] fn close() -> Unit # Lease[T] fn get() -> Result[T, PoolError] fn close() -> Unit Acquire waits cancellably for capacity. Closed admission returns PoolError.Closed. Delivery that loses to cancellation releases its lease before unwind. Pool and lease objects are shareable, opaque, and eligible for with; they have no equality or hashing.
Get returns a guarded contract view. Calls through that view admit under the lease’s lifetime, including method values saved before release. Closing the view releases the lease. Lease close stops admission, cancels and joins admitted operations, and returns capacity exactly once; concurrent closers join the same release. A later get returns Closed. Stale I/O views return IoError.Closed; stale operations without an I/O error result fault. Release during an admitted operation interrupts it; I/O reports Closed, and other contracts report a programming fault unless caller cancellation already applies.
Pool close stops acquisition, wakes waiters, invalidates every lease, joins its operations, then closes owned receivers in reverse supplied order. It is idempotent; concurrent callers observe the same release fault. A lease or pool cannot join its own active operation. Closing may wait indefinitely for uncooperative native code; shutdown escalation is separate.
See sharing , release , and background resources .

title: Local builders and immutable results
content:
Local builders and immutable results# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A builder lets you mutate a value while constructing it locally, then freeze an immutable snapshot. Aliases refer to the same builder. Freezing may seal it so later mutation returns a runtime error.
An unsynchronized mutable builder cannot be shared concurrently. Freezing transfers no compiler-tracked ownership; the frozen collection still has to meet its ordinary element bounds.
Builders with unsynchronized mutable state are not eligible for concurrent sharing. There is no consuming function type or compiler-tracked ownership transfer. Frozen contents follow the ordinary collection element bounds.
API# All builder names are exported by @std/builders.ms. They have zero-argument constructors and are opaque local references with no sharing, equality, or hashing eligibility. Type arguments can come from an explicit application or a complete expected constructor type.
Type Mutation Freeze result ListBuilder[T: Shareable] append(value: T) -> Unit List[T] MapBuilder[K: Hashable, V: Shareable] with_entry(key: K, value: V) -> Unit Map[K, V] SetBuilder[T: Hashable] with_value(value: T) -> Unit Set[T] BytesBuilder append(value: Int) -> Unit, concat(values: Bytes) -> Unit Bytes StringBuilder append(value: String) -> Unit String freeze() seals the shared local object and returns its immutable snapshot. Repeated freeze returns the same value. Every mutation through any alias after sealing is a programming fault. Byte append requires 0 through 255. Map replacement preserves insertion position; set insertion ignores an already present value. Builders have no implicit cleanup or ownership transfer.
See aggregates and collections .

title: Application hosts
content:
Application hosts# Guide index · Design index A host starts application code and sets its execution lifetime, cancellation, and limits. The CLI host invokes main once; an HTTP host gives each request its own execution context.
HTTP request hosts — Use HTTP clients or request hosts with bounded bodies and cleanup. CLI application hosts

title: HTTP request hosts
content:
HTTP request hosts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The HTTP host gives each request its own execution context and limits. It controls admission, body sizes, deadlines, disconnect cancellation, backpressure, and fault isolation. Handlers use parallel APIs for joined work and with for request resources.
If the client disconnects, the host cancels the request and its nested groups. Those groups finish joining and registered cleanup runs before the request ends.
Request handlers use parallel for joined work and with for request resources. Client disconnection cancels the request and its nested groups; those groups join and registered cleanup runs before request execution ends.
Streaming responses remain within their request lifetime until streaming finishes. WebSocket/session hosts establish explicit session lifetimes and participate in shutdown; they are not untracked background goroutines.
Application background services are constructed under the application context and passed to handlers. Accepted work uses that service’s context, not the submitting request’s deadline or disconnect signal. Jobs capture request data and application services and acquire their own resources. Admission can race with request cancellation; idempotent submissions are an application concern.
Server shutdown stops request admission, allows a configured grace period, cancels and joins remaining request/session work, closes background admission and drains/cancels/joins those services, then releases application resources. A finite grace period does not guarantee uncooperative work exits; host escalation is separate.
Bounded request API# @std/http.ms exports Network, HttpServer, HttpRequest, and HttpResponse. The CLI host supplies process.network: Network & Shareable; source cannot manufacture native network authority.
Manuscript type HttpRequest: method: String path: String query: String headers: Map[String, Bytes] body: Bytes type HttpResponse: status: Int headers: Map[String, String] body: Bytes # Network fn serve(address: String, handler: fn(request: HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse, limit: Int, max_body_bytes: Int, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration, grace: Duration) -> Result[HttpServer & Shareable, IoError] fn close() -> Unit # HttpServer fn address() -> String fn wait() -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn close() -> Unit These signatures specify library operations. A complete declaration places the entire function header inside delimiter continuation. serve requires a direct call and a proved shareable handler; its plain method signature cannot preserve that requirement as a stored value. limit and timeout are positive; byte bounds and grace are nonnegative. Invalid settings return IoError.InvalidInput; binding failure returns Unavailable; a closed network returns Closed. Port zero permits an OS-selected port reported by address().
The host admits at most limit requests; excess requests receive 503 without invoking a handler. Bodies over the bound receive 413. Each handler gets a fixed timeout/disconnect context, and all work and cleanup in it join before its lifetime ends. Handler faults are isolated as 500 and recorded by the bounded diagnostic sink. Timeout/cancellation yields 504 where the connection still permits a response. Source routes by ordinary branching on method/path; raw query remains encoded. Header values are bytes to preserve non-UTF-8 HTTP input. Header keys are visited in sorted order.
Responses require status 200 through 599, a bounded body, and valid header names/values. Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, and Connection are host-managed and cannot be supplied. Invalid responses yield 500. This API is deliberately a bounded, fully buffered request/response host. Streaming HTTP and reusable clients and WebSocket sessions have separate implemented contracts.
Server close stops admission, waits up to grace, then cancels and joins remaining requests and closes transport. It cannot be called from its own request. Network close joins all its servers. A server also registers with its construction execution lifetime, so omitting a with binding cannot detach server work. Unexpected transport release errors are cleanup faults; uncooperative handlers may delay joining beyond grace.
See background services , cancellation , and conformance programs .

title: CLI application hosts
content:
CLI application hosts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A CLI application starts at an exported fn main(process: Process) -> Int. The host creates the run context and Process value, calls main once, then waits for work and cleanup before reporting the exit code.
The selected entry module must export exactly one nongeneric main with that parameter name, type, and result. Missing or internal main, or a different signature, is a compile error. Other exports are allowed.
Explicit authority roots# Process is a standard immutable record:
Manuscript type Process: arguments: List[String] environment: Map[String, String] stdin: ReadStream & Shareable stdout: WriteStream & Shareable stderr: WriteStream & Shareable files: Files & Shareable clock: Clock & Shareable network: Network & Shareable commands: Commands & Shareable interface Clock: fn now() -> Instant interface Files: fn open(path: String) -> Result[File & Shareable, IoError] Arguments exclude the executable name. Environment is a snapshot; duplicate OS names are resolved by the host before entry. Invalid UTF-8 in process inputs is a startup failure on native stderr with exit 70 before main runs. Relative file paths use the fixed startup working directory. The specified file API opens read-only files; file creation remains an additional API contract. Network and command operations are specified in HTTP and subprocess execution .
The host creates Files, Clock, and stdio behind shared views. Those field types make Process shareable; Files.open preserves sharing in its returned File view. Applications and source fakes follow the same view-conversion rules .
Importing an interface supplies no authority. Files, clock, stdio, and environment arrive only through Process. The host closes roots after main and its scoped services finish; the application registers acquired files with with. Early root-stream closure affects every alias.
Manuscript import Process from "@std/cli.ms" export fn main(process: Process) -> Int: let message = "Arguments: {process.arguments.length()}\n" match process.stdout.write(data: message.to_bytes()): ok(_): return 0 error(_): return 1 This is a complete entry module. Only the Process type name is imported; field/method results and match cases are inferred from its public signatures. The import supplies the interface, while the host supplies the authority-bearing value. On success its transcript is Arguments: N followed by LF and exit 0. Stream signatures are defined in streams .
Exit and shutdown# Normal main results must be 0–125; other results fault. An unhandled root or cleanup fault exits 70 after attempted cleanup and reports primary/secondary diagnostics on host stderr. SIGINT/SIGTERM request cancellation; after joining and cleanup SIGINT exits 130 and SIGTERM exits 143. The first accepted stop reason is retained; a fault during joining/cleanup takes precedence and exits 70. Parent cancellation unwinds main rather than becoming a normal Result.
The ms run launcher forwards SIGINT/SIGTERM to the native host and waits for its joined shutdown before reporting that exit status.
Construct application Background services in main with with, inside their dependencies’ scopes. Shutdown stops admission, joins services, then releases roots. Uncooperative work/reporters can require host escalation ; the host exposes its watchdog policy. Escalated exit is incomplete cleanup, not conformance success.
Additional explicit roots# Process also exposes network: Network & Shareable and commands: Commands & Shareable for the bounded HTTP host and bounded subprocess execution . These capabilities are synchronized host roots. Network services register under their construction execution and join before host roots are released. The host provides no ambient networking or process constructor.
General-purpose authority roots# Process additionally supplies filesystem: FileSystem & Shareable, entropy: Entropy & Shareable, wall_clock: WallClock & Shareable, and system: System & Shareable. Imports come from @std/fs.ms, @std/random.ms, @std/time.ms, and @std/system.ms respectively. These roots are host-created; the native CLI grants its OS authority, not a restricted sandbox. Canonical operations are in general-purpose packages . Existing Files, Network and Commands identities are preserved. Network owns its acquired TCP/UDP/TLS handles and joins them during host-root shutdown.

title: General-purpose packages
content:
General-purpose packages# Standard library guide · Package coverage Find a package by the task you want to perform. Read common contracts for shared error and limit rules, and coverage to compare available functionality with Node.js or Go. The signature blocks are reference declarations, not complete programs.
Text, bytes, and collections — Work with text, bytes, encodings, collections, and regular expressions. Numbers and mathematics — Use floating-point functions and arbitrary-precision integers. Serialization and formats — Parse and write JSON, CSV, URLs, and escaped HTML text. Paths and filesystem — Manipulate paths and use an explicit filesystem service. Time and system information — Work with timestamps and query supplied clock or system services. Cryptography and randomness — Hash, authenticate, encrypt, sign, and request random bytes. Networking and TLS — Use destination policies, DNS, sockets, and verified TLS. HTTP clients and streaming hosts — Use HTTP clients or request hosts with bounded bodies and cleanup. WebSocket sessions — Send and receive messages within a WebSocket session lifetime. Subprocesses and terminal I/O — Read terminal streams and run commands through explicit authority. Compression and archives — Compress data and handle archive entries with explicit limits. Logging, testing, and diagnostics Read a signature# For example, fn parse(text: String, limits: JsonLimits) -> Result[JsonValue, JsonError] means:
Call the function with named text and limits arguments. Success returns a JsonValue; an expected failure returns a JsonError. Import the function from the module listed above its signature. Import type names separately if your own annotations use them. A heading such as “FileSystem operations” lists methods on a supplied service. Importing its interface gives you the type; obtain the service value from the host or a function parameter. Read the behavior sections for limits, cleanup, and partial effects.

title: Resources & cleanup
content:
Resource lifetimes and cleanup# Design index Use with when a file, connection, or other resource must close at the end of a block. The runtime reclaims unused memory, but you must arrange release of external resources. Keeping another reference to a resource does not keep it open.
Reading order# 1. References and sharing# Ordinary references — Understand what another reference does, and why it does not keep a resource open. Concurrent access and resource lifetime — Check whether data or a function can safely be used by concurrent operations. Aggregates and local construction — Store resources inside records or collections without assuming automatic cleanup. Assignment and branches — See what reassignment and branches do to references and registered cleanup. 2. Scoped cleanup# With scopes — Acquire a resource and close it at the end of a block with with. The Closeable contract — Implement the cleanup operation required by with. Scope-exit ordering — Follow cleanup order after a return, error, fault, or cancellation. Shielding and cleanup faults — Understand cleanup after cancellation and what happens if close itself faults. External resource release — Separate closing a handle from successfully completing its work.

title: Common package contracts
content:
Common package contracts# Standard library guide · Coverage · Package index These rules apply across the general-purpose packages. Exact types and signatures live in the pinned Manuscript files under stdlib/. The checker reads those files and verifies that native runtime signatures agree with them.
Imports and callbacks# Import each function or type you name from its module. Standard imports are pinned with the distribution. They add no ambient types, wildcard imports, user-defined generic operations, or automatic access to external services.
Function identity includes the module, so json/parse, bigint/parse, and url/parse remain distinct in generated code. Source import renaming is unsupported; use a helper module if two imports have the same spelling.
Sequential callbacks run under the caller’s execution context and may wait for operations. Collection helpers that invoke them sequentially do not require the callable-sharing proof used by concurrent APIs.
Errors# Each package returns a named error type from its own module: JsonError from @std/json.ms, EncodingError from @std/encoding.ms, FileSystemError from @std/fs.ms, and so on. Each type contains the cases relevant to that domain; its exact definition is in the generated reference . For example, JsonError has only InvalidInput, InvalidData, and LimitExceeded.
NetworkError covers sockets, DNS, and network policy; HTTP, WebSocket, and certificate operations return HttpError, WebSocketError, and TlsError respectively, including when acquired through Network. Stream helpers return IoError and preserve underlying stream failures. Logging wraps a sink failure as LogError.Io(cause: IoError).
All standard error types explicitly implement Error from @std/errors.ms, an ordinary operation contract with message() -> String. Specific API signatures retain their domain error type. A generic boundary uses Result[T, Error]; choose it explicitly with Error(value: cause) or map_error(result: outcome, transform: as_error[SpecificError]). The as_error helper is imported from @std/errors.ms and preserves the original receiver, case, and payload. See the executable filesystem/random/time example .
Handle a concrete error with its ordinary case match. Handle a generic Error by calling message(), or use a contract type match to recover a concrete error such as JsonError(cause), then match its cases. The final wildcard handles other implementations. Custom errors participate through an ordinary impl Error for CustomError in their defining module. Error does not constrain Result’s error parameter or turn faults and cancellation into expected failures.
try propagates the declared error type; it does not convert unrelated types or implicitly construct an Error view. This replaces the former shared LibraryError contract: update imports and return annotations, and qualify cases such as JsonError.InvalidData when multiple imported types define the same case name.
Use specific error cases for classification. message() and Failed(message: String) diagnostics are human-readable text, not stable error codes. A native Failed preserves its diagnostic text; a payloadless native error reports its qualified case, such as JsonError.InvalidData. LogError.Io delegates to its underlying IoError. Command, queue, pool, and task errors also implement Error while retaining their distinct cases and identities.
Situation Behavior Malformed data or unavailable OS service Return an expected Result error. Missing value Use Optional. Illegal collection slice bounds, broken programming assumptions, or explicit invariant violation Produce a programming fault. Parent cancellation Unwind; do not turn cancellation into EOF or a domain error. Local network deadline expires Return Timeout, subject to the operation’s documented error type. If cancellation wins before a newly acquired resource is delivered, native acquisition releases that resource. Delivered socket handles use with and synchronized close admission. Retaining another reference never extends the open lifetime.
Bounds and native limits# Byte, item, and depth limits are nonnegative unless a package requires a positive value. Exceeding a bound returns an error, not a truncated success.
A limit on a function’s output does not bound input already allocated by the caller. Some native operations also allocate before they can check a limit: CSV may parse one record, ZIP may read the central directory, and logging may construct a full record. Bound source reads and consult each package’s behavior section.
Facility Native limit JSON Depth ceiling of 512. HTTP Response headers limited to 64 KiB. Entropy 16 MiB per call. UDP receive At most 65535 bytes. These limits do not form a general memory or CPU sandbox.
Cancellation and partial effects# Native loops check cancellation between bounded chunks. A single math, regex, big-integer, directory, resolver, or OS call may delay cancellation until it returns. There is no forced termination.
Writing, copying, or removing data can fail after changing an external prefix. Cancellation and errors do not imply rollback or a transaction.
Access to external services# CLI Process supplies filesystem, entropy, wall_clock, and system roots, alongside network and commands. Source fakes implement the same contracts with explicit shared views.
Pure codec, path, math, and hash functions grant no OS access. Native CLI services use the process’s OS permissions. Filesystem subtree restrictions are not implemented; Network.restrict narrows destination access. Imports alone grant no authority. HTTP and socket operations use explicit service values and retain TLS verification.
Networking includes DNS, Unix sockets, verified TLS, streaming HTTP, and WebSockets. HTTP/3 is outside the supported scope. Native builds bundle pinned dependency sources and licenses rather than fetching packages.

title: References and sharing
content:
References and sharing# Guide index · Design index Several names can refer to the same object. These pages explain what happens when you pass, store, replace, or share those references. Keep two questions separate: is concurrent access safe, and is the resource still open?
Ordinary references — Understand what another reference does, and why it does not keep a resource open. Concurrent access and resource lifetime — Check whether data or a function can safely be used by concurrent operations. Aggregates and local construction — Store resources inside records or collections without assuming automatic cleanup. Assignment and branches — See what reassignment and branches do to references and registered cleanup.

title: Ordinary references
content:
Ordinary references# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Several names can refer to the same object. Passing a reference to a function, putting it in a record, or capturing it in a closure gives another way to access that object. The original reference still works.
Memory and open resources# Go’s garbage collector reclaims memory that is no longer needed. Releasing a file handle, socket, or other external resource is a separate job. Use an explicit close() call or a with block to arrange that release.
Keeping a reference keeps the object accessible in memory. It does not keep an external resource open. When one reference closes a resource, operations through its other references also see that it is closed. Dropping a reference, closure, or work ID does not itself close anything.
Returning a resource# A factory can return an open resource for its caller to put in with. But a function must not expect a resource to stay open merely because it returns it from inside a local with block. That block still closes the resource before the caller receives it.
What the function does What the caller receives Returns an open resource without registering local cleanup An open resource; the caller must arrange cleanup. Returns a resource registered in a local with block A reference to the resource after that block has closed it. Later use of a closed resource produces its runtime closed-state error.
The compiler does not catch every missing with. Libraries should provide scoped APIs and diagnostics to help callers avoid omissions. Manuscript has no move or ownership-transfer operation.
See Closeable , with scopes , and closures .

title: Text, bytes, and collections
content:
Text, bytes, and collections# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use these modules for text transformations, raw bytes, encodings, collection algorithms, and regular expressions. Import the functions you need from the module above each signature block. Read the behavior sections for indexing, ordering, and limit rules.
@std/text.ms# Manuscript fn contains(value: String, text: String) -> Bool fn ends_with(value: String, suffix: String) -> Bool fn from_scalars(values: List[Int]) -> Result[String, TextError] fn join(parts: List[String], separator: String) -> String fn lower(text: String) -> String fn repeat(text: String, count: Int, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, TextError] fn replace(text: String, old: String, new: String, max_replacements: Int) -> String fn scalar_length(text: String) -> Int fn scalar_values(text: String) -> List[Int] fn slice_scalars(text: String, start: Int, end: Int) -> Result[String, TextError] fn split(text: String, separator: String, max_parts: Int) -> List[String] fn starts_with(value: String, prefix: String) -> Bool fn trim(text: String) -> String fn upper(text: String) -> String @std/bytes.ms# Manuscript fn contains(data: Bytes, value: Bytes) -> Bool fn slice(data: Bytes, start: Int, end: Int) -> Bytes fn values(data: Bytes) -> List[Int] @std/encoding.ms# Manuscript fn base64_decode(text: String, url_safe: Bool, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, EncodingError] fn base64_encode(data: Bytes, url_safe: Bool) -> String fn hex_decode(text: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, EncodingError] fn hex_encode(data: Bytes) -> String @std/binary.ms# Manuscript fn read_float(data: Bytes, offset: Int, little_endian: Bool) -> Result[Float, BinaryError] fn read_integer(data: Bytes, offset: Int, width: Int, signed: Bool, little_endian: Bool) -> Result[Int, BinaryError] fn write_float(value: Float, little_endian: Bool) -> Bytes fn write_integer(value: Int, width: Int, signed: Bool, little_endian: Bool) -> Result[Bytes, BinaryError] @std/collections.ms# Manuscript fn difference[T: Hashable](left: Set[T], right: Set[T]) -> Set[T] fn filter[T: Shareable](values: List[T], predicate: fn(value: T) -> Bool) -> List[T] fn fold[T: Shareable, A](values: List[T], initial: A, step: fn(accumulator: A, value: T) -> A) -> A fn intersection[T: Hashable](left: Set[T], right: Set[T]) -> Set[T] fn map[T: Shareable, U: Shareable](values: List[T], transform: fn(value: T) -> U) -> List[U] fn map_keys[K: Hashable, V: Shareable](values: Map[K, V]) -> List[K] fn map_values[K: Hashable, V: Shareable](values: Map[K, V]) -> List[V] fn reverse[T: Shareable](values: List[T]) -> List[T] fn slice[T: Shareable](values: List[T], start: Int, end: Int) -> List[T] fn sort_ints(values: List[Int]) -> List[Int] fn sort_strings(values: List[String]) -> List[String] fn sorted[T: Shareable](values: List[T], compare: fn(left: T, right: T) -> Int) -> List[T] fn union[T: Hashable](left: Set[T], right: Set[T]) -> Set[T] @std/regex.ms# Manuscript fn compile(pattern: String) -> Result[Regex, RegexError] fn find_all(pattern: Regex, text: String, max_matches: Int) -> Result[List[String], RegexError] fn matches(pattern: Regex, text: String) -> Bool fn replace(pattern: Regex, text: String, replacement: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, RegexError] Text behavior# Text is valid UTF-8. Scalar operations count Unicode code points, rather than bytes or user-perceived characters such as a letter plus a combining mark.
from_scalars rejects surrogate code points and values outside the Unicode range. slice_scalars uses a half-open range: include start, exclude end. Invalid bounds return OutOfRange. trim uses Unicode White_Space. upper and lower use Go’s locale-independent Unicode mappings; they do not normalize combining sequences. split keeps empty parts. It requires a nonempty separator and positive max_parts; the final part contains any remainder. replace uses literal text. old must be nonempty and max_replacements nonnegative; zero means no replacements. repeat requires nonnegative count and max_bytes. It checks the size multiplication before allocating. An empty search string succeeds for contains, prefix, and suffix checks. Bytes and collections# Byte and collection slices also use half-open ranges. Negative, reversed, or out-of-range bounds produce a programming fault. values returns each unsigned byte as an Int.
Updates and algorithms return new immutable values. They leave the original values unchanged.
Operation Ordering rule map, filter, fold Callbacks run sequentially in input order, with ordinary cancellation and fault behavior. sorted Sorting is stable. The comparator returns a negative, zero, or positive Int and must define a consistent total preorder. Its call order and call count are unspecified. map_keys, map_values Preserve insertion order. Set intersection and difference Preserve the left set’s order. Set union Keep left order, then append previously absent right values. You may explicitly specialize a generic function and store it as a function value. These operations add no compiler bounds.
Encodings# Hex output uses lowercase. Hex input accepts either case but rejects odd digit counts and whitespace.
Base64 uses padded standard or URL-safe encoding according to url_safe. Decoding rejects whitespace, the wrong alphabet, malformed padding, and nonzero unused bits. max_bytes must be nonnegative; excess decoded output returns LimitExceeded.
Bytes.to_text strictly decodes UTF-8. Invalid text is an error; there is no decoder that silently substitutes replacement characters.
Binary numbers# Integer widths are 1, 2, 4, or 8 bytes. Signed integers use two’s complement. An unsigned 64-bit input above MaxInt64 returns OutOfRange.
Invalid widths return InvalidInput. Bad offsets, truncated input, and values that cannot fit the requested representation return OutOfRange. Float reads and writes use IEEE binary64. little_endian: true explicitly selects little-endian order. These functions do not reinterpret unsafe memory or convert numeric types implicitly.
Regular expressions# Regex is an opaque, immutable, shareable compiled Go RE2-style pattern. Backreferences and lookaround are invalid; compile failures return InvalidData.
find_all returns whole matches. max_matches must be nonnegative, and exceeding it returns LimitExceeded instead of a truncated success. Go regexp rules govern zero-width and adjacent matches.
replace uses literal replacement text, without $ capture interpolation. It enforces max_bytes and never returns a partial output as success.
Unicode normalization, grapheme segmentation, non-UTF-8 codecs, and capture-group match records remain future work.

title: Concurrent access and resource lifetime
content:
Concurrent access and resource lifetime# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Shareable means a value is safe to access concurrently. It says nothing about how long a resource stays open and does not register cleanup. A closure can keep a reference after its with block ends, but later use still reports the resource’s closed-state error.
Data and services# Immutable data derives sharing from its components. Trusted native services declare sharing only when their mutable state and resource lifecycle are synchronized. A resource may serialize simultaneous calls or reject overlapping use explicitly.
Wrappers coordinate the closed-state check, access to the underlying handle, and closure as one lifecycle protocol. A flag check followed by unprotected I/O is insufficient. A stale lease must never access a connection reused for another caller.
Contract views# A plain contract view carries no sharing guarantee. Contract & Shareable retains a statically proved safe receiver through fields, parameters, returns, and collections. Explicit conversion to a plain view discards that proof; inspecting the hidden receiver cannot recover it. Contract views define construction and conversion.
A generic behavioral bound alone does not prove sharing; concurrent code needs T: Shareable & Contract. A shared receiver does not make its operation’s parameters or results shareable.
Function values# Function signatures describe calls, not captures. Source function types never satisfy the type-level Shareable bound. The compiler instead tracks a separate proof for each named function, closure, or bound method.
Boundary Callable sharing proof Named source function Safe: no captured local environment Local closure Safe when every capture has a type-level sharing guarantee or a retained callable proof Bound method Requires a shareable receiver; a plain view cannot reveal its hidden receiver’s proof Local copy or capture Retains the known proof var assignment or branch merge Requires the proof for every possible value Source function parameter or result, function field, or generic forwarding Erases the proof; concurrent invocation is rejected Direct standard callback argument Checks the value’s retained proof rather than a generic type bound A safe local closure therefore cannot instantiate F: Shareable. Passing it through identity[T] also loses its callable proof. These rules prevent storage or generic helpers from bypassing concurrent-call checks while preserving ordinary sequential function calls.
Capture application services and job data for background work, and acquire job resources inside that work’s own with scopes. See background services , generic bounds , and resource release .

title: Numbers and mathematics
content:
Numbers and mathematics# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use math for floating-point calculations, numbers for text conversion, and bigint when values exceed the Int range. Numeric conversions are explicit. Read the behavior sections before depending on rounding or overflow results.
@std/math.ms# Manuscript fn abs(value: Float) -> Float fn abs_int(value: Int) -> Int fn acos(value: Float) -> Float fn asin(value: Float) -> Float fn atan(value: Float) -> Float fn atan2(y: Float, x: Float) -> Float fn ceil(value: Float) -> Float fn cos(value: Float) -> Float fn cosh(value: Float) -> Float fn e() -> Float fn exp(value: Float) -> Float fn floor(value: Float) -> Float fn hypot(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn is_finite(value: Float) -> Bool fn is_nan(value: Float) -> Bool fn log(value: Float) -> Float fn log10(value: Float) -> Float fn log2(value: Float) -> Float fn max(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn min(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn pi() -> Float fn pow(base: Float, exponent: Float) -> Float fn remainder(left: Float, right: Float) -> Float fn round(value: Float) -> Float fn sin(value: Float) -> Float fn sinh(value: Float) -> Float fn sqrt(value: Float) -> Float fn tan(value: Float) -> Float fn tanh(value: Float) -> Float fn truncate(value: Float) -> Float @std/numbers.ms# Manuscript fn format_float(value: Float) -> String fn format_int(value: Int, radix: Int) -> String fn parse_float(text: String) -> Result[Float, NumberError] fn parse_int(text: String, radix: Int) -> Result[Int, NumberError] @std/bigint.ms# Manuscript fn add(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn bit_and(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn bit_or(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn bit_xor(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn compare(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> Int fn divide(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> Result[BigInt, BigIntError] fn format(value: BigInt, radix: Int) -> String fn from_int(value: Int) -> BigInt fn multiply(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn parse(text: String, radix: Int, max_digits: Int) -> Result[BigInt, BigIntError] fn remainder(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> Result[BigInt, BigIntError] fn subtract(left: BigInt, right: BigInt) -> BigInt fn to_int(value: BigInt) -> Optional[Int] Floating-point behavior# Math functions use IEEE binary64 and Go’s domain and overflow rules. An invalid Float domain yields NaN; overflow can yield infinity. The last bits of transcendental results may differ across targets, so tests should use tolerances.
round uses ties-to-even. min and max propagate NaN and preserve signed-zero conventions. abs_int(MinInt64) faults because the positive result cannot fit in an Int. pi() and e() are ordinary zero-argument functions.
Parsing and formatting numbers# Integer radices are 2–36. Input may have a sign and ASCII digits or letters. Parsing consumes the whole input and rejects prefixes, whitespace, and separators. An invalid radix returns InvalidInput when parsing and faults when formatting. An integer outside the Int range returns OutOfRange.
Float parsing accepts signed decimal digits with an optional fraction or exponent. A present decimal point needs at least one digit on each side. It also accepts NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity. Finite syntax that overflows binary64 returns OutOfRange. Formatting uses the existing round-trip Float representation.
Arbitrary-precision integers# BigInt is opaque, immutable, shareable, and comparable for equality. Create it with from_int or parse; there is no source constructor, literal, arithmetic operator, or hashing guarantee. Arithmetic functions leave both operands unchanged. Conversion between Int and BigInt is explicit.
Operation Behavior Parse max_digits is positive and counts digits excluding the optional sign. Divide Truncates toward zero; division by zero returns InvalidInput. Remainder Has the dividend’s sign; a zero divisor returns InvalidInput. Compare Returns -1, 0, or 1. Convert to Int Returns none outside the signed 64-bit range. Bit operations Use mathematical two’s-complement semantics. A very large native arithmetic operation can delay cancellation until it returns. Bound input magnitudes where that matters. Decimal keeps its existing 34-digit contract; extended Decimal parse and format APIs remain future work.

title: Aggregates and local construction
content:
Aggregates and local construction# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Records, alternatives, collections, and closures can hold resource references. Storing a resource inside one of these values does not arrange for it to close or keep it open. Arrange cleanup for the resource itself.
Closing a registered resource affects all aliases, including aliases nested in aggregates. Dropping an aggregate does not recursively close its fields. A library object that deliberately manages several resources can implement Closeable and explicitly close them in its implementation.
Collections retain their ordinary element bounds; resource references are eligible when their runtime wrappers satisfy the declared sharing contract. The bound provides concurrency safety, not a resource lifetime guarantee.
Builders follow the same reference rules. Basic sealed snapshots are implemented; additional bulk mutation operations remain design work. Destructuring extracts fields and positions without changing cleanup.

title: Serialization and formats
content:
Serialization and formats# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use these modules to parse and write JSON, CSV, and URLs, or escape HTML text. Choose explicit limits for input size and nesting. Each format has its own validation rules, described after the signatures.
@std/json.ms# Manuscript fn parse(text: String, limits: JsonLimits) -> Result[JsonValue, JsonError] fn stringify(value: JsonValue, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, JsonError] @std/csv.ms# Manuscript fn parse(text: String, options: CsvOptions, max_rows: Int, max_cells: Int) -> Result[List[List[String]], CsvError] fn stringify(rows: List[List[String]], options: CsvOptions, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[String, CsvError] @std/url.ms# Manuscript fn decode_component(text: String) -> Result[String, UrlError] fn encode_component(text: String) -> String fn format(value: Url) -> Result[String, UrlError] fn format_query(entries: List[QueryEntry]) -> String fn parse(text: String) -> Result[Url, UrlError] fn parse_query(text: String, max_entries: Int) -> Result[List[QueryEntry], UrlError] fn resolve(base: Url, reference: String) -> Result[Url, UrlError] @std/html.ms# Manuscript fn escape(text: String) -> String Data records# Manuscript type JsonLimits: max_bytes: Int max_depth: Int max_values: Int type JsonValue: case Null case BoolValue(value: Bool) case NumberValue(text: String) case StringValue(value: String) case ArrayValue(values: List[JsonValue]) case ObjectValue(values: Map[String, JsonValue]) type CsvOptions: delimiter: String line_ending: String type QueryEntry: key: String value: String type Url: scheme: String host: String port: Optional[Int] path: String query: String fragment: String JSON behavior# JSON numbers keep their exact valid token text, including integers larger than 2^53. They are not automatically converted to Float. stringify also validates NumberValue text because an application can construct that case directly.
Parsing accepts one document. It rejects trailing values, duplicate decoded object keys, and unpaired surrogate escapes. Object order follows Map insertion order. There is no reflection-based record serialization or execution hook.
JsonLimits uses nonnegative limits:
Limit What it counts max_bytes UTF-8 input bytes. Stringify separately limits output bytes. max_depth Container nesting; a root container has depth one. max_values All values, including the root. Object keys are not counted as values. Both parsing and stringify enforce a native depth ceiling of 512. Malformed data returns InvalidData; exceeded limits return LimitExceeded.
Stringify produces compact JSON and uses Go’s escaping for HTML-sensitive characters. It is not a canonical format for signing.
CSV behavior# The delimiter must be one non-NUL ASCII byte other than quote, CR, or LF. line_ending is LF or CRLF. Row, cell, and output limits must be nonnegative; max_cells counts every returned cell.
Go’s encoding/csv quoting rules apply: quotes are doubled, values are not trimmed or converted to other types, rows may have different widths, and blank lines are ignored. CRLF is normalized, including inside quoted cells. Serialization ends every row with the selected terminator. Formula-like spreadsheet values are left as supplied.
Exceeded limits return LimitExceeded. The input String is already in memory, and the parser reads one record before checking its row and cell limits. Bound the source read before parsing untrusted CSV.
URL behavior# parse requires an absolute hierarchical URL and rejects user information. Scheme and host become lowercase. The optional port is in the range 0–65535.
The path keeps escaped separators, the query stays encoded, and the fragment is decoded. resolve follows Go’s net/url rules. Url is an ordinary record, so format and resolve validate values constructed by application code too. Unsupported opaque URLs return InvalidData.
Query entries retain duplicates and order. A bare key has an empty value; + represents a space. Component encoding preserves only ASCII unreserved characters. Decoding rejects invalid UTF-8.
IDNA normalization, a distinction between absent and empty queries, and browser WHATWG URL compatibility remain future work.
HTML escaping# escape handles text and quoted attribute contexts. It does not sanitize HTML or encode JavaScript, CSS, or URL contexts.

title: Assignment and branches
content:
Assignment and branches# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Reassigning a var replaces its value or reference. It does not close the previous object or invalidate other references to it. A let prevents reassignment.
A with binding is immutable and registers the initialized object itself. Reassigning another variable that references the object cannot change which object’s close() will execute. Closing early is permitted because close() is idempotent.
Every binding is initialized at declaration. Branch-local names stay inside their branch; assignments to an outer var keep its declared type. Closures snapshot the current value of a local binding at creation; they do not share mutable local cells.
See bindings , closure captures , and with scopes .

title: Paths and filesystem
content:
Paths and filesystem# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Path functions manipulate path text without accessing disk. FileSystem methods read or change files through a supplied service. A path string or an import alone does not grant filesystem access.
@std/path.ms# Manuscript fn basename(path: String) -> String fn dirname(path: String) -> String fn extension(path: String) -> String fn is_absolute(path: String) -> Bool fn join(parts: List[String]) -> String fn normalize(path: String) -> String fn relative(base: String, target: String) -> Result[String, PathError] @std/fs.ms# FileSystem operations# Manuscript fn read_file(path: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, FileSystemError] fn write_file(path: String, data: Bytes, replace: Bool) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn stat(path: String, follow_links: Bool) -> Result[FileInfo, FileSystemError] fn list(path: String, max_entries: Int) -> Result[List[DirectoryEntry], FileSystemError] fn create_directory(path: String, recursive: Bool) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn remove(path: String, recursive: Bool) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn rename(source: String, destination: String) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn copy_file(source: String, destination: String, replace: Bool, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn canonicalize(path: String) -> Result[String, FileSystemError] fn read_link(path: String) -> Result[String, FileSystemError] fn create_link(path: String, target: String) -> Result[Unit, FileSystemError] fn temporary_directory(prefix: String) -> Result[String, FileSystemError] Authority and records# Process supplies filesystem: FileSystem & Shareable. FileSystem uses a fixed startup directory for relative paths and the CLI process’s native OS permissions. It is not restricted to a sandboxed subtree. The existing Files capability remains read-only.
Importing a type or constructing a path string grants no file access. Source fakes can implement the same contract. NUL paths return InvalidInput; filenames that cannot be represented as text return Unsupported. A temporary directory must be explicitly removed; dropping its path string does not remove it.
Manuscript type FileInfo: name: String size: Int directory: Bool symlink: Bool modified: Timestamp type DirectoryEntry: name: String directory: Bool symlink: Bool Reads, writes, and replacement# read_file limits cumulative bytes and closes its handle on every exit. write_file with replace: false creates exclusively; replace: true may truncate existing data. copy_file bounds input before writing and uses the same replacement rule.
Writes and copies are not transactional. An error can leave a destination prefix. Default creation permissions are 0600 for files and 0700 for directories, subject to platform behavior.
Directories, links, and errors# Directory lists are sorted by byte-lexical order. Excess entries return LimitExceeded, rather than a truncated success. stat uses follow_links to choose link or target metadata.
rename follows the native platform’s replacement and atomicity behavior, including cross-device errors. It does not fall back to copying and deleting. Recursive remove does not intentionally follow symlinks and checks cancellation between entries; it is not transactional.
Temporary-directory prefixes must be nonempty and contain no slash, backslash, or NUL. OS failures map to NotFound, AlreadyExists, PermissionDenied, or Failed(message: ...).
Path functions# Pure path functions use the target platform’s Go filepath rules. join and normalize do not access disk. Cleaning path text does not prove that a path stays inside an authorized directory.
relative requires absolute paths and may return InvalidInput for incompatible roots. Basename, dirname, and extension follow Go filepath behavior, including treating .profile as an extension.
Seekable files, metadata mutation, watchers, secure subtree provisioning, and archive extraction remain future work. Existing Files and stream APIs provide bounded sequential reads.

title: Scoped cleanup
content:
Scoped cleanup# Guide index · Design index A with block registers a resource to close when the block ends. Cleanup also runs after early returns, errors, faults, and cancellation. Start with with scopes, then read the exact rules for close and exit order.
With scopes — Acquire a resource and close it at the end of a block with with. The Closeable contract — Implement the cleanup operation required by with. Scope-exit ordering — Follow cleanup order after a return, error, fault, or cancellation. Shielding and cleanup faults — Understand cleanup after cancellation and what happens if close itself faults. External resource release — Separate closing a handle from successfully completing its work.

title: Time and system information
content:
Time and system information# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use Timestamp for wall-clock time and Duration for a time interval. Access the current wall clock, environment, system information, and random bytes through explicit services supplied by the host.
@std/time.ms# Manuscript fn difference(left: Timestamp, right: Timestamp) -> Result[Duration, TimeError] fn format_timestamp(value: Timestamp) -> String fn nanoseconds(value: Timestamp) -> Int fn parse_timestamp(text: String) -> Result[Timestamp, TimeError] fn shift(value: Timestamp, duration: Duration) -> Result[Timestamp, TimeError] fn timestamp(seconds: Int, nanoseconds: Int) -> Result[Timestamp, TimeError] fn unix_seconds(value: Timestamp) -> Int @std/system.ms# @std/random.ms# Manuscript fn secure_int(entropy: Entropy&Shareable, min: Int, max_exclusive: Int) -> Result[Int, RandomError] fn uuid_v4(entropy: Entropy&Shareable) -> Result[String, RandomError] WallClock operations# Manuscript fn now() -> Timestamp System operations# Manuscript fn info() -> SystemInfo fn working_directory() -> String fn environment(name: String) -> Optional[String] Entropy operations# Manuscript fn bytes(count: Int) -> Result[Bytes, RandomError] Services supplied by the CLI# Process provides wall_clock: WallClock & Shareable, system: System & Shareable, and entropy: Entropy & Shareable.
Timestamp represents wall time and is opaque, immutable, shareable, and comparable for equality. Instant remains a monotonic time value; conversion between them is not implicit. Existing Clock and sleep keep their signatures and error/cancellation rules. Wall-clock changes do not affect monotonic deadlines.
Timestamp rules# Construction accepts UTC years 1–9999 and nanoseconds 0–999999999. Parsing uses strict RFC 3339: an explicit offset, uppercase T/Z, at most nine fractional digits, and no leap seconds.
Formatting uses UTC. It omits a zero fraction and removes trailing fractional zeroes. shift checks the resulting calendar range. difference returns OutOfRange if its nanosecond result cannot fit in Duration.
There are no Timestamp operators or source constructor. Use the named functions; unix_seconds and nanoseconds expose the components explicitly.
System information# SystemInfo has os: String, architecture: String, and cpu_count: Int. This is a native runtime snapshot. CPU count does not reserve resources.
working_directory returns the fixed startup directory. environment returns none if the variable is absent or its value cannot be represented as UTF-8. Process.environment remains a startup snapshot. Importing System grants no environment access; receive a service value explicitly. There is no global chdir or environment mutation API.
Randomness# Entropy.bytes returns exactly the requested number of bytes from Go’s crypto/rand. Count must be 0–16777216 per call. It never falls back to a deterministic generator.
secure_int samples uniformly from a nonempty interval that includes min and excludes max_exclusive. Rejection sampling avoids bias, including for interval widths above MaxInt64. uuid_v4 returns a canonical lowercase RFC 9562 version-4 UUID with the correct variant.
A source fake must return the exact requested byte count. Malformed fake output returns Failed.
Timezone and calendar conversion, tickers, seeded generators, and environment mutation remain future work.

title: Cryptography and randomness
content:
Cryptography and randomness# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Choose a cryptographic function by its purpose: hashing, keyed authentication, key derivation, encryption, or signatures. These transforms use supplied bytes. Random material comes from an explicit Entropy service.
@std/crypto.ms# Manuscript fn constant_time_equal(left: Bytes, right: Bytes) -> Bool fn derive_key(password: Bytes, salt: Bytes, iterations: Int, length: Int) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn hmac(key: Bytes, data: Bytes, algorithm: String) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn open(key: Bytes, nonce: Bytes, ciphertext: Bytes, associated_data: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn public_key(seed: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn seal(key: Bytes, nonce: Bytes, plaintext: Bytes, associated_data: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn sha256(data: Bytes) -> Bytes fn sha384(data: Bytes) -> Bytes fn sha512(data: Bytes) -> Bytes fn sign(seed: Bytes, data: Bytes) -> Result[Bytes, CryptoError] fn verify(key: Bytes, data: Bytes, signature: Bytes) -> Bool Choose the operation# Cryptographic transforms are pure functions. Obtain random keys and nonces through an explicit Entropy service.
Task Operation and algorithm Hash bytes sha256, sha384, or sha512. Authenticate bytes with a key HMAC with SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512. Unsupported algorithm names return Unsupported. Derive key bytes from a password derive_key, using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256. Encrypt and authenticate seal / open, using AES-256-GCM. Sign and verify Ed25519 with sign / verify. Hashing checks cancellation between chunks. Key derivation checks it periodically.
Key derivation# derive_key requires positive iterations and a length from 1 to 1048576. The application chooses the salt and work factor. The function does not define a password-storage policy.
Authenticated encryption# AES-256-GCM requires a 32-byte key and 12-byte nonce. seal appends a 16-byte authentication tag to the ciphertext. open authenticates before releasing any plaintext. The associated data must match exactly.
A nonce must not be reused with the same key. The runtime does not detect that reuse. Invalid key or nonce sizes return InvalidInput; a wrong key or tampered ciphertext returns AuthenticationFailed.
Signatures and key material# sign and public_key take a 32-byte Ed25519 seed. verify takes a 32-byte public key and signature bytes. It returns false for invalid signatures or wrong key/signature lengths. Use Entropy to generate seed material.
These APIs expose keys as Bytes, so garbage collection cannot guarantee erasure of retained copies. They provide no weak-algorithm menu, implicit randomness, automatic private-key diagnostic redaction, or certificate issuance. Verified TLS belongs to the Network and HTTP APIs.

title: With scopes
content:
With scopes# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use with to acquire a resource and close it when an indented block ends. The name introduced by with cannot be reassigned.
Manuscript with file = try files.open(path: "data.txt"): let chunk = try file.read(max_bytes: 4096) This fragment belongs inside a function returning Result[U, IoError]. The function receives files as an explicit capability. Files.open returns a shared File view. The read result is Optional[Bytes]: match it to distinguish bytes from end-of-input.
What happens, step by step# Evaluate the initializer once. Here, that means opening the file. If initialization fails, leave through the initializer’s error or fault path. No close action has been registered. If initialization succeeds, register the resource’s close operation before the next cancellation checkpoint. Run the block. Close the registered resource when execution leaves the block. Cleanup runs for every exit: reaching the end, break, continue, return, an error forwarded by try, a fault, or cancellation. Nested scopes close from inner to outer.
Which values can use with?# The compiler must be able to identify a valid close operation:
Value’s type Required evidence Concrete type An explicit implementation of standard Closeable. Contract view A declared fn close() -> Unit operation. Generic parameter A bound proving one of those operations. See Closeable for the exact checks.
Keep the lifetime tied to the block# A resource acquired inside a loop closes at the end of that iteration. Returning it or capturing it in a closure does not remove its registered cleanup. An ordinary let binding does not register cleanup.
The file, transaction, or background service supplies its own close behavior. with adds no custom enter hook or error-suppression hook.
