For compiler contributors: Go’s function-level defer lasts until the function returns, so it cannot by itself implement Manuscript’s nested block lifetimes. The compiler generates explicit cleanup for those scopes. See exit order , cleanup lowering , and the Go defer specification .

title: Networking, DNS, and TLS
content:
Networking, DNS, and TLS# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use an explicit Network service to resolve names and open sockets. Connections, listeners, and datagram sockets must close when their work ends. The sections below explain destination restrictions, cancellation, and verified TLS.
@std/net.ms# Manuscript fn contains_ip(cidr: String, address: String) -> Result[Bool, NetworkError] fn parse_cidr(text: String) -> Result[String, NetworkError] fn parse_ip(text: String) -> Result[String, NetworkError] @std/tls.ms# Manuscript fn parse_certificates(pem: String, max_certificates: Int) -> Result[List[CertificateInfo], TlsError] fn verify_certificates(chain_pem: String, roots_pem: String, server_name: String, now: Timestamp) -> Result[Unit, TlsError] Connection operations# Manuscript fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn shutdown_write() -> Result[Unit, NetworkError] fn local_address() -> String fn peer_address() -> String fn close() -> Unit fn read_timeout(max_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn write_timeout(data: Bytes, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn tls_info() -> Result[TlsInfo, TlsError] Listener operations# Manuscript fn accept() -> Result[Connection&Shareable, NetworkError] fn address() -> String fn close() -> Unit fn accept_timeout(timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection&Shareable, NetworkError] DatagramSocket operations# Manuscript fn send(data: Bytes, address: String) -> Result[Unit, NetworkError] fn receive(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Datagram, NetworkError] fn address() -> String fn close() -> Unit fn receive_timeout(max_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Datagram, NetworkError] fn send_timeout(data: Bytes, address: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Unit, NetworkError] Authority and restrictions# process.network: Network & Shareable remains the authority root, imported from @std/http.ms. Acquired Connection, Listener and DatagramSocket views are individually imported from @std/net.ms, closed with with, and also owned by Network. Network.close stops admission, cancels and joins in-flight DNS/dials/HTTP acquisition, closes owned services and handles, and waits for admitted I/O. Concurrent close callers join the same shutdown. Imports never manufacture native network authority.
Narrowing destination access# Use restrict to create a child Network with narrower access. The child cannot grant access its parent denied. Host entries are exact DNS names, compared without case and ignoring a trailing dot. CIDR entries authorize numeric address ranges. DNS-name dialing requires the name to be allowed. If CIDRs are supplied, every chosen resolved destination must also belong to those CIDRs; raw IP dialing never bypasses a host-only restriction. Empty hosts/CIDRs deny all outbound destinations.
allow_listen permits binding explicitly allowed numeric addresses; inbound listener peers are not an additional outbound grant. Restricted roots reject Unix socket acquisitions. Redirect hops retain the same policy. Restrictions are enforced on actual resolved addresses at dial time, not by URL string prefixes.
Choosing a resolver# with_resolver provisions a child with an explicit numeric DNS server address. The parent policy must authorize that server. Resolver configuration is scoped to the child; it does not mutate process-wide DNS. Lookup/resolve and UDP destination resolution use cancellable native resolver calls. Parent shutdown closes child capabilities. An unrestricted CLI root retains ordinary OS network authority; restrictions are explicit opt-in narrowing.
Records# Manuscript type Datagram: data: Bytes sender: String type DnsRecord: kind: String value: String priority: Int weight: Int port: Int type TlsOptions: server_name: String roots_pem: String certificate_pem: String private_key_pem: String alpn: List[String] require_client_certificate: Bool type CertificateInfo: subject: String issuer: String dns_names: List[String] not_before: Timestamp not_after: Timestamp der: Bytes type TlsInfo: version: Int cipher_suite: Int alpn: String peer_certificates: List[Bytes] verified: Bool DNS result fields# Resolve accepts A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, PTR and SRV. PTR takes a numeric address; SRV takes the full service name. CNAME returns the native canonical-name result. MX fills priority; SRV fills priority/weight/port; other numeric fields are zero. TXT joins the native record’s fragments. If results exceed max_records, the call returns an error rather than a truncated successful list. TXT/domain text that is not valid UTF-8 returns InvalidData rather than constructing an invalid String. The native resolver does not expose TTL; the API does not invent TTL values. Parse_ip/parse_cidr normalize numeric addresses/prefixes, and contains_ip checks prefix membership without DNS or authority.
Socket lifecycle and deadlines# Connect/listen addresses use native host:port notation, with port zero selecting an ephemeral local port on bind/listen. Unix methods use native Unix-domain paths. Read and write use separate synchronization gates, allowing one of each to progress together. Calls in the same direction are serialized. Closing a handle interrupts blocking I/O and waits for admitted operations. Metadata remains readable after close. A half-close ends writing while leaving reads available. It is supported for TCP, Unix, and TLS connections. Read follows the existing IoError/Optional Bytes contract: positive bounded chunks, none for EOF, and Closed for stale aliases. Writes accept all bytes or return an error after a possible external prefix.
Accept and handshake cancellation# Listener accept cancellation uses an interruptible deadline and restores it before releasing the accept gate. Cancellation and accept_timeout do not destroy the listener: it can admit another accept afterwards. A TLS listener additionally bounds each handshake; shutdown cancels admitted handshakes. Accepted handles retain Network ownership. Unix socket availability follows the target OS, not a separate deferred API.
Datagrams and operation timeouts# UDP preserves message boundaries, including empty messages. Receive accepts max_bytes 1–65535 and returns LimitExceeded on an oversized consumed packet, never a truncated success. UDP name resolution responds to caller cancellation and Network/socket closure. Timeout variants take nonnegative durations: zero is an immediate deadline. Expected local timeouts return NetworkError.Timeout; Connection timeout variants retain IoError and use Failed with a timeout diagnostic. Parent cancellation always unwinds. Operation deadlines are cleared under the direction gate before the next operation starts.
TLS and certificates# TLS supports 1.2 and newer with native authenticated ciphers. connect_tls uses system trust plus a required server_name; connect_tls_config accepts explicit trust PEM, client certificate/key, and ALPN. listen_tls uses a server certificate/key and can require verified client certificates. Empty roots select system trust for clients; supplied roots replace that client trust store. There is no insecure-skip-verification switch or retry. Configured names are checked against certificates; chain validation and expiration remain enabled. ALPN values must be nonempty protocol tokens of at most 255 bytes.
Hostnames and certificate helpers# HTTP/WebSocket clients validate each URL hostname; the generic client TLS server_name field does not override subsequent origins. Private-key PEM is explicit input, not an imported ambient secret. Parse_certificates validates PEM/DER syntax with a certificate count bound and exposes metadata. Verify_certificates takes an explicit PEM chain, trust roots, a nonempty name and Timestamp for pure deterministic chain/hostname/expiry validation. Tls_info exposes negotiated version/cipher/ALPN and peer DER certificates, without exposing private keys.
HTTP/3 is intentionally excluded at the user’s request. The HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSocket contracts are in their own pages.
Network operations# Manuscript fn lookup(name: String, max_records: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[List[String], NetworkError] fn connect(address: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection&Shareable, NetworkError] fn connect_tls(address: String, server_name: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection&Shareable, NetworkError] fn listen(address: String) -> Result[Listener&Shareable, NetworkError] fn bind_datagram(address: String) -> Result[DatagramSocket&Shareable, NetworkError] fn restrict(hosts: List[String], cidrs: List[String], allow_listen: Bool) -> Result[Network&Shareable, NetworkError] fn with_resolver(address: String) -> Result[Network&Shareable, NetworkError] fn resolve(name: String, kind: String, max_records: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[List[DnsRecord], NetworkError] fn connect_unix(path: String, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection&Shareable, NetworkError] fn listen_unix(path: String) -> Result[Listener&Shareable, NetworkError] fn connect_tls_config(address: String, options: TlsOptions, timeout: Duration) -> Result[Connection&Shareable, NetworkError] fn listen_tls(address: String, options: TlsOptions, handshake_timeout: Duration) -> Result[Listener&Shareable, NetworkError]

title: The Closeable contract
content:
The Closeable contract# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Closeable is the standard cleanup contract. Import it from @std/cleanup.ms to name or implement it. A with block checks the identity of that standard contract, so an unrelated interface with the same spelling does not replace it. Its declaration is:
Manuscript interface Closeable: fn close() -> Unit For a concrete value the compiler requires its explicit Closeable implementation, resolves that method, and registers a call to it. A contract value is also eligible when its own declaration explicitly contains the exact operation fn close() -> Unit; register that declared operation without a contract-to-contract conversion. A similarly named concrete method without impl Closeable remains insufficient. This rule lets standard File, ReadStream, and WriteStream contracts expose cleanup and admit source test fakes without inheritance. It has no special knowledge of a particular file or transaction. Libraries can implement the same cleanup contract for their own managed objects.
A generic parameter with a Closeable bound also supplies the implementation proof needed by with; dispatch its bound close operation directly without constructing a view or adding Shareable. A generic bound naming a contract that explicitly declares the exact close signature is likewise sufficient. An unconstrained type parameter or a merely similarly named method is insufficient.
close() is idempotent, may suspend like any other function, and finishes the object’s release/shutdown obligation before returning. Repeated or concurrent calls do not release an underlying handle twice. An implementation must coordinate ongoing access with closure and ensure that later accesses report closed state.
Expected failures that application code needs to handle belong to explicit operations such as commit(), flush(), or finish(), returning Result. The automatic close hook returns Unit; an unexpected release failure is a programming/cleanup fault, not a discarded error value.
A close failure does not skip other registered actions. Implementations must leave the object unusable or safely quarantined after a failed release rather than exposing an invalid/reused native handle. Faults and remaining release obligations are reported to the host.
General user defer syntax is unsupported. Custom scope cleanup can be packaged in a library object implementing Closeable.
See with scopes , cleanup faults , and operation contracts .

title: HTTP clients and streaming hosts
content:
HTTP clients and streaming hosts# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use HttpClient for reusable outbound requests and HttpExchange for streaming request handling. Response bodies are resources: read them in chunks and close them. A received HTTP error status is still a response you can inspect.
@std/http.ms# HttpClient operations# Manuscript fn send(method: String, url: String, headers: Map[String, String], body: Bytes, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[ResponseBody&Shareable, HttpError] fn send_stream(method: String, url: String, headers: Map[String, String], body: ReadStream&Shareable, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[ResponseBody&Shareable, HttpError] fn close() -> Unit ResponseBody operations# Manuscript fn status() -> Int fn headers() -> Map[String, List[String]] fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn close() -> Unit HttpExchange operations# Manuscript fn method() -> String fn path() -> String fn query() -> String fn headers() -> Map[String, List[String]] fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError] fn send_headers(status: Int, headers: Map[String, List[String]]) -> Result[Unit, HttpError] fn write(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, IoError] fn upgrade(allowed_origins: List[String], subprotocols: List[String], max_message_bytes: Int) -> Result[WebSocket&Shareable, WebSocketError] fn close() -> Unit Compatibility# The original bounded buffered HTTP host and Network.request remain supported. The new reusable client and streaming host provide HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 without changing those existing record types. HTTP/3 is excluded by user instruction.
Configuration# Manuscript type HttpClientOptions: max_redirects: Int max_idle_connections: Int max_header_bytes: Int idle_timeout: Duration decompress: Bool cookies: Bool tls: TlsOptions type HttpServerOptions: max_requests: Int max_body_bytes: Int max_response_bytes: Int max_header_bytes: Int timeout: Duration grace: Duration tls: Optional[TlsOptions] Option limits# Client redirect counts, idle capacity, and timeouts must be nonnegative. The header limit must be positive, and idle capacity cannot exceed 65536. Server request capacity is 1–65536. Header limits and timeout must be positive. Body and response limits and grace must be nonnegative. With no TLS configuration, the server uses plain HTTP/1.1. With TLS configured, native ALPN negotiation selects HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. Credentials/trust come from explicit TlsOptions. No ambient HTTP proxy is read.
Client lifetime# Create a shared HttpClient through Network.http_client. It implements Closeable, so keep it in a with scope. It owns a pooled transport and optional public-suffix-aware cookie jar. Idle connections and lifetime are explicit options. Close stops admission, cancels in-flight requests, closes outstanding response bodies, joins their upload/read work and releases idle connections. Network close owns and joins clients too.
Reading a response# send returns a ResponseBody that you read incrementally. Reads follow the stream contract. max_response_bytes limits the cumulative decoded output. Status and duplicate headers remain available as metadata. Close before EOF cancels/discards the body; consumed bodies can reuse the pooled connection. Timeout covers DNS through body lifetime; parent cancellation unwinds. Gzip decoding is enabled only with decompress and remains subject to the expanded-byte bound. Invalid UTF-8 header values are rejected before constructing source Strings.
Streaming an upload# Send_stream borrows an explicitly shared ReadStream for the upload and does not close it. The response owns the upload work until response closure/completion: keep the input’s scope open through the response scope. Under HTTP/1.1, streaming server responses enable full duplex so a response does not silently drain/close the outstanding upload. Upload faults retain source fault identity, not a generic transport success. Redirects requiring replay are returned to the caller for streaming bodies; immutable Bytes sends can follow configured redirects. A consumed prefix cannot be rolled back after failure.
Redirects and HTTP status# Redirects honor max_redirects (zero returns the redirect response), reject TLS downgrade, recheck the Network policy on every destination, and remove explicit Authorization/Cookie/Proxy-Authorization when the origin changes. Automatic cookies are selected by the destination jar rather than copying source-origin headers. HTTP 4xx and 5xx statuses are returned responses, rather than transport errors. Header names/values reject injection and callers cannot set host-managed framing fields.
Streaming request host# Call Network.serve_stream directly; it cannot be stored as a function value. Its handler must be proved safe to call concurrently and have type fn(exchange: HttpExchange & Shareable) -> Result[Unit, HttpError]. The server establishes a fixed request execution context, bounded admission, body/output/header limits, disconnect cancellation and timeout. The handler may read incrementally, emit headers once and write/flush bounded output, or upgrade to a WebSocket session. Route requests with ordinary branches on method and path.
Response ordering and limits# Read and write have separate synchronized gates. Send_headers accepts status 200–599 and ordered duplicate header values; it rejects repeated headers emission, CR/LF/NUL values, and caller-supplied framing. Write requires headers first, counts cumulative output bytes, applies native backpressure and disallows bodies for HEAD/204/304. Body bound failures return IoError.Failed with a limit diagnostic. Before headers, handler faults/domain errors produce a generic 500, or 504 for timeout where possible; after headers the host aborts transport rather than returning a misleading complete body. Returning success without headers produces 204.
Request and server lifetime# HttpExchange belongs to its request: retained aliases report Closed once request cleanup ends. Server shutdown stops admission, waits grace, cancels remaining requests/sessions and joins them before returning. Hijacked WebSocket transports are explicitly included in request cleanup and joining. A server or Network cannot close from its own handler. Streaming source code needs no new function kind or detached task syntax.
Network operations# Manuscript fn request(method: String, url: String, headers: Map[String, String], body: Bytes, max_response_bytes: Int, timeout: Duration) -> Result[ClientResponse, HttpError] fn http_client(options: HttpClientOptions) -> Result[HttpClient&Shareable, HttpError] fn serve_stream(address: String, handler: fn(exchange: HttpExchange&Shareable) -> Result[Unit, HttpError], options: HttpServerOptions) -> Result[HttpServer&Shareable, HttpError]

title: Scope-exit ordering
content:
Scope-exit ordering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index When a scope ends, the runtime runs the cleanup registered by with. It closes inner resources before outer ones. Another reference to a resource, including one stored in a record, does not register another close action.
Evaluate the pending return value or select the initiating error, fault, or cancellation. Finish any active joined API call: it cancels unfinished operations if needed and joins them before unwinding into the caller’s cleanup. Call registered close() methods in reverse registration/nesting order. A Background.close() performs its own service cancellation and joining here. Deliver the pending return/error, unless cleanup selected a programming fault; otherwise propagate the selected fault or cancellation. A cleanup fault suppresses a pending normal return or domain error. The unreturned value is released for garbage collection; it is not recursively closed. Resource factories retain explicit responsibility for resources acquired but never delivered.
Returned references do not bypass registered cleanup. A returned file registered in the exiting scope is already closed when the caller receives it. There is no staged ownership transfer or result escrow.
Register dependencies outside the background service’s with scope so that service shutdown finishes before those dependencies close. See background services and fault selection .

title: Shielding and cleanup faults
content:
Shielding and cleanup faults# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Cleanup still runs when cancellation or a fault ends ordinary work. It ignores the cancellation signal and expired work deadline that caused the exit. This is called shielding. Cleanup keeps the original access to external services and may wait for operations to finish.
If close itself faults# Every registered close action is attempted once during scope exit. A fault in one action does not skip the rest.
Outcome before cleanup If cleanup faults If cleanup succeeds A programming fault is already pending Keep the original fault as primary; record cleanup faults as secondary diagnostics. Keep the original fault. A normal return, expected error, or cancellation is pending The first cleanup fault becomes primary; record later faults as secondary diagnostics. Keep the pending outcome. A concurrency API reports an operation fault as ExecutionError.Crashed. A background service reports it through its failure observer. Root hosts isolate and report request failures.
Cleanup can outlast a timeout# Shielding gives cleanup a chance to release resources; it cannot force uncooperative code to finish. Hosts set cleanup watchdogs separately from request timeouts. If close or join cannot finish, the host may need process-level escalation . A timer expiring does not mean cleanup completed.
If an operation can fail in an expected way, handle that through an explicit fallible completion method before leaving the scope. For example, commit a transaction before relying on close to release it. See Closeable , timeouts , and resource release .

title: Subprocesses and terminal I/O
content:
Subprocesses and terminal I/O# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use stream helpers for bounded reads and copies, and Commands for buffered subprocess execution. The caller supplies the streams or command service. Helpers do not acquire authority or close the streams for you.
@std/io.ms# Manuscript fn copy(input: ReadStream&Shareable, output: WriteStream&Shareable, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Int, IoError] fn read_all(input: ReadStream&Shareable, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, IoError] fn read_line(input: ReadStream&Shareable, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[String], IoError] Running commands# Commands.run uses explicit process.commands access. Supply the program, arguments, input, aggregate output bound, and timeout. It waits for execution and returns captured exit_code, stdout, and stderr. A nonzero exit is returned data. Running a shell must be explicit.
Stream helpers# These helpers use shared stream views without closing them. Keep the streams’ own cleanup scopes open for the whole call. All helpers cooperate with cancellation and enforce cumulative byte limits.
Helper Behavior copy Returns the number of bytes copied. An error may occur after a prefix was written; there is no rollback. read_all Returns all bytes only on success. read_line Reads one byte at a time so it does not consume the next line. It strips LF and a preceding CR, and accepts a final line without a terminator. read_line returns none only if EOF occurs before any data. Its positive max_bytes includes terminator bytes. Invalid UTF-8 returns InvalidData; overflow returns LimitExceeded and may consume a prefix plus one boundary byte. Copy and read_all allow a zero limit for an empty source.
Source streams must return nonempty chunks within the requested size. A malformed stream implementation causes Failed.
Expected stream failures preserve their original IoError case and payload. Invalid UTF-8 returns IoError.InvalidData; an exceeded byte bound returns IoError.LimitExceeded. Helpers do not flatten Result or catch cancellation and faults. Convert a File view explicitly to ReadStream when required by the contract-view rules.
Interactive subprocess handles, terminal raw mode and secret reads, REPL/history, and richer child environment or working-directory options remain future work. Buffered Commands is the current subprocess API; there is no new Process/Child hierarchy.

title: WebSocket sessions
content:
WebSocket sessions# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts A WebSocket session sends and receives complete text or binary messages over a connection. Client sessions come from Network; server sessions come from an HTTP upgrade. Keep each session inside its cleanup and host lifetime.
@std/websocket.ms# WebSocket operations# Manuscript fn receive() -> Result[Optional[WebSocketMessage], WebSocketError] fn send(data: Bytes, text: Bool) -> Result[Unit, WebSocketError] fn ping(data: Bytes) -> Result[Unit, WebSocketError] fn subprotocol() -> String fn close() -> Unit Acquiring a session# Network.web_socket acquires a client WebSocket for an explicit ws/wss URL, headers, subprotocols and WebSocketOptions. HttpExchange.upgrade acquires the server session inside an admitted request. Both return shared views with synchronized operations and explicit close. Wss retains hostname/chain verification, explicit TLS roots/client certificates and destination restrictions.
Manuscript type WebSocketOptions: max_message_bytes: Int timeout: Duration tls: TlsOptions compression: Bool type WebSocketMessage: data: Bytes text: Bool Message limits and errors# Client max_message_bytes and handshake timeout must be positive. Clients negotiate permessage-deflate only when compression is explicitly enabled. Server upgrade currently accepts uncompressed messages. Bounds apply to decompressed message data as well as wire frames. receive returns one complete text or binary message, or none when the peer closes normally. Oversized messages return LimitExceeded and terminate transport; invalid text UTF-8 returns InvalidData. Repeated reads after a protocol failure return Closed rather than spinning inside the protocol implementation. Send validates text UTF-8 and bounds outbound message bytes. Ping limits control payloads to 125 bytes.
Concurrent calls and protocol rules# One read and one write can run concurrently. Two reads, or two writes, are serialized. Fragmentation, masking, control frames and close codes follow RFC 6455 through the pinned Gorilla implementation. Subprotocol tokens are validated and the selected protocol is observable. Client callers cannot override Sec-WebSocket handshake/framing headers. Server upgrade accepts absent Origin, and by default same-host origins; an explicit allowed_origins list authorizes exact http/https origins, never a wildcard implicit grant.
Session lifetime# The server session remains inside the HTTP request lifetime. Disconnect, request timeout and server/Network shutdown interrupt blocking receives/writes, close the hijacked socket and join the handler’s nested work. Close is idempotent, attempts a normal close control frame with a short bounded write deadline, then releases the handle and joins admitted operations. Source must not retain a session as detached work outside the request. Client sessions remain owned by their Network and lexical with scope. HTTP/3 is unrelated to the supported WebSocket transport and is excluded from this expansion by user request.
Manuscript fn web_socket(url: String, headers: Map[String, String], subprotocols: List[String], options: WebSocketOptions) -> Result[WebSocket&Shareable, WebSocketError]

title: Compression and archives
content:
Compression and archives# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Use compress for a byte stream and archive for named file or directory entries. Both operate on data in memory. Set limits on expanded output; unpacking an archive does not write its entries to disk.
@std/compress.ms# Manuscript fn compress(data: Bytes, format: String, level: Int, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, CompressionError] fn decompress(data: Bytes, format: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, CompressionError] @std/archive.ms# Manuscript fn pack(entries: List[ArchiveEntry], format: String, max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Bytes, ArchiveError] fn unpack(data: Bytes, format: String, limits: ArchiveLimits) -> Result[List[ArchiveEntry], ArchiveError] Compression behavior# Supported format strings are gzip, zlib, and deflate; others return Unsupported. Compression levels are 0–9, and output limits must be nonnegative.
Decompression validates checksums and rejects trailing bytes that do not belong to the format. Concatenated gzip members share one cumulative output limit. Chunk processing checks cancellation. Excess expanded output returns LimitExceeded before the decoder retains output beyond max_bytes.
Gzip output has a zero timestamp and no platform or name metadata.
Archive records and limits# ArchiveEntry contains path: String, data: Bytes, and directory: Bool. ArchiveLimits contains max_entries: Int, max_entry_bytes: Int, and max_total_bytes: Int. All limits are nonnegative and count expanded content.
Pack and unpack support zip and tar, with regular files and directories. Names must be UTF-8 portable relative paths. They reject absolute roots, backslashes, colons, NUL, and empty, dot, or dot-dot components. Duplicate normalized paths are rejected. Directory data must be empty.
Encrypted archives, devices, sparse files, links, and non-UTF-8 names are unsupported. ZIP supports stored and deflated entries and validates checksums. Pack preserves entry order with deterministic metadata: TAR uses the epoch and ZIP uses its 1980 minimum date.
Problem Error Unsupported entry type Unsupported Malformed archive or decoded path InvalidData Invalid source entry InvalidInput Unpacking does not write files# unpack returns immutable entries. It performs no filesystem writes and grants no filesystem access. Automatic extraction is future work.
Bound compressed input reads as well as expanded output. ZIP parses central-directory metadata before checking max_entries. TAR uses native header validation; it makes no canonical guarantee about arbitrary trailing padding or metadata.
An application can validate entries and write them through an explicit FileSystem service. Secure extraction into an existing directory still needs a trusted containment adapter; a lexical path check alone is insufficient. Brotli and Zstd remain future work.

title: External resource release
content:
External resource release# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Files, sockets, stream bodies, transactions, and pool leases need explicit release. Their object memory is garbage collected, but their external handles or activity are released through close() or a with block. These resource objects implement Closeable.
Object Automatic close behavior File, socket, stream body Release the external handle Transaction Roll back if not committed; then release its lease Connection lease Return the connection only after outstanding access has ended Background service Stop admission, cancel as configured, and join work Closing is shared state: all aliases see the same closed object. Resource methods return resource-specific errors such as IoError.Closed after closure. The wrapper must synchronize access and close; checking a flag before accessing a native handle is not sufficient. Old lease references must never access a connection reused for another caller.
Cleanup is not successful completion. Explicit commit, finish, or flush operations expose expected errors with Result. Unexpected release failures become cleanup faults. A plain let, function call, aggregate, or closure does not add implicit close behavior.
Factories close newly acquired native resources when cancellation or an error prevents delivery. A with initializer registers successful acquisition before cancellation can unwind it. See completion and acquisition , sharing , and Closeable .

title: Concurrency
content:
Concurrency guide# Design index An ordinary function call finishes before the caller moves on. Use a concurrency API when operations should run at the same time. Every function can wait for work; there is no separate async declaration.
Choose how the work ends# Need Use When it finishes Run a fixed set of functions together parallel Before the call returns, including on failure. Start work under a longer-lived service Background The service tracks it and waits for unfinished work during shutdown. Parallel APIs join: they wait for every started operation to finish its body and cleanup. A timeout requests a stop; it does not let the call return with work still running.
Start with parallel operations for a complete example. Then read joined groups for error outcomes and cancellation for stopping and time budgets. Runtime contracts contains the implementation details.
Functions passed to a concurrency API must be safe to call concurrently. Closures keep snapshots of the surrounding bindings they use. Keeping a resource reference does not keep the resource open; see sharing .
Importing concurrency APIs# Concurrency adds no intrinsic names or compiler bounds. Import each API or type that the module names:
Manuscript import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" import Background from "@std/tasks.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import OperationId from "@std/tasks.ms" import StartError from "@std/tasks.ms" import check_cancelled from "@std/tasks.ms" import Duration from "@std/time.ms" These are independent imports, not a required bundle. Importing one does not expose the others. Work status and failure reporting are also explicit standard exports; the standard API contract lists their paths. Ordinary Result annotations and error-adaptation helpers use their own imports from @std/result.ms.
Scheduling, cancellation, joining, time budgets, and service shutdown belong to these library/runtime APIs. The compiler checks callable sharing and the fixed parallel pack shape by the resolved standard binding identity. Its hidden execution context is an internal calling convention, not an ambient source capability or a new intrinsic type. A user function named parallel remains an ordinary function.
Fixed lifetimes# Every operation starts under a fixed execution lifetime. That relationship is chosen before work starts and does not change while it runs.
API Execution lifetime Ordinary call Current execution context parallel Joined group nested under the caller Background.start The chosen background service’s fixed host/component lifetime A helper may call parallel and return its completed result. It cannot return running work for another scope to adopt. Background work is started directly through the chosen service.
Passing a Background reference shares access to that service. It does not prolong the service’s lifetime, move its existing work, change its cancellation parent, or reset deadlines. The creating scope registers shutdown with with; aliases reject admission after closure.
A request can submit work through an application background service, but accepted work uses the service’s execution context. Request resources captured by that work can still close when the request exits; later use reports the resource’s closed-state error. Pass request data and application services, and acquire the operation’s resources inside it.
There is no task adoption, task reparenting, source-level detached work, or dynamic ownership graph. Scoped resources and ordinary references follow resource lifetimes .
Reading order# Parallel operations : calling parallel, argument preparation, and typed results Joined groups : the normative stop, join, and outcome contract for parallel Cancellation and budgets : cancellation requests, checkpoints, timeouts, and deadlines Runtime contracts : atomic transitions, resource acquisition, adapter contexts, and host escalation The standard library describes background services .

title: Logging
content:
Logging# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts Write structured logs to an explicit output stream. Logging returns expected errors. Tests use ordinary conditional returns to check their results.
@std/log.ms# Manuscript fn write(output: WriteStream&Shareable, level: String, message: String, fields: Map[String, String], max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Unit, LogError] write emits one compact UTF-8 JSON line to the supplied shared WriteStream. It contains level, message, and fields. Allowed levels are debug, info, warn, and error. Fields are a Map[String, String], sorted by the native JSON serializer.
max_bytes must be nonnegative and includes the final LF. Excess output returns LimitExceeded; it is not truncated. Stream failures become Failed. Writes use the stream’s existing synchronization, backpressure, and cancellation behavior.
The caller chooses the output and sensitive fields. The function provides no implicit stderr access, arbitrary object inspection, automatic redaction, or recursive failure logging. Serialization may allocate a complete record before checking the byte limit, so bound untrusted inputs too.
Tests# Tests use ordinary if/return guards; see semantic conformance tests . No expected-fault-catching syntax or authority injection is added. Heap/CPU profiling and richer runtime metrics remain future work. Existing inspect, diagram, and debug metadata contracts are unchanged.

title: Node.js and Go coverage
content:
Node.js and Go coverage# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts This table maps common Node.js and Go tasks to Manuscript facilities. It tells you what runs today and what remains future work. The mapping is about functionality, not compatibility with those platforms’ APIs.
Node.js / Go capability Manuscript option Availability Buffer, bytes, encoding/hex/base64/binary Immutable Bytes, strict UTF-8/hex/base64, binary Int/Float Implemented strings, Unicode scalar operations, regexp Text functions and opaque RE2-style Regex Implemented; normalization/graphemes/legacy encodings deferred Array/Map/Set, slices/maps/sort Immutable collections, sequential map/filter/fold/stable sort, builders Implemented Math, strconv, math/big Float math, strict number conversion, BigInt, existing Decimal Implemented; complex/advanced distributions deferred JSON, encoding/json/csv, net/url, html Exact-number JsonValue, bounded CSV, ordered query codecs, URL records, escaping Implemented path/filepath, fs/io/fs Native pure paths, explicit read/write/copy/stat/list/create/remove/rename/links Implemented; seek/watch/permissions APIs deferred stream, io, bufio/readline Existing ReadStream/WriteStream plus bounded copy/read_all/read_line Implemented functional option; no Node stream events time/timers/os/process info Monotonic Clock/sleep, wall Timestamp, System snapshots/environment Implemented; timezone/calendar/ticker APIs deferred crypto/crypto/rand Entropy, UUID, unbiased integers, SHA/HMAC/PBKDF2, AES-GCM, Ed25519 Implemented; broader algorithms/key containers deferred net/dgram/dns TCP/Unix sockets, UDP, bounded DNS A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/NS/TXT/PTR/SRV, scoped resolver and destination policy Implemented tls/https Verified TLS, custom trust/client certificates, mutual TLS listener, certificate parsing/verification and negotiated metadata Implemented http/net/http Buffered and streaming HTTP/1.1/HTTP/2, pooled clients, cookies, redirects, WebSocket sessions Implemented; HTTP/3 excluded by user request child_process/os/exec Existing Commands.run, bounded captured output, timeout, joined execution Implemented functional option; interactive child handles deferred zlib/compress, archive/tar/zip Bounded gzip/zlib/deflate, ZIP/TAR immutable encode/decode Implemented; extraction/Brotli/Zstd deferred events/sync/channels/context/worker_threads Queue, State, Pool/Lease, joined parallel and Background contexts Implemented; no JS worker VM or detached tasks console/log/testing Explicit streams/structured JSON log, conditional checks, existing runner Implemented; interactive terminal and advanced diagnostics deferred XML/gob/ASN.1/MIME/image/database/sql Application/adaptor implementations using Bytes/streams/capabilities Deferred; not claimed as standard-package coverage vm/v8/module/async_hooks/inspector/repl, Go reflect/unsafe/plugin/syscall Ordinary suspending functions, checked source tooling, trusted host adapters Runtime-specific APIs omitted; no sandbox VM equivalent claimed The canonical callable surface lives on the linked package pages. Existing host/service APIs retain their identities. Deferred entries stay explicit; future implementations should add declarations to the Manuscript standard library sources and matching native implementations, semantic/boundary tests, and source-level compiler conformance fixtures together. The distribution remains self-contained with pinned vendored Go dependencies; native builds need no downloads.

title: Parallel operations
content:
Parallel operations# Guide index · Design index Use parallel to run a fixed set of operations at the same time. Pass functions in the named tasks argument. The API starts them and waits for every started operation, including cleanup, before returning. Passing a function call would execute it before parallel starts.
Calling parallel# Manuscript import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" type User: id: Int type Order: id: Int type UserError: case Missing type OrderError: case Unavailable interface Users: fn get(id: Int) -> Result[User, UserError] interface Orders: fn for_user(user_id: Int) -> Result[List[Order], OrderError] type Summary: user: User orders: List[Order] type LoadError: case Execution(cause: ExecutionError) case UserFailure(cause: UserError) case OrderFailure(cause: OrderError) fn load(user_id: Int, users: Users & Shareable, orders: Orders & Shareable) -> Result[Summary, LoadError]: let first = fn() -> Result[User, UserError]: return users.get(id: user_id) let second = fn() -> Result[List[Order], OrderError]: return orders.for_user(user_id: user_id) let [resA, resB] = try map_error( result: parallel(tasks: [first, second]), transform: fn(cause: ExecutionError) -> LoadError: return LoadError.Execution(cause: cause) ) let user = try map_error( result: resA, transform: fn(cause: UserError) -> LoadError: return LoadError.UserFailure(cause: cause) ) let user_orders = try map_error( result: resB, transform: fn(cause: OrderError) -> LoadError: return LoadError.OrderFailure(cause: cause) ) return ok(value: Summary(user: user, orders: user_orders)) Preparation# Before parallel starts anything, the caller evaluates arguments, task-pack entries, receivers, and captured values in written order. In this example, creating first and second captures snapshots of user_id and the shared services. Their bodies run later, after preparation succeeds and parallel starts the operations under its group execution context.
If preparation fails, no operation has started. Preparation may have external effects; the runtime does not undo them. Resources acquired during preparation require their own with scopes or acquisition API contracts.
Passing users.get(...) instead of a function executes that call during preparation; it is not a way to schedule the call concurrently, and it is a type error when the result is not callable. Ordinary calls inside a function remain sequential unless another concurrency API is invoked.
Concurrent scheduling and external effect order are nondeterministic. Sharing a resource does not imply that simultaneous operations on it are semantically valid; its API must serialize access or report unsupported concurrent use. See closures and resource sharing .
Ordered, typed results# A literal task pack is a fixed set of positions, each holding a zero-argument function. Positions may have different return types. The result preserves both their types and their input order. Here, resA is Result[User, UserError] and resB is Result[List[Order], OrderError], whichever operation finishes first.
The brackets do not force these different types into a homogeneous List[T]. Fixed positional packs require type-system support for heterogeneous inputs and outputs; parallel itself remains an API call, with no special concurrency keyword. Ordinary list literals outside a positional-pack contract keep their homogeneous list rules.
Pack arity is preserved: parallel(tasks: [first]) returns a one-position successful result, destructured with let [resA] = ...; an empty pack returns an empty successful result and starts no work. Destructuring a fixed positional result with the wrong number of positions is a compile error. Parenthesized binding patterns such as let (resA, resB) = ... are not supported. See destructuring bindings .
Return values and errors# parallel returns an outer Result[Pack, ExecutionError]. The outer Result describes execution of the whole group. Each operation’s return value is preserved unchanged at its position:
Function returns Result position contains String String Result[Stock, OrderError] Result[Stock, OrderError] Optional[String] Optional[String] A returned domain error(cause: ...) is ordinary completion. It does not stop sibling operations and is not flattened into the outer Result. In the example, explicit map_error calls translate execution and domain errors into LoadError before each try; propagation still requires one exact error type. Matching each Result directly is also valid. There is no source task-result wrapper beyond the outer Result.
No operation remains running after parallel exits, on any path. An operation fault or an expired timeout stops and joins the group; caller cancellation joins the group and then unwinds the caller. The complete rules are in joined groups .
Results follow the ordinary reference rules ; returning a resource does not keep it open. Unreturned references become eligible for garbage collection; the runtime does not recursively close arbitrary results or captures. Resource cleanup comes from with or an acquisition-specific delivery contract. See completion and acquisition .
The optional named timeout argument shortens the inherited deadline; it never waives joining. See timeouts . Functions must meet the concurrent sharing contract . The standard API contract fixes the callable/result mapping and legal uses of inferred packs; general source declaration syntax for packs is unsupported.

title: Expanded library conformance
content:
Expanded library conformance# Standard library guide · Coverage · Common contracts These executable checks exercise package behavior through the compiler and native runtime. Use the listed fixtures and tests to verify data handling, limits, errors, and cleanup.
tests/e2e/testdata/accept/library*.ms: compiler-to-native execution for exact JSON numbers, duplicate-key/depth failures, codecs, hashes, binary range limits, compression, ZIP, and generic sequential callbacks/function values. runtime/library_test.go: malformed strict encodings/numbers, signed 64-bit binary boundaries, surrogate/duplicate-key JSON validation, PBKDF2 vector, AEAD tampering, Ed25519, compression trailing bytes/bombs, ZIP/TAR paths/limits, exclusive filesystem writes, symlink-safe removal, HTTP duplicate headers/status/redirect/limits, and TCP half-close/round-trip, empty/oversized UDP datagrams, socket close/cancellation, and Network close interrupting active HTTP requests. tests/e2e/testdata/projects/library/main.ms: native CLI acquisition/use of FileSystem, Entropy, WallClock/Timestamp and System roots, including exclusive creation and removal. compiler/library_test.go: every registered function is importable, and opaque BigInt/Regex/Timestamp constructors are rejected. Existing host, service, compiler/cache and e2e tests remain required. The runtime embeds all new implementation sources for standalone builds and content pinning; test sources are excluded from the runtime bundle. Run go test ./..., go test -race ./runtime ./checker ./compiler ./tooling, and go vet ./... with Go 1.25 or newer. Native platform limitations are documented per package rather than inferred from a familiar module name. Written future requirements are not counted as passed tests.
Networking checks additionally cover scoped host/CIDR policy (including raw-IP bypass rejection), custom DNS records, listener reuse after timeout, Unix half-close, cancellation during acquisition, pooled cookies/redirects, HTTP/2, custom trust/hostname validation, mutual TLS, duplex streamed upload/response, decompressed WebSocket bounds and shutdown joining hijacked sessions. tests/e2e/testdata/projects/networking/main.ms exercises HTTP streaming and WebSocket echo through the compiler and an offline native build.

title: Joined groups
content:
Joined groups and execution outcomes# Guide index · Design index A parallel call waits for all the operations it started, including their cleanup. This waiting is called joining. A failure or timeout first asks unfinished work to stop, then waits for it. This page defines the exact lifecycle and which outcome the caller receives.
Terms# Term Meaning Operation One invocation of a function passed to a concurrency API: a tasks position or one Background.start submission Group The operations started by one parallel call Caller The execution that called the API; its context is the group’s fixed parent Joined Every started operation has finished its body and scope cleanup Execution errors# ExecutionError is exported by @std/tasks.ms; import it when naming the result type. Its Crashed payload uses OperationId, also exported by @std/tasks.ms. The standard declaration is:
Manuscript type ExecutionError: case TimedOut case Crashed(operation: OperationId, message: String) OperationId identifies runtime work for diagnostics; it does not grant scheduling, joining, or transfer authority. Secondary faults are retained in runtime diagnostics associated with the primary outcome.
Group lifecycle# Prepare. The caller evaluates arguments in written order. If preparation fails, no operation starts. See preparation . Start. An empty pack returns ok immediately and starts no work, whatever the timeout. A zero timeout on nonempty input stops the group before any operation starts. Otherwise parallel starts every position. Stop. The first of these triggers stops the group: an operation faults, the group’s timeout expires, or the caller’s context is cancelled or reaches its inherited deadline. Stopping prevents further starts and requests cancellation of unfinished operations. Returning a domain error(cause: ...) is ordinary completion and never stops the group. Join. The API waits for every started operation, including its cleanup. Joining is not bounded by the timeout; uncooperative work falls to host escalation . Report. After joining, the caller observes the first matching row: Condition after joining Caller observes The caller’s own context was cancelled or reached its inherited deadline The caller unwinds; no Result is delivered. Operation faults become secondary diagnostics An operation faulted, in its body or cleanup error(cause: Crashed(...)) for the primary fault The group’s timeout expired before every operation committed error(cause: TimedOut) Otherwise ok(value: ...) with each operation’s exact return value in input order The first row is checked against the caller’s context, not the group’s derived context. Both can report an expired deadline; only the group’s own timer yields TimedOut, and only to a caller that is still active.
The primary fault is the first fault committed to the group’s outcome. When operations fault concurrently, which one is primary depends on scheduling. Successful value order never does. Commitment of an operation’s outcome and acceptance of a stop are atomic; an operation that committed before the stop keeps its outcome. See atomic transitions .
Faults are isolated at the group boundary# An operation fault becomes Crashed rather than unwinding the caller. This is intentional and matches how hosts isolate a failed request: the faulted operation has already unwound through its own cleanup, its siblings have been cancelled and joined, and the caller is the only remaining place that can respond. No faulted state is resumed. The caller’s own faults still unwind it; try propagates only Result errors.
No per-operation cancellation# No source or adapter API cancels a single operation of a joined group. An adapter that ends a foreign call early reports that through the operation’s declared return value, such as an IoError; it is not a fault. Joined APIs therefore have no separate cancelled outcome. Background work, which can be cancelled individually, reports cancellation through WorkStatus.Cancelled.
See parallel operations , cancellation , and scope cleanup .

title: Cancellation and budgets
content:
Cancellation and budgets# Guide index · Design index Cancellation asks work to stop. It does not mean the work has already stopped; code must reach a checkpoint, leave its scopes, and finish cleanup. Request work follows the request’s execution lifetime. Accepted background work follows its background service’s lifetime.
Requests# Hosts signal requests, joined groups signal their operations, and background services expose cancellation of admitted work:
Manuscript let id = try background.start(operation: work) background.cancel(id: id) The submission fragment belongs to a function returning Result[U, StartError]; work must have the standard API contract callable type. Other application error types need explicit adaptation.
Successful Background.start admission yields an OperationId through Result[OperationId, StartError]. cancel(id: id) returns Unit, is idempotent for an admitted ID, and requests cancellation without joining. Dropping an ID has no effect. The service retains responsibility for work until it finishes or service shutdown joins it. IDs the service did not admit, including IDs from other services or from joined groups, and IDs whose status has been evicted are harmless no-ops; an ID never identifies unrelated work.
cancel, status, and close are receiver operations of the imported Background service; there are no ambient cancellation or join functions. Using an already-typed service does not require importing its otherwise unused type name. background.close() is the waiting boundary: it stops admission and performs the configured drain, cancellation, and joining sequence. A closed service stays closed through all aliases.
Late cancellation cannot overwrite an already committed completion. For background work, the first accepted stop reason determines WorkStatus, except that a programming fault during cleanup takes precedence and reports Crashed. Joined groups have no per-operation cancellation; their caller-visible outcomes are defined in joined groups .
Propagation and checkpoints# Cancellation is cooperative: stopped work unwinds at its next checkpoint. These are checkpoints:
runtime operation entry and completion; blocking I/O and other adapter calls; each loop back-edge, before the next iteration of for or while starts; an explicit check_cancelled() call. Loop checkpoints make CPU-bound loops respond promptly without source changes; they cost one poll of the context’s stop signal per iteration. check_cancelled() remains available for long straight-line work. It is an imported standard function, not a language intrinsic:
Manuscript import check_cancelled from "@std/tasks.ms" Importing it supplies the operation declaration; the runtime supplies the current execution context when it is called. Cleanup runs under a shielded context, so checkpoints inside cleanup do not observe the initiating cancellation. No checkpoint occurs between with acquisition and cleanup registration; see completion and acquisition .
Cancelling a request or current operation cancels its nested groups. Each group joins its operations, each operation runs its registered with cleanup, and the caller unwinds.
Background service cancellation reaches the work admitted under that service. Cancellation of a submitting request does not cancel accepted work, because the background lifetime was selected at admission. Cancellation before admission must not start work. Admission and acknowledgement can race with request cancellation; callers must use application idempotency keys if a retried submission must not duplicate work.
Completed external writes remain completed. Cancellation does not provide rollback; a transaction’s explicit resource contract does.
Cleanup is shielded from the initiating cancellation and expired work deadline. It may exceed that deadline; it retains capability authority and remains subject to host escalation . See foreign cancellation and cleanup faults .
Timeouts# Timeouts are named library arguments, not syntax annotations. Duration values come from the standard time API; naming Duration requires its own import from @std/time.ms.
parallel(tasks: [first, second], timeout: 2.seconds) sets one budget for the group’s execution, starting on API entry after argument preparation. timeout is the only budget argument; there is no absolute deadline argument.
Argument validation is part of the standard API contract ; zero-timeout and empty-input behavior is in joined groups . On expiry, the group stops, joins, and reports as defined in joined groups . Results are never delivered while work remains outstanding.
A timeout bounds ordinary work, not cleanup or joining. Foreign code that does not cooperate can delay joining indefinitely; host escalation is the final fallback. An API must not report successful joining merely because its timer expired.
To share one budget across several steps, put the steps in one function and give that function the budget. Nested groups inherit the deadline:
Manuscript let sync = fn() -> Result[Unit, SyncError]: try download_all(sources: sources) try upload_all(targets: targets) return ok(value: unit) let [outcome] = try parallel(tasks: [sync], timeout: 2.seconds) This fragment requires an enclosing Result[U, ExecutionError] function; outcome is the unchanged Result[Unit, SyncError]. Any parallel inside download_all or upload_all inherits the same deadline.
Deadlines# Hosts establish deadlines for application, session, CLI, and request execution contexts. Every operation inherits its fixed parent’s deadline. A joined group can only shorten it with timeout; nothing in source can extend an inherited deadline. The effective deadline is the earliest of the inherited deadline and any group timeout.
Budgets use the runtime’s monotonic timer, not a Clock capability or calendar time. A test runner may virtualize that timer; a fake Clock value does not affect execution budgets.
When the caller’s own deadline expires, the caller unwinds after its groups join; it does not receive TimedOut. Only a group’s own timeout produces TimedOut.
Background work inherits the service’s fixed execution context, including that context’s deadline. It does not inherit the submitting request’s deadline. A service cannot revive cancelled work or extend its host’s deadline. Its context is selected at construction, not at each call to start.
Deadline configuration is a host operation. There are no source task handles to mutate, deadline annotations on functions, or absolute deadline arguments. See background services for drain budgets and adapter contexts .

title: Runtime contracts
content:
Runtime concurrency contracts# Guide index · Design index This page is for runtime implementers. The runtime provides the mechanisms to start, stop, join, and synchronize work. Library objects decide whether to accept work, how to report failures, and how shutdown proceeds.
Source programs use standard concurrency APIs . The compiler checks their types, safe callable sharing, and cleanup contracts. Internal contexts and scheduler mechanisms add no source names or compiler bounds.
Atomic transitions# Each runtime operation has a stable OperationId, a fixed execution parent, a stop signal, an effective deadline, and one completion outcome. Cancellation acceptance and completion commitment have atomic linearization points. There is no reparenting or task-transfer transaction.
Background admission, closing admission, and reserving capacity must be coordinated atomically. If admission wins, the service tracks the accepted operation even if the submitting request stops before receiving its ID. If closure or cancellation wins before admission, the operation never starts. Capacity reservations are released exactly once: on rejection, or when the operation’s completion commits. Pending failure reports have their own bound and do not hold admission capacity.
Completion is not published until registered cleanup and nested joins have finished. A pending cancellation accepted before commitment prevents an ordinary successful outcome from being delivered. Already committed outcomes are stable.
User callbacks, failure reporters, resource cleanup, and joining run outside transition locks. Shutdown is idempotent; concurrent calls to close() observe one shutdown sequence and all wait for it to finish.
An operation must not join itself or an execution ancestor. Closing its own background service, including from nested parallel descendants or reporter callbacks joined by that service, faults before initiating shutdown. Check the fixed execution-parent chain, not just the current operation ID. Hosts close services from outside their admitted work. Cross-service cyclic shutdown is invalid library usage and must be avoided by host shutdown ordering.
The conformance suite uses controlled barriers and race stress for admission versus closure, cancellation versus completion, and concurrent shutdown. See semantic tests .
Completion and resource acquisition# Completion records an operation’s outcome after its body, nested concurrency groups, and registered cleanup finish. Cancellation and completion commitment race atomically; a late stop does not overwrite a committed outcome.
Parallel results are ordinary values, with references to existing objects where appropriate. If the group fails, unreturned references are released for garbage collection. The runtime does not recursively call close() on arbitrary result fields or closure captures: those references may alias resources still used elsewhere. Cleanup responsibility comes from explicit with registration or an acquisition API’s delivery contract, not a result-ownership escrow.
A native acquisition API must close a newly acquired resource if cancellation or a fault prevents it from being delivered. Successful acquisition and registration by with form one protected sequence: no cancellation checkpoint may occur between delivery to the binding and registration of its close() action.
Race outcome Required handling Cancellation wins before delivery Acquisition adapter closes the undelivered resource with acquires successfully Register cleanup before exposing cancellation Cancellation arrives after registration Unwind the scope and run registered cleanup Closure/result retains a resource reference after scope exit The reference remains valid memory; operations report that the resource is closed A source helper returning an open resource must handle resources it acquires but fails to return. Its resource factory/delivery contract is explicit. Merely returning a resource reference cannot cancel a with registration or keep the resource open.
Background operations have no resource-valued result delivery; each operation manages acquisitions through its own scopes. See adapter acquisition and resource release .
Adapter execution contexts# Generated calls carry a hidden execution context. An adapter observes the current operation’s fixed parent context, cancellation signal, deadline, and cleanup mode.
Parallel operations derive contexts from their caller. Background operations derive contexts from their service’s construction-time context. The runtime does not substitute the submitting request’s context merely because start was invoked from that request.
Fixed parent relationships can use Go context derivation directly; there is no movable cancellation ancestry or separate ownership graph. Operation IDs support diagnostics and traces. Go context documentation Cleanup receives a shielded context that ignores the initiating cancellation and expired ordinary-work deadline. It preserves authority; a host cleanup/escalation policy is separate from the request budget. Adapters must support safe resource closure and must not return from a cancelled operation while its foreign work is still outstanding.
See blocking adapters , deadlines , and runtime/library layering .
Host escalation# Joining and cleanup wait for work to actually end. The runtime cannot safely terminate an arbitrary goroutine, so work that ignores cancellation can delay a join forever. Escalation is the host’s last resort for that case. It ends the process; it never reports the stuck work as joined.
Each host runs one watchdog. It starts when the host begins shutdown or receives a stop request, such as SIGINT, SIGTERM, or server shutdown. Ordinary timeouts and request deadlines do not start it. Once started, it covers every waiting boundary: group joins, Background.close(), with cleanup, and resource close.
Setting Default Grace period after the stop request 30 seconds A second stop request during the grace period Escalates immediately Hosts may configure a different grace period. A zero grace period escalates on the first stop request whenever work is still outstanding.
On escalation the host:
writes one diagnostic per outstanding operation to host stderr, containing its OperationId, the source location of its current suspension, and its accepted stop reason; writes any retained primary and secondary fault diagnostics; terminates the process without running further cleanup. The CLI host exits 70 and labels the exit as incomplete cleanup. Conformance treats an escalated exit as a failure of the program, not as successful shutdown. See CLI exit and shutdown , HTTP shutdown , and cleanup faults .

title: Modules and capabilities
content:
Modules and capabilities guide# Design index Organize code into files, choose what each file exports, and pass external services into the functions that need them. A capability is an object that grants access to a service such as files or the network. Adapter pages explain the planned bridge to foreign code.
Reading order# 1. Module boundaries # Modules, exports, and imports Boundary contracts 2. Authority and effects # Explicit capability authority — Make file, network, and other external access visible in function inputs. Inferred effects and call relationships — Follow external behavior through a function and the functions it calls. 3. Foreign adapter contracts # Adapter manifests — Declare a foreign adapter API and the facts the compiler trusts. Foreign values and the trust boundary — Validate foreign values before they enter Manuscript. Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition — Arrange for foreign calls and resource acquisition to respond to stopping.

title: Module boundaries
content:
Module boundaries# Guide index · Design index Each .ms file is a module. Import individual declarations from other files and use export for declarations other modules may use. Boundary contracts describe the data and operations those modules expose.
Modules, exports, and imports Boundary contracts

title: Modules, exports, and imports
content:
Modules, exports, and imports# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Each .ms file is a module: a group of declarations with its own boundary. Use export to make a declaration available to other files and import to bring an individual exported declaration into the current file. Resolved file paths identify modules. There is no module declaration, wildcard import, or cyclic module dependency.
Names and declaration order# Import multiple symbols with import { Name, OtherName } from "./module.ms". The braces contain a nonempty, comma-separated list; a trailing comma and multiple lines are permitted. Each name selects an export and enters the same module namespace as a single-symbol import. Duplicate names and collisions are errors. Single-symbol import Name from "./module.ms" remains supported.
Types, interfaces, module functions, and imported symbols share one ordinary module namespace. Duplicate names, import/declaration collisions, and function overloading are rejected. Imports and declarations may appear in any order: collect names and signatures before checking bodies, so forward references and mutually recursive functions work. Type layout cycles follow the separate recursive data rule , not module-cycle rules.
The intrinsic core type names are only Bool, Int, Float, String, Unit, and Never. They cover primitive literals, ordinary arithmetic, and function/control-flow typing. The compiler bounds Shareable, Equal, and Hashable also have fixed identities. A module declaration, import, or type parameter cannot redefine these names. They are resolved names rather than lexical keywords. Ordinary local bindings may shadow outer names, but a shadowed value name cannot be used as a type.
All other standard declarations are explicit imports from the compiler-supplied @std directory, including Decimal, Bytes, collections, Optional, Result, Closeable, and runtime/host APIs. The standard imports and API typing page lists their modules. These names are ordinary exports: without an import, a module may declare its own Result, List, or parallel. Import/declaration collisions still fail. Compiler support follows the canonical standard declaration identity, never its spelling. Optional/Result case shorthand becomes visible when its alternative type is imported and follows ordinary lookup and ambiguity rules; qualify Result[T, E].error when a local spelling shadows it.
An unqualified case shorthand is considered only when ordinary lexical name lookup finds no binding or declaration of that name. The candidate cases come from visible alternative types declared in the module or imported by name. Exactly one candidate is required; an expected type cannot choose among multiple candidates. Type.Case explicitly selects the nominal alternative. Match-pattern case lookup uses the scrutinee type, as specified by pattern matching .
Import renaming, namespace imports, re-exports, and wildcard imports have no syntax. A dotted type path does not create a module namespace; callers import each needed exported type by its own name. Qualified alternative constructors remain supported. Module-level executable statements and bindings are rejected; local-value examples elsewhere are function-body fragments.
A visible contract# The file src/domain/customers.ms exports a nominal identifier type:
Manuscript export type CustomerId: value: String The file src/main.ms imports the individual symbol:
Manuscript import CustomerId from "./domain/customers.ms" Exporting a type makes it part of the module boundary; an internal declaration stays within that boundary. A relative import resolves from the importing file’s directory. Paths include the .ms extension and identify a file, with no implicit directory entry or extension lookup.
Public signature closure# An exported function, data type, or contract cannot expose an internal nominal type through a parameter, result, field, case payload, generic bound, or operation signature. Check the transitive public type surface through nested applications and exposed data members. Exported types from other modules may appear in a public signature without automatically re-exporting their names. Generic parameters themselves are not private nominal declarations.
Manuscript type PrivateToken: value: String # Rejected: callers cannot name the internal result type. export fn issue() -> PrivateToken: return PrivateToken(value: "token") Exporting a record exposes every field and its constructor; exporting an alternative exposes every case and payload field; exporting an interface exposes every operation. Opaque exports and selective member visibility are unsupported. See public data surfaces .
An impl belongs to the receiver’s nominal data type’s defining module and becomes available when that module is loaded. Imported public contracts can be implemented there. Concrete and generic implementations do not re-export declarations. Duplicate or overlapping receiver/instantiated contract pairs are rejected, ignoring bounds when checking overlap; bounds cannot choose competing implementations. These coherence rules prevent behavior from depending on unrelated imports.
Standard-library imports# Manuscript import List from "@std/collections.ms" import { Result, map_error } from "@std/result.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" @std is always available without an [aliases] entry and cannot be overridden. Importing one export does not bring its signature’s other type names into scope. For example, importing parallel permits matching its inferred result, but writing Result or ExecutionError in an annotation requires their own imports. Importing a contract supplies its interface, not an authority-bearing value.
Optional aliases# A project-root ms.toml can define file and directory aliases. With @domain mapped to ./src/domain and @customers mapped to ./src/domain/customers.ms, either import selects the same exported type:
Manuscript import CustomerId from "@domain/customers.ms" Manuscript import CustomerId from "@customers" Each example is an alternative import spelling for the same CustomerId. Aliases change how a path is written; module identity and visibility still follow the resolved file. Relative imports and aliases that resolve to the same file refer to the same module.
Missing files, unknown aliases, missing exports, and cyclic module dependencies are compile errors. The project configuration defines alias resolution and filesystem identity.
See source structure and boundary contracts .
Next: Boundary contracts

title: Boundary contracts
content:
Boundary contracts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A module boundary tells callers which data and operations they may use. Keep those exported contracts explicit so a caller can see inputs, outputs, expected errors, and required access to external services.
Example: ordinary operations# The following uses application-defined Item, Stock, and OrderError types:
Manuscript interface Inventory: fn check(items: List[Item]) -> Result[Stock, OrderError] fn check_stock( inventory: Inventory & Shareable, items: List[Item], ) -> Result[Stock, OrderError]: return inventory.check(items: items) let first = fn() -> Result[Stock, OrderError]: return check_stock(inventory: inventory, items: items) let [stock] = try parallel(tasks: [first]) The closure/call fragment belongs to an enclosing function returning Result[U, ExecutionError]. To propagate OrderError in the same function, first translate it explicitly with map_error; parallel gives a complete example.
The operation accepts its capability explicitly and returns the unchanged domain Result. In this concurrent example the enclosing function’s inventory input has the shared Inventory & Shareable type, preserving the receiver proof in the captured capability and across check_stock’s parameter. A plain Inventory view would support sequential calls but could not be captured by this concurrent closure. The caller chooses concurrent execution through an ordinary API. The outer try handles execution failure; stock still contains the inventory domain outcome. The captured data must also meet the API’s sharing requirements.
Submitting work to a Background service instead chooses that service’s fixed lifetime. Passing a reference does not transfer cleanup or keep a scoped resource open.
See parallel operations , fixed work lifetimes , and derived effects .
Previous: Modules, exports, and imports · Next: Explicit capability authority

title: Authority and effects
content:
Authority and effects# Guide index · Design index A capability gives a function access to an external service. An effect describes what the function can do through that access, including through other functions it calls. Read authority first, then the rules for inferred effect summaries.
Explicit capability authority — Make file, network, and other external access visible in function inputs. Inferred effects and call relationships — Follow external behavior through a function and the functions it calls.

title: Explicit capability authority
content:
Explicit capability authority# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A capability is a passed-in object that lets a function use an external service. For example, a function that reads files receives a file service rather than silently accessing a global filesystem. Look at capability parameters to see which services the function can use.
Capabilities represent external authority such as storage, network access, a clock, or a model client. They are explicit inputs. Manuscript source has no ambient application access to these services. Standard shareable capability implementations support concurrent calls; shared internal state must be synchronized. Resource methods also enforce closed state.
The language requires explicit authority inputs. Tooling still needs a precise classification rule for distinguishing a capability interface from a pure operation contract, including wrappers and function values that retain authority. Until that rule is settled, a diagram cannot claim to enumerate all reachable authority from parameter names alone.
Sharing an implementation# A shareable network or storage implementation can receive concurrent calls. Its mutable internal state must be synchronized. References do not extend a resource’s open lifetime; methods coordinate active calls with close.
Passing a capability explicitly makes the dependency visible to reviewers and compiler-derived diagrams. It also makes it possible to substitute controlled implementations when testing.
See resource sharing and the foreign-code trust boundary .
Previous: Boundary contracts · Next: Inferred effects and call relationships

title: Inferred effects and call relationships
content:
Inferred effects and call relationships# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index An effect describes external behavior reachable from a function. If a function calls another function that writes to storage, that write is also part of the caller’s effect summary.
Transitive analysis# The compiler follows calls and combines their known effects. The vocabulary is read, write, external-call, and unknown.
Call target How it contributes to the summary Known source target Include its effects, including the effects of its callees. Several known targets Include the union of their effects. Unresolved function value or contract call Include unknown; do not treat it as having no effects. Foreign adapter Use its declared summary, which foreign code is trusted to honor. These summaries describe reachable behavior. Manuscript has no source syntax that promises static purity or restricts a function to an effect set.
Effects and cancellation# Cancellation can stop unfinished work and run cleanup. It cannot undo an external write that already completed. Review both a boundary’s returned errors and its external effects when deciding how to retry or recover.
See diagram views and architecture changes .
Previous: Explicit capability authority · Next: Adapter manifests
