title: Foreign adapter contracts
content:
Foreign adapter contracts# Guide index · Design index Adapters connect Manuscript code to foreign implementations such as Go. These design contracts explain how an adapter declares its API, validates values, and cooperates with cancellation and cleanup. Check implementation coverage before relying on external adapters.
Adapter manifests — Declare a foreign adapter API and the facts the compiler trusts. Foreign values and the trust boundary — Validate foreign values before they enter Manuscript. Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition — Arrange for foreign calls and resource acquisition to respond to stopping.

title: Adapter manifests
content:
Adapter manifests# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index An adapter connects a Manuscript operation contract to a trusted Go implementation. Its manifest declares the facts the compiler needs, including whether its receiver is safe to share concurrently. A standard adapter must implement the standard API rules , rather than change them.
Interface modules and package direction# A local adapter ships a .ms interface module containing exported data and contracts, with no function bodies, tests, or implementation blocks. It may import standard modules through @std/...ms and other registered interface modules. Signatures use intrinsic types, explicitly imported standard types, or public declarations in that interface graph, never application-defined types. Source imports interface declarations through ordinary .ms paths.
Each interface module generates a separate Go schema package. The native adapter imports schemas and runtime; the application imports schemas, adapters, and runtime. Schemas never import adapters or application packages. Standard schemas belong to the pinned standard-library/runtime distribution. This prevents Go import cycles. An application contract over application Money types can have source implementations or explicitly wrap an adapter interface using data conversion, but cannot directly bind a separately compiled native adapter to application types.
Native receivers remain opaque. The host creates them and exposes contract views. Source fakes implement the interface contract for their own concrete type under ordinary coherence. The standard CLI host supplies only its enumerated roots; custom host construction still needs a concrete contract.
Manifest version 1# The manifest is UTF-8 TOML with closed fields; unknown keys, duplicate bindings, unsupported versions, missing fields, and signature mismatches are compile errors.
toml format = 1 interface = "./files.ms" go_package = "example.org/nativefiles" go_version = "v1.0.0" go_checksum = "h1:example-content-checksum" [[bindings]] contract = "Files" operation = "open" symbol = "Open" effects = ["read", "external-call"] shareable_receiver = true cancellation = "cooperative" acquisition = "dispose-undelivered" disposer = "DisposeFile" This is a schema example; its package and checksum are placeholders. Interface paths resolve relative to the manifest, and the Go fields pin the native package.
Binding field Rule contract, operation, symbol Select an exported interface/standard contract operation and an exported Go symbol; bind each operation exactly once effects Explicit subset of read, write, external-call, and unknown; use [] for an empty summary shareable_receiver Required audited boolean, consistent across the receiver’s operations; true permits shared views, false permits only plain views cancellation cooperative, completion-only, or nonblocking acquisition none or dispose-undelivered disposer Required exported symbol for dispose-undelivered; forbidden for none Resource bindings include a matching close operation. A standard host boundary requiring sharing rejects a nonshareable receiver. Source code can still explicitly discard a native receiver’s sharing guarantee by constructing a plain view.
Generated bindings# Interface declarations determine parameter labels/order and result types; manifests do not duplicate them. Each Go operation receives the hidden execution context, opaque receiver, and generated parameters in declaration order, then returns the generated exact result type.
A disposer receives a shielded context and the acquired generated resource value. It completes release before returning. The fixed constructor New accepts runtime HostInputs and returns an opaque receiver token. Standard host packages follow the same convention.
The concrete Go declarations for HostInputs, receiver tokens, results, and disposers still need a pinned runtime ABI. Symbol/type mismatches must fail validation before linking; referring to an ABI alone does not define those declarations.
Wrappers enforce the foreign value invariants . Disposal of an undelivered acquisition finishes before unwind, and no wrapper returns with outstanding foreign work. Native code requires separate cancellation, sharing, conversion, and release tests.
Acceptance requires a minimal interface/native-adapter/application fixture whose Go builds without cycles, rejection of interface imports from the application, source fake implementations, and invalid-value/acquisition race fixtures.

title: Foreign values and the trust boundary
content:
Foreign values and the trust boundary# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index An adapter must validate foreign values before exposing them as Manuscript values. For example, a Go string may contain invalid UTF-8, while a Manuscript String may not. Conversion must preserve every guarantee of the source type.
Adapters validate UTF-8, alternative tags and payloads, required non-nil values, and numeric ranges. They preserve immutability and copy buffers unless exclusive ownership can be established. Mutable Go storage, unrestricted Go interfaces, and runtime task internals are not exposed to Manuscript source. Raw Go dependencies may use ambient authority, so source capability checking is not a sandbox for adapter code.
Preserving invariants# A converted string must be valid UTF-8. An alternative must carry a valid tag. A buffer must not become mutable through a hidden Go alias after being exposed as immutable source data. Exclusive native buffer transfer is an optimization only when the adapter proves no mutable Go aliases remain; source code has no move or ownership checker.
An invalid foreign value is a programming fault with the operation, expected type, and value path in its diagnostic. It is not an expected input error: untrusted data should remain Bytes until explicitly decoded. The manifest binding defines wrapper validation and release obligations.
See Go representations and text and byte values .
Previous: Adapter manifests · Next: Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition

title: Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition
content:
Foreign cancellation and resource acquisition# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A blocking adapter must pass cancellation to its underlying operation and wait until outstanding work actually ends. Returning early while a foreign call keeps running would break Manuscript’s join and cleanup guarantees.
Each blocking adapter defines how cancellation reaches the underlying operation and when cleanup completes. An uncancellable foreign call remains outstanding until it finishes; wrapping it in a goroutine and returning early violates joining guarantees. Host escalation is the final fallback. Adapters report acquired resources even when cancellation races with acquisition, so the runtime can close newly acquired undelivered resources.
An acquisition race# Suppose a connection is acquired just as cancellation is accepted. The acquisition adapter must close it if delivery loses the race. Once delivered into with, cleanup registration has no intervening cancellation checkpoint. This contract applies to newly acquired resources, not arbitrary result references that may alias existing objects.
See stable adapter contexts and result commitment .
Previous: Foreign values and the trust boundary

title: Compiler design
content:
Compiler design guide# Design index This chapter is for compiler contributors and readers who need to understand builds. Follow a program from parsing and checking to generated Go, then read how builds are pinned and tested. For ordinary application code, you can start with project configuration .
Reading order# 1. Parsing and checking # Compilation pipeline — Follow a program from project loading to the native executable. Type checking and source contracts Scope and capture checking Typed intermediate representation 2. Go lowering # Function and concurrency API lowering Source guarantees and Go representations Evaluation order and call preparation Cleanup and fault lowering 3. Builds and dependencies # Project configuration and module paths — Set the source directory, entry file, and import paths in ms.toml. Pinned dependencies and deterministic output — Record versions and inputs so builds use the intended distribution. Caching and Go package boundaries — Understand what can be cached and when Go must rebuild a package. 4. Conformance and scope # Core-language fixtures — Check complete modules and rejected variants.
Runtime binding fixtures — Check standard imports, sharing, and host bindings.
Semantic conformance tests — Test required behavior, including cancellation races and cleanup.
Complete-program conformance — Check that guarantees work together in complete applications.
Scope and implementation order — Find remaining decisions and the order in which work depends on them.

title: Parsing and checking
content:
Parsing and checking# Guide index · Design index Before generating Go, the compiler reads the source and checks names, types, scopes, and captured values. It records the checked facts in a typed intermediate representation, or typed IR. These pages explain each stage.
Compilation pipeline — Follow a program from project loading to the native executable. Type checking and source contracts Scope and capture checking Typed intermediate representation

title: Compilation pipeline
content:
Compilation pipeline# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler turns Manuscript source into Go, then uses Go to build a native executable. Before generating code, it checks Manuscript’s own rules; Go accepting the generated program is not enough to prove the source is valid.
Following a program through compilation# Load the project. Read ms.toml, locate the entry .ms file, and follow imports. Resolve relative paths and aliases to canonical file identities so different spellings of one path identify the same module. Parse the source. Read declarations, expressions, and indented blocks. Each file is already a module; it needs no module declaration. Resolve imports and names. Find exported declarations and reject module dependency cycles. Check the program. Validate types, scopes, captured values, and source contracts. Record checked facts. Produce a typed intermediate representation, or typed IR. It records evaluation order, closure captures, cleanup scopes, effects, and source locations. Generate Go and build. Translate those facts into Go and invoke the pinned Go toolchain with the versioned runtime and adapters. Package boundaries in the design# The compiler is written in Go. The backend design emits one application Go package and separate packages for adapter interface schemas. Schema packages cannot depend on the application package; see adapter bindings for the dependency direction.
This page defines required behavior. It does not prescribe a parser library, syntax-tree schema, or internal package layout. External adapters remain design work; implementation coverage identifies the working compiler’s limits.
Continue with project configuration , type checking , scope and capture checking , and typed IR .
Next: Type checking and source contracts

title: Type checking and source contracts
content:
Type checking and source contracts# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The type checker decides whether source operations satisfy Manuscript’s rules before the compiler generates Go. The fact that a value can be represented in Go does not make every use of it legal in Manuscript.
Required checks# Accept source according to the normative grammar ; then resolve names and check the compatibility rules . Each rejected program must identify the violated source rule. Backend assignability and Go compiler acceptance are not substitutes for those checks.
Source rule Checker responsibility Explicit function signatures Check parameter and result types against calls and returns Names and scopes Collect module signatures, reject duplicate names, resolve locals in declaration order, and check assignments against fixed mutable binding types Operators Use the closed precedence and operand table; enforce Bool conditions and short-circuit evaluation without implicit numeric conversion Function values Preserve parameter labels/order and exact types; require explicit specialization of generic function values and explicit anonymous signatures Return completeness Allow Unit fallthrough/bare returns; reject reachable non-Unit fallthrough; track Never and function-local loop/return boundaries Argument labels Resolve an omitted label for a single-parameter function; require labels for multi-parameter functions and constructors; reject unknown labels, duplicate arguments, and missing required arguments, including function-value calls List literals Require the canonical standard List import; check homogeneous shareable element types and use annotations or the expected parameter type for empty lists Parallel API packs Check zero-argument functions in literal tasks: [...] packs and preserve each position’s exact return type; see parallel operations Destructuring bindings Check positional arity, record fields, renaming, nesting, and duplicate bindings; infer each local’s type independently; see destructuring bindings Nominal records and tagged alternatives Preserve type identity and check declared fields and cases Expected types Propagate annotations/substituted constructor context through literals, fields, and parentheses; reject incomplete types and avoid result-context inference for generic calls Exhaustive match Check the scrutinee alternative, positional payload arity/bindings, exact qualified cases, missing alternatives, duplicate arms, and final nonredundant wildcard Generic bounds Check arity, invariant arguments, argument-only inference, every nested application’s bounds, and generic bodies under their declared assumptions Recursive types and specialization Reject inline storage cycles and expanding generic type/function specialization, including mutual calls and specialized function values; permit regular recursion guarded by immutable collection storage Equality and hashing Derive only the specified properties; reject Float/collection keys and data containing ineligible components Explicit implementations Match substituted operation names/labels/order/types exactly, check generic bodies and receiver-determined parameters, reject overlap ignoring bounds, enforce defining-module coherence, and require explicit contract views Standard bindings and sharing Resolve the minimal intrinsic prelude and explicit standard imports by canonical declaration identity, distinguish plain and shared contract views, require receiver sharing proof only for shared views, reject implicit guarantee removal or recovery, and retain callable sharing proofs independently of function signature identity Public signatures Reject internal nominal types leaking through exported fields, signatures, bounds, or operation surfaces Iteration Admit List/Set/Map only, bind immutable element/MapEntry types, evaluate iterable once, and reject loop control outside the current function’s loops Result propagation Recognize the canonical standard Result identity; require the same exact error type at a try expression in the current function; do not infer missing operand type arguments backward String literals Validate escape/scalar syntax, check interpolated scalar eligibility, and preserve left-to-right evaluation These requirements derive from the core language guide , with accepted and rejected modules in core conformance . The rules specify observable inference and compatibility; checker data structures and internal pass organization remain implementation choices. A module-level test body is a zero-parameter Unit function for static checking: ordinary local scopes, bare-return/fallthrough rules, and Result propagation restrictions apply. Test discovery and runner execution remain separate tooling contracts.
Type information feeds typed IR , generated representations , and structural tools .
Previous: Compilation pipeline · Next: Scope and capture checking

title: Scope and capture checking
content:
Scope and closure checking# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler checks which names a closure captures and which cleanup actions each scope must run. It does not prove that every resource reference stays within its open lifetime. Runtime closed-state checks still matter.
Source operation Required check with initializer Require the concrete, contract-view, or generic-bound proof defined by Closeable ; register the resolved operation Scope exit Identify exited cleanup scopes for return, loop exits, errors, faults, and cancellation Closure creation Identify captured bindings and snapshot them once Assignment to captured outer local Reject implicit shared mutable cells Reassignment and branch scope Require initializers, enforce let/var, and keep branch-local names inside their scope Concurrency eligibility Retain type-level sharing through generic data/shared-contract boundaries; check callable value proofs separately at standard API entry Callable proof erasure Retain safe local capture proofs for direct standard callable arguments; erase them through generic forwarding, fields, and source function parameter/result boundaries; function types never satisfy Shareable Call-only standard bindings For resolved standard declaration identities only, reject extracting parallel, Background constructors, or Background.start as function/bound-method values; validate every direct call’s required callable proofs. Same-spelled application functions follow ordinary function-value rules Capturing a scoped resource is not a compile error merely because it may outlive its scope. Methods report closed state at runtime. Storing or returning a reference does not transfer a cleanup action. There are no moved-binding states, borrow lifetimes, partial-move restrictions, or source task-ownership checks.
See with scopes , closures , and typed IR .

title: Typed intermediate representation
content:
Typed intermediate representation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index After checking source, the compiler stores the program in a typed intermediate representation, or typed IR. It keeps the facts code generation and tooling need, rather than trying to rediscover them later.
Fact Why it remains explicit Types, sharing bounds, and resolved operations Preserve plain/shared contract identity, receiver-sharing proofs, and substituted generic implementation selection; select representations and validate API contracts Argument names and parameters Resolve omitted single-parameter labels and preserve checked parameter mapping and written evaluation order Lists and fixed positional packs Retain homogeneous element types or each position’s exact type Destructuring Retain shapes, field bindings, and extraction order Closure environments Record snapshot captures and receiver references with registration and cleanup scopes Resolve close() and unwind exited scopes Effects and concurrency API boundaries Derive host/service relationships and diagrams Source locations Connect generated behavior back to source There are no ownership-transfer instructions or affine states. Runtime operation IDs and fixed execution parents belong to the concurrency runtime; source IR records the API calls and contexts used to establish them.
See pipeline , evaluation lowering , and metadata .

title: Go lowering
content:
Go lowering# Guide index · Design index Lowering translates checked Manuscript into Go. The generated code must preserve evaluation order, closure captures, concurrency, and block-level cleanup. These pages describe how the compiler carries those guarantees across the translation.
Function and concurrency API lowering Source guarantees and Go representations Evaluation order and call preparation Cleanup and fault lowering

title: Function and concurrency API lowering
content:
Function and concurrency API lowering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler turns functions, closures, and contract methods into Go calls. Each generated call carries an internal execution context for cancellation and deadlines. A closure also keeps its captured snapshots in an environment object. Source code still has one function kind; every function can wait for work.
Explicitly imported parallel, and Background methods lower as typed library calls. Scheduling, cancellation, joining, admission, and shutdown policy live in the standard library/runtime rather than an expanded source intrinsic list. Native runtime primitives start goroutines, signal cancellation, join completion, and synchronize state. The compiler checks the resolved standard API declarations and their callable-proof requirements; a same-spelled application declaration acquires none of that special typing. There is no special background class or task transfer. Go concurrency specification The hidden context carries the current operation, fixed cancellation parent, effective deadline, and cleanup mode. Parallel operations derive it from the caller; a background service supplies its stored construction-time context. Creating a closure does not capture the caller’s execution context as a hidden source dependency; invocation supplies the execution context. Each loop back-edge polls the context’s stop signal and unwinds through the iteration’s cleanup if it has stopped; cleanup contexts are shielded, so the poll never fires during cleanup.
The frontend implements the standard library’s fixed heterogeneous callable/result mapping , preserving inferred packs through locals, generic helpers, and Result matches. This is type-system/interop support for the API. General source pack syntax is unsupported; the standard mapping is normative and cannot be altered by an adapter manifest.
Policy can be implemented over native primitives. No goroutine-ID lookup, custom coroutine lowering, stack implementation, or memory collector is required. See parallel and background layering .

title: Source guarantees and Go representations
content:
Source guarantees and Go representations# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A Go value must preserve the behavior promised by its Manuscript type. For example, generated Int arithmetic must detect overflow, and generated collections must prevent mutation through an alias. The compiler and runtime enforce guarantees that unrestricted Go values do not provide on their own.
The frontend enforces semantics that Go representations do not provide:
Source guarantee Go lowering Checked Int int64 with checked operations and conversions Decimal Versioned finite decimal implementation honoring the coefficient/exponent grid, exact literals, and per-operator rounding in the numeric contract Valid UTF-8 String Validated construction and conversion; no raw string escape Immutable bytes and collections Encapsulated storage; copies or exclusive adapter transfer Ordered maps and sets Ordered wrappers Tagged alternatives Generated typed tags and payloads; exhaustive frontend checking Guarded recursive data Inline records/alternatives with immutable container indirection; reject invalid layouts before Go emission Value equality and hashing Generated operations for eligible types Explicit contract implementation Frontend selection of a unique applicable concrete/generic implementation, then Go interfaces and wrappers Closures and resource references GC-retained environments, snapshot captures, and synchronized native closed-state checks Lexical cleanup Explicit with registrations, shielded Closeable.close(), and scope unwind operations Parallel results Typed positional packs preserving each exact return value Use Go generics where suitable; generated typed pack wrappers handle heterogeneous parallel results without exposing unchecked casts to source.
Representation boundaries# For example, emitting a raw int64 does not supply checked arithmetic. A raw Go slice does not establish immutable source bytes. The frontend and runtime cooperate with generated wrappers and operations to preserve those contracts.
Explicit view constructors create contract wrappers. Plain and shared views may use the same runtime representation, while the frontend and IR retain distinct identities and sharing proofs. Go interface assignment or runtime receiver inspection cannot restore an erased proof.
Generic implementation bodies use checked substitutions; Go method selection cannot resolve overlapping source implementations. Function wrappers retain source labels/order in frontend identity even though Go erases labels. Check recursive storage rules before emission; a generated-Go error is not a source type check.
Int division/remainder overflow handling, Float non-finite outcomes, Decimal underflow/overflow, and checked truncation conversions follow runtime numeric outcomes , including parameterized runtime operands. Unchecked Go casts or a decimal package’s defaults do not establish these semantics.
See foreign conversions , type checking , and scope and capture checking .
Previous: Function and concurrency API lowering · Next: Evaluation order and call preparation

title: Evaluation order and call preparation
content:
Evaluation order and call preparation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Named arguments can be written in a different order from the parameters in a declaration. Generated Go must still evaluate them in the order the caller wrote. Resolve the names first, including an omitted label on a single-parameter function. Evaluate each argument into a temporary value, then arrange those values for the Go call. Preserve short-circuit behavior too.
A tasks: [...] literal constructs a typed pack of function values in source order. Constructing closures snapshots their local captures; it does not invoke their bodies. If preparation fails, the concurrency API has not started work. Native acquisitions during preparation retain their explicit delivery/cleanup contracts.
Ordinary list elements evaluate left to right; an existing list argument evaluates once. Destructuring evaluates the initializer once and extracts bindings in written pattern order, retaining each positional result type.
A with initializer evaluates once, then registers the initialized object’s resolved close method before exposing another cancellation checkpoint. Later alias assignment does not change that receiver.
See source call order , operation preparation , and with scopes .

title: Cleanup and fault lowering
content:
Cleanup and fault lowering# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The compiler registers Closeable.close() after successful with initialization and generates cleanup for each block exit. A Go defer that runs only when a function returns is not enough for resources whose lifetime ends at a nested block or loop iteration.
The backend implements scope-exit order and fault selection as follows:
Use private tagged Go panics for nonlocal language faults and cancellation. Give each function with active registrations a local scope stack and one deferred unwind handler. Normal block exits drain and pop explicitly; panic paths drain the remaining stack. Pop an action before invoking it, and recover each close separately so a secondary panic cannot skip later cleanup. Give cleanup a context without the initiating cancellation or expired work deadline, retaining authority and cleanup mode. Rethrow the selected fault or cancellation after draining, until its operation or host boundary handles it. Recoverable unexpected adapter panics become programming faults; concurrency boundaries report them as Crashed. Active parallel APIs join before the caller’s cleanup begins. Ordinary values and captures are never recursively disposed. Process-fatal out-of-memory or stack exhaustion has no cleanup guarantee.
Resources acquired but not delivered require cleanup from the acquisition adapter or factory. Returned references do not suppress an existing with registration. See exit order , fault selection , and acquisition races .

title: Builds and dependencies
content:
Builds and dependencies# Guide index · Design index These pages explain how the compiler locates source files, records the versions used by a build, and reuses cached work. Start with the project manifest if you are setting up an application.
Project configuration and module paths — Set the source directory, entry file, and import paths in ms.toml. Pinned dependencies and deterministic output — Record versions and inputs so builds use the intended distribution. Caching and Go package boundaries — Understand what can be cached and when Go must rebuild a package.

title: Project configuration and module paths
content:
Project configuration and module paths# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A project has an ms.toml file at its root. The compiler reads this file to locate source and the entry file and to resolve optional import aliases. Each .ms file is one module; no source-level module declaration is required or accepted.
A project manifest# toml [project] name = "store" source = "./src" entry = "./src/main.ms" [aliases] "@domain" = "./src/domain" "@customers" = "./src/domain/customers.ms" project.name names the project. project.source identifies its source directory, and project.entry identifies its entry .ms file. All filesystem paths in the manifest resolve relative to the directory containing ms.toml, including the entry path; the entry path is not relative to project.source.
Commands and module discovery# Command Behavior ms check <ms.toml> Check the program and its entry signature ms build <ms.toml> Check, generate Go, and build the executable A relative manifest argument resolves from the invocation directory. Its containing directory then becomes the project root for configuration paths. The entry follows the CLI main contract .
The compiler discovers application modules by following imports from entry. The manifest does not enumerate them. Optional [adapters] entries map identifiers to project-relative manifest paths, for example files = "./adapters/files.toml". Adapter bindings define their interfaces and native symbols. Unknown manifest tables or keys are rejected.
The compiler supplies the minimal intrinsic prelude and the standard modules under @std, alongside local adapter interfaces. Third-party Manuscript packages are unsupported; native dependencies follow build pinning .
Resolving an import# Imports name an exported symbol and a path:
Manuscript import CustomerId from "./domain/customers.ms" import Order from "@domain/orders.ms" For an import in src/main.ms, the first path resolves to src/domain/customers.ms. The second expands @domain using the manifest and resolves to src/domain/orders.ms.
A path beginning with ./ or ../ resolves relative to the importing file’s directory. A path beginning with @std/ resolves within the compiler-supplied standard-library directory. @std alone selects no module. The [aliases] key @std is rejected, so an application cannot override standard identities. Other paths beginning with @ resolve through the importing project’s aliases. Alias keys consist of @ followed by one identifier, such as @domain. A directory alias matches its complete first path segment and appends the remaining path. @domain does not match @domain_extra. A directory alias alone does not select a module. A file alias selects exactly its target .ms file and accepts no appended path segments. Alias targets are filesystem paths relative to ms.toml; aliases do not expand other aliases. Direct paths and paths appended to directory aliases must include .ms. Resolution does not infer extensions or search for directory entry files. A file alias can omit the extension in the import because its configured target supplies it. Bare logical module names and absolute filesystem paths are not import forms. Paths use / as the separator. [aliases] is optional. Ordinary relative imports work without it. Missing source directories or entry files, invalid alias definitions, unknown aliases, and imports that do not resolve to an existing .ms file are compile errors. Import checking also rejects missing or internal symbols, wildcard imports, and cyclic module dependencies.
Module identity and configuration scope# The compiler normalizes resolved paths, including . and .., and resolves symbolic links to establish one canonical file identity within a build. Importing the same file through a relative path, a file alias, or a directory alias does not create separate modules. Cycle detection and module caching use this identity, so alternate path spellings cannot bypass cycle checks. Stable build metadata records paths relative to the owning project root rather than checkout-specific absolute paths.
Application paths, source directories, user aliases, adapter manifests, and interface modules must resolve inside the project root after symlink resolution. Escapes are compile errors. @std/...ms is the sole exception: paths resolve inside the pinned standard-library directory, and normalization/symlinks cannot escape that directory or reach application files. Standard module identity is its distribution version/content identity plus canonical distribution-relative path, independent of its installation location. Standard modules cannot import application modules.
Interfaces may use intrinsic types and import standard declarations or other registered interfaces, never application modules. Native Go dependencies are pinned adapter inputs. External Manuscript dependency projects and package acquisition syntax are unsupported.
Changes to source roots, entry files, aliases, or the pinned standard-library distribution can change the resolved module graph. The compiler includes relevant manifest settings in build and analysis cache identity, alongside source and dependency identities.
See module exports and imports , the compilation pipeline , and incremental compilation .
Previous: Cleanup and fault lowering · Next: Pinned dependencies and deterministic output

title: Pinned dependencies and deterministic output
content:
Pinned dependencies and deterministic output# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A reproducible build records which inputs and tool versions produced it. Those inputs include source, relevant ms.toml settings, the compiler and runtime, the Go toolchain, adapters, and dependencies. The project manifest chooses the entry file, source directory, and import aliases.
Pin the Go toolchain, compiler-supplied standard-library modules and their content identity, runtime, native adapters, and their dependencies. @std resolves only to that pinned distribution; a build does not fetch or silently substitute a newer library. Include this identity in module, analysis, and generated-code caches. Debug builds also pin the supported Delve version.
Generate deterministic symbol names and declaration order; do not rewrite unchanged output. This promises stable generated source for the same inputs. Byte-identical binaries need a separate toolchain and environment contract.
Details still needed# ms lock ms.toml explicitly creates or updates project-root ms.lock, a JSON object with closed fields: format: 1, compiler: "0.1.0", implementation_sha256, and toolchain. The implementation digest covers sorted compiler/frontend and embedded runtime source contents, excluding tests and checkout paths. Toolchain records Go version, OS/architecture, CGO, experiments, and architecture tuning from the embedded build payload, or an explicit MANUSCRIPT_GO override. Pins and builds share toolchain selection. The payload is extracted into a cache identified by its content hash and supplies its own GOROOT. Native commands use GOENV=off, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, and CGO_ENABLED=0; they need no system Go or C compiler and cannot automatically download another Go version. Pinned builds require empty GOFLAGS and use explicit -trimpath; --debug additionally disables optimization and inlining.
Project build, run, and test reject missing or mismatched pins and instruct the caller to explicitly run lock. Check/format/inspect/emit do not require a native toolchain pin. Standalone module builds record the selected toolchain without claiming a project lock. There are no third-party native dependencies in the supplied runtime. External adapter dependency pins and Delve remain separate future distribution contracts.
Native artifacts are cached under project .ms-cache/ by generated source, original module/configuration hashes, implementation content, target/toolchain, and debug flags. Cache hits verify metadata and binary content hashes; corruption rebuilds. A matching output is not rewritten. <executable>.ms-build.json carries source/configuration hashes and executable identity. compiler.VerifyBuild rejects mismatched binaries or supplied source/configuration snapshots before source interpretation. This pins source generation and artifact identity; byte-identical binary reproducibility across environments is not promised.
Pinning Delve keeps the native transport contract aligned with debugger integration .
Build identity and source hashes must travel with debug and trace metadata . See incremental compilation for caching and package boundaries.
Previous: Project configuration and module paths · Next: Caching and Go package boundaries

title: Caching and Go package boundaries
content:
Caching and Go package boundaries# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Caching can save the compiler from repeating parsing and checking. It cannot always save Go from rebuilding an application package. This page separates those two boundaries and explains what must be included in a cache key.
Cache parsing, checking, and module summaries by source, relevant project configuration, and dependency identity. Use canonical resolved file identity for modules; imports through different path spellings or aliases share a module summary.
Runtime, adapter schemas, and native adapters compile as separate packages. Native adapters and the application import schemas; schemas never import either. Adapter interfaces cannot use application types. Changing application code rebuilds its package; multiple generated files do not create independent compilation units. Go build documentation See project configuration , the pipeline , and deterministic generation .
Previous: Pinned dependencies and deterministic output · Next: Semantic conformance tests

title: Conformance and scope
content:
Conformance and scope# Guide index · Design index Conformance tests check whether the implementation follows the language rules. Some fixtures check that source is accepted or rejected; others must execute code and check observable behavior. Use the scope page to see remaining work and its dependencies.
Core-language conformance fixtures Runtime binding acceptance cases Semantic conformance tests — Test required behavior, including cancellation races and cleanup. Complete-program conformance — Check that guarantees work together in complete applications. Scope and implementation order — Find remaining decisions and the order in which work depends on them.

title: Core-language conformance fixtures
content:
Core-language conformance fixtures# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index These fixtures check whether the compiler accepts or rejects core-language programs and whether executed expressions behave as specified. They complement the semantic test plan . Host behavior, resource lifetimes, and concurrency have separate fixtures.
Each fenced accepted fixture is an independent .ms module, with its application types and helper functions included. Its module-level test body has the ordinary Unit return contract. A rejected variant replaces or removes exactly the indicated text in that fixture, leaving the rest unchanged. If a variant introduces a standard declaration, add its individual import unless missing-import rejection is the behavior under test. Test each variant independently: combining unrelated errors makes the expected diagnostic ambiguous.
The expected stage identifies the violated contract: parse for invalid source structure; resolution for an unknown or ambiguous symbol; type for incompatible types, shapes, labels, bounds, or control flow after parsing and resolution. A checker may combine its resolution and type passes, but must identify the specified cause at the offending source span. Diagnostic wording and internal pass layout are implementation choices. Accepted fixtures must satisfy the stated checks, rather than merely generate Go that compiles.
CL-01: Layout and named-call syntax# Contract: source syntax and declarations and calls .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn subtract(amount: Int, deduction: Int) -> Int: return amount - deduction test "named multiline call": let remaining = subtract( deduction: 2, amount: 9, ) if not (remaining == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") This accepts trailing commas and multiline calls while mapping labels to declared parameters. Reordering the written labels does not change the parameter mapping.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the call with subtract(amount: 9, deduction: 2) Accept; remaining is Int and equals 7 Replace it with subtract(9, 2) Type rejection: multi-parameter functions require argument labels Replace it with subtract(amount: 9, amount: 2) Type rejection: duplicate supplied argument and missing deduction Replace it with subtract(amount: 9) Type rejection: missing required deduction Replace it with subtract(amount: 9, discount: 2) Type rejection: unknown argument name discount Replace return amount - deduction with return missing Resolution rejection: unknown binding missing Remove the indentation before the function’s return Parse rejection: missing function block/module-level return Add lexical rejection fixtures for tabs, inconsistent dedentation, and unterminated delimiters as specified by the syntax chapter. Preserve the error’s actual cause rather than reporting a later missing return.
CL-02: Arithmetic grouping and Boolean short-circuiting# Contract: expressions and operators and numeric operations .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn invalid_division(zero: Int) -> Bool: return 1 / zero == 0 test "grouping and short circuit": if not (2 + 3 * 4 == 14): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ((2 + 3) * 4 == 20): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (10 - 3 - 2 == 5): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (true or invalid_division(zero: 0)): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (not (false and invalid_division(zero: 0))): return panic(message: "check failed") Both short-circuit checks must complete without invoking the invalid division. This observes control flow, not only operator result types.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace 2 + 3 * 4 with 2 + 3.0 * 4.0 Type rejection: mixed Int and Float, without implicit conversion Replace true or invalid_division(zero: 0) with 1 or invalid_division(zero: 0) Type rejection: logical operand must be Bool Replace a comparison with 1 < 2 < 3 Parse rejection: comparison operators cannot chain Replace true or invalid_division(zero: 0) with true or panic(message: "skipped") Accept and evaluate to true: the skipped Never operand is admissible as Bool Replace false and invalid_division(zero: 0) with false and panic(message: "skipped") Accept and evaluate to false: the right Never operand is not evaluated Integer overflow and division-by-zero fixtures must expect programming faults even if the backend could evaluate a wrapping Go operation. Use parameterized helpers to exercise runtime inputs rather than relying only on constant folding. Literal-range rejection is a separate compile-time fixture.
CL-03: Nominal constructors and record bindings# Contract: records and destructuring .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" type CustomerId: value: String type OrderId: value: String type Customer: id: CustomerId name: String fn customer_name(customer: Customer) -> String: let {id: {value}, name: display_name} = customer return "{value}: {display_name}" test "nominal record and nested binding": let customer = Customer(id: CustomerId(value: "c1"), name: "Ada") if not (customer_name(customer: customer) == "c1: Ada"): return panic(message: "check failed") Independent variant Expected outcome Use OrderId(value: "c1") for the customer’s id Type rejection: nominal OrderId is not CustomerId Omit name in Customer(...) Type rejection: missing field Add active: true to Customer(...) Type rejection: unknown field Supply name twice Type rejection: duplicate field Bind {email} from customer Type rejection: unknown record field Bind {id: value, name: value} Type rejection: duplicate local binding Assign customer.name = "Grace" after construction Parse rejection: assignment accepts a binding name, not a field target Public-surface rejection fixture:
Manuscript import List from "@std/collections.ms" type PrivateId: value: String export type PublicRecord: ids: List[PrivateId] Reject at type checking: the exported field exposes the internal nominal PrivateId through a nested application. Changing type PrivateId to export type PrivateId accepts the module. Public closure is not satisfied merely because the outer standard List type is public.
CL-04: Positional bindings and list shape# Contract: collections and destructuring .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" fn difference(values: List[Int]) -> Int: let [first, second] = values return first - second test "list binding": if not (difference(values: [9, 4]) == 5): return panic(message: "check failed") let empty: List[Int] = [] let {value: label} = Label(value: "ready") if not (label == "ready"): return panic(message: "check failed") type Label: value: String The empty literal gets its type from the annotation. difference’s binding is checked against List[Int]; its exact length is validated when the function runs.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace [9, 4] with [9, 4.0] Type rejection: heterogeneous numeric list without explicit conversion Replace let empty: List[Int] = [] with let empty = [] Type rejection: insufficient element-type information Replace the binding with let (first, second) = values Parse rejection: parenthesized positional binding is unsupported Replace the test call with difference(values: [9]) Function accepts List[Int]; evaluation faults at dynamic destructuring Replace the empty declaration with let [only] = [1, 2] Type rejection: statically known length mismatch; no extra value is discarded Annotate let [first, second]: List[Int] = values Parse rejection: only simple name bindings accept annotations A literal-length mismatch in the binding itself is a compile-time shape error; a list parameter’s runtime length is a programming-fault check. Optional optimization must not turn acceptance of the parameterized function into an invented fixed-length parameter type.
CL-05: Function values retain parameter labels# Contract: function values .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn increase(value: Int) -> Int: return value + 1 fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) test "function label compatibility": let transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int = increase if not (apply(value: 4, transform: transform) == 5): return panic(message: "check failed") Independent variant Expected outcome Rename only increase’s parameter and body binding to item Type rejection: fn(item: Int) -> Int is incompatible with fn(value: Int) -> Int Call transform(item: value) in apply Type rejection: unknown function-value argument label Change increase to return Float with body return 1.0 Type rejection at assignment/call: function result contract differs Change it to return Never with body panic(message: "stop") Type rejection at assignment: Never expression compatibility does not make function result types covariant Change the apply call to omit transform Type rejection: required function argument is missing CL-06: Return completeness and Boolean conditions# Contract: declarations and calls , conditionals , and faults .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn positive(value: Int) -> Int: if value > 0: return value else: panic(message: "positive value required") fn discard(value: Int) -> Unit: if not (value > 0): return panic(message: "check failed") test "return contracts": if not (positive(value: 3) == 3): return panic(message: "check failed") discard(value: 1) The faulting branch has no normal successor. discard accepts normal fallthrough because it returns Unit.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove the else branch in positive Type rejection: a reachable path falls through a non-Unit function Replace if value > 0 with if value Type rejection: condition must be Bool Replace return value with return true Type rejection: returned value is not Int Replace discard’s body with return 1 Type rejection: Int result in a Unit function Replace it with return or return unit Accept: explicit Unit return, like fallthrough Unreachable statements must still parse, resolve, and type-check; they do not repair a missing return on a reachable path.
CL-07: Alternatives, positional payload patterns, and exhaustiveness# Contract: alternatives and pattern matching .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" type Outcome: case Ready(value: Int) case Failed(reason: String) fn score(outcome: Outcome) -> Int: match outcome: Ready(value): return value Failed(_): return 0 test "alternative result": if not (score(outcome: Outcome.Ready(value: 8)) == 8): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (score(outcome: Outcome.Failed(reason: "unavailable")) == 0): return panic(message: "check failed") Constructors name payload fields; payload patterns bind positions in declaration order. Matching has no fallthrough.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove Failed arm Type rejection: non-exhaustive match Add another Ready(other) arm Type rejection: duplicate/unreachable arm Replace Ready(value) with Ready(value, extra) Type rejection: payload arity mismatch Replace Ready(value) with Ready(value: local) Parse rejection: payload patterns are positional, not named-call syntax Use Outcome.Ready(amount: 8) in the constructor Type rejection: wrong payload field name Add a final _: arm instead of Failed Accept; wildcard covers the remaining case Add _: with body return 0 after both existing arms Type rejection: every case is already covered, so the wildcard is unreachable Add ambiguity fixtures with two visible alternative types declaring Ready: unqualified construction must be rejected at resolution even when an expected result type could identify one; qualified construction succeeds. Match-case lookup is governed by the scrutinee type.
CL-08: Iteration and nearest-loop control flow# Contract: loops .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" fn selected_sum(values: List[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: if value == 0: continue if value < 0: break total = total + value return total test "iteration control": if not (selected_sum(values: [2, 0, 3, -1, 9]) == 5): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (selected_sum(values: []) == 0): return panic(message: "check failed") Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the iterable values with 3 Type rejection: Int is not an admitted iterable Assign value = 4 in the loop body Type rejection: iteration binding is immutable Put break in the test body outside a loop Type rejection: no enclosing loop Put continue inside a nested anonymous function without its own loop Type rejection: loop control cannot cross a function boundary For nested loops, verify that break and continue select the nearest enclosing loop. For while, verify that the condition is reevaluated and must have type Bool.
CL-09: Generic declaration, inference, and bounds# Contract: generics and equality .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" type Box[T: Shareable]: value: T fn unwrap[T: Shareable](box: Box[T]) -> T: return box.value fn same[T: Shareable & Equal](left: T, right: T) -> Bool: return left == right test "generic argument inference": let box = Box[Int](value: 6) if not (unwrap(box: box) == 6): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (unwrap[Int](box: box) == 6): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (same(left: 6, right: 6)): return panic(message: "check failed") Inference uses independently typed supplied arguments. Explicit and inferred applications must select the same substitution. Generic bodies are checked against declared bounds, not only the concrete types used by these tests.
Independent variant Expected outcome Use Box[Int, String](value: 6) Type rejection: generic arity mismatch Use Box[String](value: 6) Type rejection: field is not the substituted String type Use unwrap[String](box: box) Type rejection: invariant Box[Int] is not Box[String] Use same(left: 6, right: 6.0) Type rejection: supplied types do not yield one exact T Remove Equal from same’s bound Type rejection in generic body: T does not establish equality Use the undeclared type parameter U in Box’s field Resolution rejection: unknown type U Separate fixture:
Manuscript import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn absent[T: Shareable]() -> Optional[T]: return none test "result context does not infer function arguments": let value: Optional[Int] = absent[Int]() Accept the explicit call. Replacing absent[Int]() with absent() is a type rejection: result context cannot infer a generic function’s type arguments. An expected constructor payload type may provide context for none or an empty list without introducing result-context function inference.
Intrinsic-name rejection fixture:
Manuscript type Box[Int]: value: Int Reject at resolution: a type parameter cannot redefine the intrinsic Int identity. Int is a resolved name rather than a lexical keyword, so this is not a grammar rejection. Apply the same namespace check to module declarations/imports and fixed compiler-bound names, without prohibiting ordinary local shadowing where the module rules permit it.
CL-10: Explicit implementations and contract conversion# Contract: operation contracts .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" interface Increment: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int type Offset: delta: Int impl Increment for Offset: fn apply(value: Int) -> Int: return value + self.delta fn use_increment(operation: Increment) -> Int: return operation.apply(value: 4) test "explicit contract conversion": let offset = Offset(delta: 1) let operation = Increment(value: offset) let same_view = Increment(value: operation) if not (use_increment(operation: same_view) == 5): return panic(message: "check failed") self is implicit in the implementation body, never a source call argument. Conversion retains the concrete value; applying the same view constructor to an existing exact contract value is an identity conversion. The contract cannot be constructed without a value providing its declared implementation or already having that exact contract type.
Independent variant Expected outcome Pass offset directly as operation Type rejection: conversion to the contract must be explicit Remove the impl declaration Type rejection at conversion: Offset does not implement Increment Rename implementation parameter/body binding from value to item Type rejection: operation labels do not match the contract Change implementation result/body to Float/return 1.0 Type rejection: result signature mismatch Add self: Offset to the implementation parameter list Parse rejection: reserved self cannot be declared as a parameter Repeat the same impl Increment for Offset declaration Type rejection: duplicate implementation Replace Increment(value: offset) with Increment() Type rejection: conversion requires the concrete value argument Add a multi-module rejection fixture for an implementation outside the concrete type’s defining module; path/import mechanics follow module conformance . Contract method ambiguity on a concrete value is resolved by explicit conversion to the selected contract.
CL-10a: Generic implementations and nonoverlap# Contract: generic implementations .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" interface ReadValue[T]: fn get() -> T interface SameValue[T: Equal]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool type Box[T]: value: T impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T]: fn get() -> T: return self.value impl SameValue[T] for Box[T]: fn same(other: T) -> Bool: return self.value == other fn compare[T: Equal](box: Box[T], other: T) -> Bool: return box.same(other: other) test "generic implementations": let number = Box[Int](value: 7) let text = Box[String](value: "hello") let number_view = ReadValue[Int](value: number) let text_view = ReadValue[String](value: text) if not (number_view.get() == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (text_view.get() == "hello"): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (compare(box: number, other: 7)): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (not compare(box: number, other: 8)): return panic(message: "check failed") The first block needs no bound to read and return its field. The second inherits Equal from the SameValue interface to compare it. compare proves that implementation’s availability while checking its generic body, without waiting for a concrete instantiation.
Independent variant Expected outcome Add a concrete impl ReadValue[Int] for Box[Int] supplying get() -> Int Type rejection at declaration: overlap with the generic block, even if the body is identical Add another impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T] supplying get() -> T Type rejection at declaration: bounds cannot distinguish overlapping blocks Replace the first block’s ReadValue[T] with ReadValue[Int] Type rejection at declaration: get() -> T does not match the substituted contract result Int Remove Equal from SameValue’s interface parameters Type rejection at declaration: unconstrained field values cannot be compared Remove Equal from compare’s parameters Type rejection in the generic function body: the implementation’s bound is not proved Replace the first block’s receiver Box[T] with bare T Type rejection at declaration: receiver must have a defining nominal data declaration Add [U] to an implementation method Parse rejection: methods cannot introduce their own parameters Also accept disjoint concrete implementations for different receiver applications when no generic block covers them, and two different contract applications for one receiver. For the latter, use explicit views to disambiguate equal operation names. Reject expanding recursive implementation specialization under the ordinary finite-application check. The defining-module rule applies equally to concrete and generic blocks.
CL-10b: Plain and shared contract views# Contract: shared contract views and sharing .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" interface ReadValue[T]: fn get() -> T type Box[T]: value: T type SharedReader: reader: ReadValue[Int] & Shareable type CallbackReader: read_value: fn() -> Int impl ReadValue[T] for Box[T]: fn get() -> T: return self.value impl ReadValue[Int] for CallbackReader: fn get() -> Int: return self.read_value() fn seven() -> Int: return 7 fn local_view[T: ReadValue[Int]](source: T) -> ReadValue[Int]: return ReadValue[Int](value: source) fn shared_view[T: ReadValue[Int] & Shareable](source: T) -> ReadValue[Int] & Shareable: return (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: source) fn consume_shared[T: ReadValue[Int] & Shareable](source: T) -> Int: return source.get() test "plain and shared views": let box = Box[Int](value: 7) let plain = local_view(source: box) let shared = shared_view(source: box) let identity = (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: shared) let erased = ReadValue[Int](value: identity) let holder = SharedReader(reader: identity) let readers: List[ReadValue[Int] & Shareable] = [holder.reader] let optional: Optional[ReadValue[Int] & Shareable] = some(value: shared) let callback = CallbackReader(read_value: seven) let local_callback = ReadValue[Int](value: callback) if not (plain.get() == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (erased.get() == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (local_callback.get() == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (consume_shared(source: holder.reader) == 7): return panic(message: "check failed") local_view must be accepted with no sharing bound on its generic receiver. shared_view retains its proof through the returned type and the record field; the same implementation supplies every view. CallbackReader’s bare function field carries no callable-sharing promise, so the record is nonshareable even though this particular initializer is a safe named function. Its plain view and sequential call are accepted. View conversion evaluates the receiver once and neither copies nor closes native state. The collection and optional declarations exercise refined types inside generic arguments.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove Shareable from shared_view’s generic bound Type rejection in its body: receiver sharing is not proved Construct (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: plain) or use erased instead Type rejection: a plain view cannot recover its hidden receiver’s sharing guarantee Replace the callback’s plain view constructor with (ReadValue[Int] & Shareable)(value: callback) Type rejection: the bare function field gives its receiver no sharing proof Pass plain to consume_shared Type rejection at the generic application: named contract bound holds, sharing bound does not Change the list to List[ReadValue[Int]] = [plain] Type rejection: plain contract type fails the collection element bound Initialize SharedReader(reader: plain) Type rejection: plain and shared field types differ Replace ReadValue[Int](value: identity) with identity Accepted: the inferred local retains the shared type rather than erasing it Annotate that replacement as let erased: ReadValue[Int] = identity Type rejection: discarding sharing is not implicit Replace the shared constructor in shared_view with ReadValue[Int](value: source) Type rejection at return: expected shared type cannot refine a plain constructor Replace ReadValue[Int] & Shareable in the record field with Int & Shareable Type rejection: only an operation contract can have this refinement Replace the field type with Shareable & ReadValue[Int] Parse rejection: reversed order is not a value-type form Replace the field type with ReadValue[Int] & Equal Parse rejection: only the Shareable refinement is admitted With a trusted native nonshareable receiver fixture, accept a plain view and sequential calls, reject its shared view construction, and reject concurrently used closures retaining its plain view or bound method. A shared receiver’s method supplies receiver-sharing proof, subject to the existing callable-boundary rules. Verify that a shared service may return a nonshareable local result without making that result shareable. These checks must use frontend proofs rather than Go interface assignability or runtime receiver inspection.
CL-11: Recursive records require immutable-container indirection# Contract: records and generics .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" type Tree[T: Shareable]: value: T children: List[Tree[T]] test "recursive immutable collection": let leaf = Tree[Int](value: 1, children: []) let root = Tree[Int](value: 2, children: [leaf]) if not (root.value == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") Accept: removing the List storage edge leaves no inline record/alternative cycle, and recursive applications preserve T unchanged.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the children field type with Tree[T] Type rejection at declaration: unguarded inline cycle Replace it with Optional[Tree[T]] Type rejection at declaration: Optional does not provide storage indirection Replace it with Result[Tree[T], String] Type rejection at declaration: Result does not provide storage indirection Replace it with List[Tree[List[T]]] Type rejection at declaration: recursive application expands the type parameter The declaration check must reject the offending type before constructor errors in the test obscure the cycle. Mutual-recursion fixtures within one module must apply the same graph rule across every participating record/alternative. An import cycle is a separate module rejection, not a substitute for the inline-layout check.
CL-12: Collection iteration has concrete element types# Contract: loops and collections .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Map from "@std/collections.ms" import MapEntry from "@std/collections.ms" import Set from "@std/collections.ms" fn map_total(values: Map[String, Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for entry in values: let {key, value} = entry let label: String = key total = total + value return total fn set_total(values: Set[Int]) -> Int: var total = 0 for value in values: total = total + value return total test "map entry type": let entry = MapEntry[String, Int](key: "a", value: 3) if not (entry.key == "a"): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (entry.value == 3): return panic(message: "check failed") Accept these functions with the minimum collection API . The map loop element is MapEntry[String, Int], whose record fields are key: String and value: Int; the set loop element is Int.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace map-loop entry with [key, value] Parse rejection: a loop introduces one identifier, not a destructuring pattern Bind {missing} from entry Type rejection: unknown map-entry record field Declare let label: Int = key Type rejection: map key is String, not Int Replace Set[Int] with Set[Float] Type rejection: Float is not Hashable Replace Map[String, Int] with Map[List[Int], Int] Type rejection: collections are not hashable keys Runtime collection fixtures use the minimum constructor/update API: verify insertion-order traversal for maps and sets, and evaluate an effectful iterable expression exactly once. The concrete expectations are in runtime bindings .
CL-13: Lexical text forms and declaration-only modules# Contract: source grammar and text .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn echo(value: String) -> String: return value test "text source forms": if not (echo(value: "\{literal\}") == "\{literal\}"): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ("\u{1F600}" == "😀"): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ("value: {3}" == "value: 3"): return panic(message: "check failed") let no_value: Unit = unit Escaped braces are literal text; unescaped braces select interpolation. Source UTF-8 encoding and Unicode scalar validation are part of parsing text, independent of later text-conversion APIs.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the scalar escape with "\u{D800}" Parse rejection: surrogate is not a Unicode scalar Replace it with "\u{110000}" Parse rejection: scalar exceeds the Unicode range Replace an escape with "\q" Parse rejection: unknown escape Replace echo’s function name with the reserved word if Parse rejection: reserved word is not an identifier Add module-level let extra = 1 after the test Parse rejection: executable bindings belong in a block Replace let no_value: Unit = unit with let no_value: Unit = 0 Type rejection: Int is not Unit Replace it with let smallest: Int = -9223372036854775808 Accept: directly negated minimum Int literal Replace it with let too_large = 9223372036854775808 Type rejection: positive literal is outside Int range Replace it with let too_large = 1e400 Type rejection: Float literal would round to infinity Replace it with let unknown = 01 Parse rejection: leading-zero numeric spelling is not supported Equivalent LF and CRLF encodings must produce the same parsed structure after documented newline normalization. Invalid UTF-8 input must be rejected rather than silently replaced. Blank/comment-only lines do not introduce suites, and comment markers within text remain text.
CL-14: Result propagation preserves the declared error type# Contract: Result and try propagation .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" type Problem: case Missing(reason: String) type OtherProblem: case Invalid(reason: String) fn checked(value: Int) -> Result[Int, Problem]: if value < 0: return error(cause: Problem.Missing(reason: "negative")) return ok(value: value) fn doubled(value: Int) -> Result[Int, Problem]: let accepted = try checked(value: value) return ok(value: accepted * 2) fn summarize(outcome: Result[Int, Problem]) -> Int: match outcome: ok(value): return value error(_): return -1 test "unchanged propagated error": if not (summarize(outcome: doubled(value: 3)) == 6): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (summarize(outcome: doubled(value: -1)) == -1): return panic(message: "check failed") Successful construction obtains the complete Result[Int, Problem] type from the declared return contract. Propagation leaves the remaining body unexecuted on an expected error; it does not introduce an implicit error union or conversion.
Independent variant Expected outcome Change only doubled’s declared error type to OtherProblem Type rejection at try: incompatible propagated error Change doubled to return Int, and its final return to return accepted * 2 Type rejection at try: enclosing function must return compatible Result Replace ok(value: value) with ok(value: true) Type rejection: wrong successful payload type Replace the error payload with OtherProblem.Invalid(reason: "negative") Type rejection: wrong declared error payload type Replace the try operand with value Type rejection: operand is not Result Replace the local binding with let accepted: Int = try ok(value: 3) Type rejection: annotation does not propagate through try to infer the missing error type Replace the local binding with let accepted = try Result[Int, Problem].ok(value: value) Accept: qualification establishes both Result arguments before propagation An anonymous function establishes its own propagation boundary. Test that an inner Unit closure cannot use try merely because its enclosing function returns Result; the inner function’s signature controls compatibility.
CL-15: Equality eligibility does not imply hashing eligibility# Contract: equality and hashing .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Decimal from "@std/decimal.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" type Callback: handler: fn(value: Int) -> Int fn increment(value: Int) -> Int: return value + 1 fn preserve_key[K: Hashable](value: K) -> K: return value test "derived value equality": let present: Optional[Int] = some(value: 1) let same: Optional[Int] = some(value: 1) let missing: Optional[Int] = none if not (present == same): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (present != missing): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (1.00d == 1d): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ([1, 2] == [1, 2]): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ([1, 2] != [2, 1]): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (preserve_key(value: "key") == "key"): return panic(message: "check failed") let callback = Callback(handler: increment) Optional equality compares its tag and eligible payload. Decimal equality compares numeric values despite different trailing zeroes. List equality observes positions rather than treating a list as a set. Eligibility is checked recursively on record fields.
Independent variant Expected outcome Add if callback == callback: with a return body Type rejection: a function field makes Callback ineligible for equality Add if increment == increment: with a return body Type rejection: function values have no equality Use preserve_key(value: [1, 2]) Type rejection: equal lists are not hashable Use preserve_key(value: 1.0) Type rejection: Float is equal-comparable but not hashable Declare let wrong: Optional[Float] = present Type rejection: invariant optional applications differ Test generated record/alternative equality with eligible scalar leaves and reject derivations containing a noneligible leaf. Do not treat sharing eligibility, identical object references, or a user-written marker implementation as evidence of equality.
CL-16: Expected data types supply constructor context# Contract: compatibility and expected types , Optional , and Result .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" type Input: names: List[Optional[String]] fn outcome_value(outcome: Result[Int, String]) -> Int: match outcome: ok(value): return value error(_): return -1 test "data constructor context": let input = Input(names: [none, some(value: "Ada")]) let success: Result[Int, String] = ok(value: 3) let failure: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "unavailable") let absent: Optional[Int] = none let nested: List[List[Int]] = [[], [1]] if not (outcome_value(outcome: success) == 3): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (outcome_value(outcome: failure) == -1): return panic(message: "check failed") The field, binding annotation, or substituted parameter determines missing data arguments; it does not convert an independently known incompatible type. Forward declarations and contextual list elements do not require module-level execution.
Independent variant Expected outcome Remove : Result[Int, String] from success Type rejection: ok’s payload does not determine the error type Remove it from failure Type rejection: error’s payload does not determine the success type Remove : Optional[Int] from absent Type rejection: none supplies no payload type Change some(value: "Ada") to some(value: 3) Type rejection: independently known payload conflicts with expected String Replace none for absent with 3 Type rejection: no implicit Optional wrapping Replace ok(value: 3) for success with 3 Type rejection: no implicit Result wrapping Add a nonempty-list fixture [none, some(value: 1)]: the independently typed some determines Optional[Int] for the absent element. Reject [some(value: 1), some(value: "one")]; no implicit union is formed. These data-constructor rules do not infer a missing generic function specialization from its result context; CL-09 checks that separate boundary.
CL-17: Nonreturning subexpressions determine control-flow exits# Contract: Unit and Never .
The following independent module is a type-checking fixture; its faulting functions are not invoked as passing tests.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn failed_initializer() -> Never: let impossible: Int = panic(message: "initializer cannot return") fn returned_failure() -> Int: return panic(message: "result cannot return") fn endless() -> Int: while true: continue Accept: the initializer and return expression cannot produce values; the literal-true loop has no reachable break and therefore no normal exit. An expected annotation does not make a Never expression return an Int at runtime.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace the initializer with 0 Type rejection: the Never function now reaches normal fallthrough Replace the binding with let impossible: Int = 1 + panic(message: "stop") Accept: the operator result is Int, but its required right operand cannot return Replace the binding with let impossible: Bool = not panic(message: "stop") Accept: not selects Bool, but its required operand cannot return Replace the binding with let impossible: Int = panic(message: "left") + panic(message: "right") Type rejection: two Never operands supply no numeric candidate, even under an Int annotation Replace the binding with let impossible: Int = -panic(message: "stop") Type rejection: unary numeric selection requires an independently known numeric operand Replace the binding with let possible: Bool = false and panic(message: "skipped") Type rejection: the Never function has reachable fallthrough because the right operand is skipped Replace the binding with let possible: Bool = true or panic(message: "skipped") Type rejection: short circuiting permits normal fallthrough Add return unit after its initializer Type rejection: unreachable returns still must match the declared result type Replace return panic(...) with bare return Type rejection: a non-Unit function requires a value Replace while true with while not false Type rejection: nonliteral conditions retain a possible exit; no constant folding proves return completeness Add a reachable break inside endless Type rejection: the loop can exit and the Int function then falls through Extend the fixture with a nested loop whose own break does not exit the outer literal-true loop. A closure’s return likewise does not return from its enclosing function. Nonreturning callable/argument evaluation prevents later arguments and the outer call from running, under the ordinary evaluation-order contract.
CL-18: Suite-bodied function expressions resume the enclosing layout# Contract: anonymous-function suites and function values .
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" fn apply(value: Int, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int) -> Int: return transform(value: value) test "function suite boundaries": let dormant = fn() -> Int: return panic(message: "body is not run at creation") let grouped = apply( transform: ( fn(value: Int) -> Int: if value > 0: return value - 1 return 0 ), value: 3, ) let final_argument = apply( value: 3, transform: fn(value: Int) -> Int: return value - 1 ) if not (grouped == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (final_argument == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") The unused closure’s body must not run. Its dedent terminates both the function expression and the surrounding binding statement, so the next binding does not require an extra blank line. The grouped closure ends before the outer argument comma; the final ungrouped closure resumes the still-open call’s continuation when its body dedents. The nested if dedents within the active function suite rather than ending the enclosing call.
Independent variant Expected outcome Replace dormant’s function expression with fn() -> Int: 1 Parse rejection: a function body requires a statement suite Indent the final call-closing ) to the closure-body level Parse rejection: a delimiter opened outside the function body cannot close at body indentation Add let after = 1 at the next test-body indentation without a blank line after dormant Accept: synthetic statement boundary follows the function-expression suite Replace the anonymous expression with a nested named fn dormant() -> Int: declaration Parse rejection: named functions are not local statements Coverage and evidence# Maintain one independently checked fixture for each accepted module and each rejected variant. Record actual compiler results separately from the expected outcomes here. Scalar conversions, collection construction, and numeric edge behavior have runtime acceptance cases .

title: Runtime binding acceptance cases
content:
