Runtime binding acceptance cases# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index These fixtures check standard imports and API identities, concurrent sharing, data operations, hosts, and adapter rules. Run each accepted module and each rejected change independently. Use them alongside the core-language fixtures .
Standard imports and declaration identity# Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import List from "@std/collections.ms" import Decimal from "@std/decimal.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" fn amount() -> Result[Decimal, String]: return ok(value: 12.50d) test "explicit standard imports": if not ([1, 2].length() == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") let outcome = map_error( result: amount(), transform: fn(cause: String) -> Int: return cause.byte_length() ) match outcome: ok(value): if not (value == 12.50d): return panic(message: "check failed") error(_): return panic(message: "Unexpected case") Accept without an [aliases] table. Independently remove List and reject its bracket literal; remove Decimal and reject its annotation/literal; remove Result and reject its annotation and expression constructor lookup; remove map_error and reject its call. Importing Result alone must not expose map_error, and importing a function must not expose the type names in its signature. Match cases remain available from an inferred scrutinee even when its type name is not imported, as in the CLI entry fixture .
Accept this independent module without standard imports:
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" type List: count: Int type Result: case Value(value: Int) fn parallel(value: Int) -> Int: return value fn ordinary() -> Result: return Result.Value(value: parallel(value: 3)) test "standard spellings are ordinary names": if not (List(count: 2).count == 2): return panic(message: "check failed") let forward = parallel if not (forward(value: 4) == 4): return panic(message: "check failed") match ordinary(): Value(value): if not (value == 3): return panic(message: "check failed") Adding the canonical List or Result import rejects its collision with the local declaration. try ordinary() is rejected: this Result is not the standard alternative. A bracket literal is rejected without the standard List import even though a local List exists. Calling this local parallel with a tasks pack does not activate the standard binding’s special typing. Extracting the local parallel above is accepted as an ordinary function value.
Preserve the imported parallel/Background callable restrictions in all existing sharing fixtures. Independently reject unimported parallel, Background, ExecutionError, OperationId, StartError, and check_cancelled in otherwise well-formed calls or annotations; importing one standard export must not expose the rest. A local check_cancelled function remains an ordinary function and receives no runtime checkpoint behavior.
Module-resolution cases reject an [aliases] entry for @std, @std without a module path, a missing standard file/export, and paths or symlinks escaping the standard-library directory. Resolving a standard module in two installation directories with identical pinned contents preserves identity; changing its pinned distribution invalidates module/analysis/code-generation caches. Adapter interfaces may import standard declarations but cannot use that exception to import application files. Imports alone acquire no external authority.
Error adaptation and inferred packs# Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" import map_error from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" fn identity[T](value: T) -> T: return value fn probe() -> Result[Unit, ExecutionError]: let first = fn() -> Result[Int, String]: return ok(value: 3) let second = fn() -> Bool: return true let packed = try parallel(tasks: [first, second]) let copied = identity(value: packed) let [number, flag] = copied if not (flag): return panic(message: "check failed") match number: ok(value): if not (value == 3): return panic(message: "check failed") error(_): return panic(message: "Unexpected case") return ok(value: unit) test "pack helper": match probe(): ok(_): let completed = unit error(_): return panic(message: "Unexpected case") test "explicit error conversion": let failed: Result[Int, Int] = error(cause: 7) let translate = fn(cause: Int) -> String: return "Error {cause}" let converted = map_error(result: failed, transform: translate) let expected: Result[Int, String] = error(cause: "Error 7") if not (converted == expected): return panic(message: "check failed") Accept the complete load module in parallel too. Replace any error adapter with direct try under LoadError and reject the incompatible error type. Moving the probe’s try parallel directly into the Unit test is rejected. Changing the copied pack pattern to [number] is rejected for arity. Passing an existing list as tasks is rejected; qualifying or annotating a source type Pack is an unknown-name rejection. parallel(tasks: []) can be matched and its success destructured as [].
For mapping, accept fn(item: Int) -> Int and reject an otherwise identical fn(id: Int) -> Int. Reject start operations returning Int or plain Unit; accept only shareable fn() -> Result[Unit, String]. Use controlled reporter fixtures to verify String errors, crashes, status expiry, bounded overflow fallback, and reporter-fault fallback without recursive reporting.
Sharing and contract cleanup# Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Bytes from "@std/bytes.ms" import File from "@std/io.ms" import IoError from "@std/io.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" import Result from "@std/result.ms" type ClosedFile: marker: Unit impl File for ClosedFile: fn read(max_bytes: Int) -> Result[Optional[Bytes], IoError]: return error(cause: IoError.Closed) fn close() -> Unit: return test "contract-valued cleanup": with file = File(value: ClosedFile(marker: unit)): match file.read(max_bytes: 1): ok(_): return panic(message: "Unexpected case") error(cause): if not (cause == IoError.Closed): return panic(message: "check failed") This fake represents an already-closed stream, so its close is idempotent and has no external release obligation. Also accept (File & Shareable)(value: ClosedFile(marker: unit)) as the with initializer: cleanup works with either view. Reject with over a concrete type merely having a method named close without impl Closeable. Reject a contract with the wrong close signature. Verify native and source fake shared File values are interchangeable through Files.open’s Result[File & Shareable, IoError] result.
A bare function parameter carries no sharing proof. Reject a parallel closure capturing that parameter, even if a particular caller passes a safe named function. Accept a plain view over an implementing record containing a bare function field or unsynchronized native state for sequential use, but reject its shared view construction; such storage lacks a type-level sharing guarantee.
Accept concurrent captures of shared contract views, shareable concrete receivers, and generic values bounded by both Shareable and the behavioral contract. Reject concurrent captures of plain contract views and bound methods extracted from them, even when a particular runtime receiver is safe.
Test captured-function wrappers and branch/var merges so an unsafe alternative cannot retain a safe callable proof.
Independently reject this complete module at the parallel call: generic forwarding erases the callable proof even for this safe input.
Manuscript import Result from "@std/result.ms" import ExecutionError from "@std/tasks.ms" import parallel from "@std/tasks.ms" fn identity[T](value: T) -> T: return value fn rejected_forwarding() -> Result[Unit, ExecutionError]: let safe = fn() -> Int: return 1 let forwarded = identity(value: safe) let [value] = try parallel(tasks: [forwarded]) return ok(value: unit) Replacing forwarded with safe accepts the function. A generic function with T: Shareable instead rejects passing safe at bound checking. A Box[T] field storing a function does not restore the erased proof; Box[T: Shareable] rejects a function type argument. Ordinary generic data values and inferred result packs retain their type-level sharing properties; their behavior is unchanged.
Independently reject extracting let launch = background.start, let constructor = Background, a bare parallel reference, and forwarding these references to identity or a function parameter. These call-only bindings have requirements a plain function type cannot retain. A source wrapper that accepts an ordinary function parameter and forwards it to Background.start is rejected for missing callable proof at that direct call.
Data and numeric outcomes# Use the accepted modules in minimum data operations . In addition:
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" import Decimal from "@std/decimal.ms" import Optional from "@std/optional.ms" fn quotient(value: Int, divisor: Int) -> Int: return value / divisor fn remainder(value: Int, divisor: Int) -> Int: return value % divisor test "numeric boundary rules": if not (quotient(value: -7, divisor: 2) == -3): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (remainder(value: -7, divisor: 3) == -1): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (remainder(value: -9223372036854775808, divisor: -1) == 0): return panic(message: "check failed") let infinity = 1.0 / 0.0 let nan = 0.0 / 0.0 if not ("{infinity}" == "Infinity"): return panic(message: "check failed") if not (nan != nan): return panic(message: "check failed") let third = 1d / 3d if not ("{third}" == "0.3333333333333333333333333333333333"): return panic(message: "check failed") let absent: Optional[Int] = none if not (1e300.truncate_to_int() == absent): return panic(message: "check failed") if not ((2.seconds + 1.seconds) == 3.seconds): return panic(message: "check failed") Runner-level fault probes use parameters for division by zero, minimum Int/-1, unary minimum Int negation, duration overflow, Decimal overflow, and invalid byte construction. Check normal subnormal/zero Decimal underflow and halfway ties-to-even. Reject out-of-grid Decimal literals and more than 34 significant digits; accept insignificant trailing zeroes. Map mutation tests verify a/b/a-replacement traversal as a→3,b→2, original snapshot retention, and remove/reinsert ordering. Reject source implementations for standard native collection types.
Entry, adapter, and lifetime integration# Build the complete CLI main module with an ms.toml selecting it, pass two arguments, and expect Arguments: 2 plus LF and exit 0. Missing/internal/generic/wrong-signature main must fail checking. Inject SIGINT and SIGTERM during joined work and verify joins/cleanup before exits 130/143. A cleanup fault exits 70. Host escalation is separately classified as incomplete cleanup.
Generate a separate schema package for a minimal interface, a native adapter package importing it, and an application importing both; the pinned Go toolchain must build this without an import cycle. Reject interface imports of an application module, invalid/duplicate bindings, absent acquisition disposers, wrong native symbol signatures, and mutable/invalid foreign result values.
Controlled race probes cover acquisition versus cancellation, completion versus stop, admission versus close, repeated close, and close from an admitted job’s nested parallel descendant or reporter. The latter must fault before shutdown instead of self-joining. Generic function specialization probes accept regular self/mutual recursion and reject expanding specialization through calls or stored function values before Go emission.

title: Semantic conformance tests
content:
Semantic conformance tests# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A conformance test checks a required rule by observing a program. For concurrency, use controlled transitions to exercise specific races and stress tests to exercise real scheduling.
Core-language fixtures specify independent accepted modules and rejected variants for the grammar, operators, inference, contracts, and control flow. Their parse/resolution/type outcomes are authoritative for this core pass; the runtime coverage below remains a separate conformance track.
Tests use test "name": blocks and ordinary if/return guards. Import panic from @std/faults.ms and return panic(message: ...) when a check fails; a bare return completes a Unit test successfully. Control fake I/O, virtual clocks, and barriers around runtime transitions; Go goroutine scheduling remains nondeterministic. Stress and race tests exercise real transitions. Required coverage includes source-order preparation, exact heterogeneous results, domain errors, snapshot captures, sharing bounds, with registration and cleanup, closed-resource aliases, atomic admission/completion/close races, cleanup faults, and fixed deadline parents.
Test runner# A source test body is checked as a zero-parameter Unit function. Discovery and execution are still unspecified: the runner needs a command, file selection rules, stable test identities, duplicate-name handling, isolation, authority inputs, and a way to expect a programming fault. It must also define whether test bodies enter ordinary builds. The examples here fix expected behavior without assuming those runner decisions.
Tests in source# The parallel API requires coverage for empty, one-position, and heterogeneous literal task packs; source-order preparation; result ordering despite reversed completion; unchanged domain results; and cancellation/fault paths that join all started work.
Cover each row of the joining outcome table with a virtual timer: caller cancellation during a group timeout unwinds the caller, a cleanup fault after a timeout reports Crashed, an empty pack with a zero timeout succeeds, and a nonempty pack with a zero timeout reports TimedOut without running any body. Verify that a while loop with no explicit checkpoint unwinds at its next back-edge after cancellation. Reject non-function task entries and functions requiring arguments.
Verify that let [resA, resB] = try parallel(tasks: [first, second]) preserves each result’s type inside a helper returning Result[Unit, ExecutionError]; the Unit test matches that helper’s result and checks success. Direct try parallel(...) in a Unit test is rejected. Mixed domain/execution errors use map_error, as in the complete parallel example.
Destructuring conformance covers array and record patterns, shorthand, renaming, nesting, let and var, and single evaluation of the initializer. Reject parenthesized positional bindings, fixed-pack arity mismatches, unknown fields, and duplicate local names. Check that dynamic list length mismatches fault rather than introducing missing values or discarding extra elements.
Module conformance covers relative, user-alias, and explicit standard imports, the reserved @std alias, standard declaration identity independent of installation path, rejection of missing imports and standard-name collisions, manifest-relative configuration, canonical file identity, project containment after symlink resolution, visibility, and cycle rejection. Check aliases at complete segment boundaries and invalidate cached analysis when relevant configuration changes. Project configuration defines the accepted and rejected paths; external Manuscript dependency projects are unsupported.
List-argument conformance covers empty, one-element, and multi-element lists, passing existing lists, multiple list parameters, and calls through function values. Check both labeled and unlabeled single-parameter calls, including generic inference and contextual empty lists. Require labels for multi-parameter functions; reject unknown labels, duplicate arguments, missing arguments, incompatible list element types, and nonshareable list elements. Use controlled capability calls to verify left-to-right list-element evaluation and source order between arguments, including closure creation and with initialization.
Manuscript import panic from "@std/faults.ms" test "checked decrement": let value = 3 if not (value - 1 > 0): return panic(message: "check failed") This illustrates the test-block syntax and ordinary conditional returns for failed checks. Runtime tests need fake capabilities, virtual clocks, and barriers to arrange meaningful races, rather than assuming a fixed goroutine schedule.
For an acquisition race, verify that the adapter closes a newly acquired resource if delivery loses to cancellation, and that with registers a delivered resource without a cancellation gap. Never recursively close arbitrary parallel result fields or captures. Test aliases invoked after scope exit, concurrent operation/close races, stale pooled leases, reverse close order, and idempotent shutdown. Background tests cover bounded rejection, closed admission, independent siblings, observed domain errors and faults, bounded reporting state, optional drain, cancellation, and joining. A captured var keeps its creation-time value; assignment to an outer captured local is rejected.
See completion and acquisition and complete-program evidence .
Previous: Caching and Go package boundaries · Next: Complete-program conformance

title: Complete-program conformance
content:
Complete-program conformance# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A feature can pass an isolated test and still fail when combined with other features. These complete-program checks combine cleanup, concurrency, external I/O, and tooling to catch those interactions.
Validate these complete programs as their APIs become concrete:
Program Required evidence CLI argument output and bounded file reads exact Process entry, explicit authority, specified stream signatures, cleanup, and exit behavior CLI draining subprocess stdout/stderr concurrent streaming and deterministic resource release Bounded HTTP server with slow clients admission, backpressure, limits, failure isolation Background worker surviving a submitting helper’s completion fixed service parent, bounded admission, error observation, and joined shutdown Cancellation during resource acquisition atomic completion and disposal of undelivered resources Nested cleanup with a fault every remaining cleanup runs exactly once; secondary diagnostics retained Debug session through parallel, Background, and with source stepping, value rendering, and task inspection Fixture contents# Each fixture includes complete source, ms.toml, adapter inputs, arguments and environment, and an expected transcript and exit outcome. Race fixtures also specify controlled barriers, allowed outcomes, and which resources must be released. Debug fixtures specify source stops and the values visible at each stop. A scenario description alone is not executable evidence.
The subprocess, HTTP, and debugger fixtures depend on the outstanding API and tooling decisions .
See semantic coverage and implementation priorities .
Previous: Semantic conformance tests · Next: Scope and implementation order

title: Scope and implementation order
content:
Scope and implementation order# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Use this page to see which parts of the design depend on others and which decisions remain open. The implementation order starts with language checking, adds runtime and library behavior, then builds tooling on those checked facts.
Implementation order# Parse and check the language, including named calls, exact types, contracts, captures, and sharing. Implement lexical cleanup and atomic start, cancellation, completion, and close transitions together. Connect standard imports, data operations, CLI host, streams, and adapters; validate complete programs. Complete the queue, pool, builder, HTTP, and subprocess APIs using the same lifetime and cancellation rules. Build source tools, diagrams, traces, and debugging on checked compiler facts and matching runtime metadata. Use the semantic tests and complete programs to check that these parts agree. A written acceptance case becomes evidence only when an implementation runs it and records the result.
Outstanding decisions# These gaps still need concrete contracts.
Area Details still needed Authoritative page Test runner Discovery, test identity, duplicate names, isolation, authority inputs, expected faults, and build inclusion Semantic tests Build distribution External adapter/dependency locks and supported debugger distribution Reproducibility Native adapter ABI Generated Go declarations, receiver construction, disposer types, and compatibility validation Adapter manifests Capability analysis Classification of adapter interfaces, pure contracts, wrappers, and indirect authority Authority Queue extensions Fairness and additional channel patterns beyond the bounded FIFO contract Queues State and pool extensions Atomic update APIs, native resource factories, and additional lease contracts State and pools Builder extensions Additional bulk mutation operations beyond sealed snapshot construction Builders HTTP and subprocess extensions Additional host contracts, interactive subprocess streams, and uniform cross-platform descendant supervision; current HTTP clients, streaming hosts, and WebSockets are covered in package coverage HTTP hosts , streams Source tools Rich diagnostic spans, transactional structural edits, and failed-write recovery Source tools Diagrams and debugging Stable node identity, diff/trace formats, stepping behavior, value rendering, and supported debugger versions Developer tooling For each gap, add exact signatures or data fields, success and failure behavior, an accepted example, and a boundary or rejected example to its concept page. Then add observable conformance expectations. Other guides should link to the rule rather than repeat it.
Unsupported features# Actors, detached tasks, task adoption, racing combinators, inheritance, macros, operator overloading, implicit conversions, and user-defined metaprogramming have no supported forms. More specific syntax exclusions appear on the relevant concept pages.
Forced task termination is unsupported. Uncooperative work can delay joining indefinitely; host escalation is an incomplete shutdown, not successful cleanup. See cancellation and background shutdown .

title: Developer tooling
content:
Developer tooling guide# Design index Use the tools to format source, read diagnostics, and inspect program structure. Later sections describe diagrams, traces, and planned source-level debugging. Consult implementation coverage for features that are still design work.
Reading order# 1. Source tools # Canonical formatting and generated views Structural edits and revision guards Readable and structured diagnostics 2. Diagrams and traces # System, flow, and detail views Reading a concurrent-flow diagram Architecture diffs Execution traces and overlays 3. Debugging # Build, source, and task metadata Generated Go source mapping Debugger transport and source interpretation

title: Source tools
content:
Source tools# Guide index · Design index Source tools help you keep code consistently formatted and understand errors. The structural-editing design also describes how tools can propose an edit against a specific source revision.
Canonical formatting and generated views Structural edits and revision guards Readable and structured diagnostics

title: Canonical formatting and generated views
content:
Canonical formatting and generated views# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The source file defines the program. The formatter gives it a consistent layout, and tools can regenerate diagrams and explanations from it.
Format a file# sh ms fmt file.ms ms fmt file.ms --check The first command formats in place. --check writes nothing and returns a nonzero status if formatting would change the file. Invalid input produces diagnostics and no write.
Formatter contract# Formatting preserves program meaning and comments. It uses four-space indentation and LF line endings with a final newline. Formatting twice produces the same text; this property is called idempotence.
The current formatter applies these layout rules:
Keep token spellings and physical code lines; do not rewrap lines. Put one space around operators and after argument/type colons and commas. Remove spaces next to delimiters and put two spaces before inline comments. Collapse blank runs to one line and remove leading and trailing blank lines. Keep comment text but remove trailing whitespace. Round comment-only indentation down to a multiple of four. Golden-output and token-equivalence tests verify these choices. A valid rewrite replaces the file through an atomic rename in the same directory.
Generated explanations# Compilation and task creation never invoke AI implicitly. Model output enters through an explicit capability call and validation. A generated explanation cannot change compilation behavior or replace a source edit.
See source layout and capability inputs .
Next: Structural edits and revision guards

title: Structural edits and revision guards
content:
Structural edits and revision guards# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Structural editing changes a program entity, such as a function or a resolved symbol. For example, a rename follows references to that symbol instead of replacing every matching word. Revision guards ensure the source has not changed since the edit was prepared.
The compiler exposes typed syntax, symbol references, effect summaries, scope/capture/sharing checks, and control flow. Operations include replacing a function, renaming a symbol, and adding a match case.
A guarded edit# Resolve the entities to change and record revisions for every source/configuration input read, including ms.toml and referenced modules. Prepare all affected files together. Renames follow symbol identity rather than matching text spellings. Parse, resolve, and check the proposed program before writing. Recheck every revision guard. A stale input or validation failure rejects the entire edit with zero writes. Apply the accepted edit as one transaction; report success only when all intended files are updated. For example, a cross-file rename is stale when a referenced file changes, even if the file containing the declaration did not. The tool must reread and prepare a new edit.
The wire schema and recovery from I/O failure or process interruption still need definitions. The implementation must provide recovery before claiming transactional multi-file edits.
See typed compiler facts and structured diagnostics .
Previous: Canonical formatting and generated views · Next: Readable and structured diagnostics

title: Readable and structured diagnostics
content:
Readable and structured diagnostics# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A diagnostic explains a problem and points to the source that caused it. Human-readable output helps you fix the code; structured output lets editor tools locate the same problem.
Each diagnostic has a stable rule code, a readable message, and a primary source span. Related declarations or call sites use secondary spans. Source coordinates follow the metadata span contract .
Explaining a violated rule# For example, a non-function entry in a parallel pack should identify the required callable type and source position. An invalid with initializer should identify the missing concrete implementation, contract operation, or generic-bound proof. A missing match alternative or unnamed argument should identify the relevant declaration and call-site location. Runtime closed-resource errors carry operation and source locations separately from static diagnostics.
ms check file.ms --json emits {"format": 1, "diagnostics": [...]}. Each diagnostic has code, phase, message, and position with file, one-based line/UTF-8 byte column, and original-byte offset. Empty results use []. CRLF normalization preserves original offsets.
Codes identify rule families: MS1000 grammar, MS1001 literals/text, MS1002 layout; MS2001 names/members, MS2002 modules; MS3000 general typing, MS3001 exact types/operators, MS3002–3004 duplicate/missing/unknown arguments, MS3010–3012 implementations, MS3020 sharing, MS3021 hashing, MS3030 captures, MS3040 recursion, MS3050 exhaustiveness, MS3060 mutation, MS3070 numeric literals, MS3080 generic inference; MS4000 lowering. Full token-range and related-declaration spans remain a richer diagnostic revision. The rules being reported are defined by type checking and scope and capture checking .
Previous: Structural edits and revision guards · Next: System, flow, and detail views

title: Diagrams and traces
content:
Diagrams and traces# Guide index · Design index Diagrams show relationships derived from checked source: which functions call each other, where work runs concurrently, and what changes across revisions. Execution traces add what actually happened during a run.
System, flow, and detail views Reading a concurrent-flow diagram Architecture diffs Execution traces and overlays

title: System, flow, and detail views
content:
System, flow, and detail views# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Choose a diagram based on the question you need to answer: which modules depend on each other, how work runs, or how data changes. These views come from checked source, so reviewers can follow links back to the code.
The compiler emits three views:
View Contents System Modules, exported operations, capabilities, external resources Flow Calls, branches, loops, parallel groups, background admission, joins, errors, cancellation, deadlines Detail Data transformations, types, implementations, source locations Nodes link to typed source and contracts. System and detailed flow views label execution-lifetime and cancellation edges separately from value dependencies. Loops remain loops; the compiler does not expand them into hypothetical executions. Dynamic dispatch shows a contract and known targets; unresolved behavior remains explicitly unresolved.
Choosing the view# Start with the system view to inspect dependencies and authority. Use a flow view to examine concurrent APIs, errors, and cleanup. Use detail to connect transformations and types back to source.
See a concurrent-flow example , architecture diffs , and observed execution overlays .
Previous: Readable and structured diagnostics · Next: Reading a concurrent-flow diagram

title: Reading a concurrent-flow diagram
content:
Reading a concurrent-flow diagram# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Read this diagram from the preparation step downward. The two branches run concurrently, then meet at a join. It shows how parallel handles ordinary results, faults, timeouts, and caller cancellation.
flowchart TD R[Prepare first and second functions] --> A[Call parallel with a 2 second timeout] A --> I[Start first operation] A --> S[Start second operation] I --> W[Observe completion outcomes] S --> W W -->|Both complete normally| J[Join operations and cleanup] J --> V[Return ordered domain Results] W -->|Operation fault or API timeout| C[Cancel unfinished operations] P[Caller cancellation or deadline] -.-> C C --> K[Join all operations and cleanup] K -->|Execution failure| E[Return ExecutionError] K -->|Caller stopped| U[Unwind caller]The API prepares all arguments before starting work. Successful positions follow input order regardless of completion order. A domain error is an ordinary returned value; it does not cancel siblings.
Every exit joins all operations, even if joining exceeds the initiating timeout. Caller cancellation unwinds the caller after joining. Resource cleanup follows explicit with registrations; no result or capture is recursively closed merely because it is unreturned.
Background submission has a different lifetime edge: an accepted operation runs under its service’s fixed parent, survives a submitting request, and is joined during service shutdown. See Background , cancellation propagation , and cleanup ordering .
Previous: System, flow, and detail views · Next: Architecture diffs

title: Architecture diffs
content:
Architecture diffs# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A small source edit can change what a system can access or how long work runs. An architecture diff highlights those changes to boundaries and behavior, alongside the ordinary text diff.
Architecture diffs report changed boundaries, capabilities, effects, error types, cleanup scopes, concurrency, and deadlines. These facts derive from compiler analysis. Explanations of intent are supplementary.
Reviewing a changed boundary# For example, adding a capability parameter changes accepted authority. Adding background submission changes a service lifetime boundary. Adding with changes an explicit cleanup boundary. Adding a domain error changes the caller’s expected alternatives. These changes belong in the derived architecture view because they follow from checked source.
The draft defines the reported facts, but does not prescribe a diff rendering format. See boundary contracts and effect summaries .
Previous: Reading a concurrent-flow diagram · Next: Execution traces and overlays

title: Execution traces and overlays
content:
Execution traces and overlays# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index A flow diagram shows what a program can do. A trace records what happened during one run. A trace overlay places those observations on the matching diagram so you can follow timing and outcomes.
Matching observations to source# Concurrent task scheduling and external effects can vary between executions. The overlay should report the observed timing and outcomes rather than imply that one observed order is guaranteed.
Trace overlays are enabled only when metadata matches the executable. Operation identities, fixed execution parents and API join relationships, and effective deadlines come from the build/runtime metadata contract.
See metadata identity checks and scheduling guarantees .
Previous: Architecture diffs · Next: Build, source, and task metadata

title: Debugging
content:
Debugging# Guide index · Design index These pages describe the source locations and runtime metadata needed to debug Manuscript through generated Go. They also explain the planned debugger bridge. Start with metadata before reading the integration details.
Build, source, and task metadata Generated Go source mapping Debugger transport and source interpretation

title: Build, source, and task metadata
content:
Build, source, and task metadata# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Metadata connects an executable and its runtime events to the exact source that produced them. Debugging and trace tools must check that connection before showing events on source code.
Keep static build facts separate from runtime observations:
Record Required information Build manifest Build identity, source hashes, source spans and statement boundaries, generated symbol/local mappings, type and variant descriptions, and static API sites Run records Run identity, operation IDs, fixed execution parents, join relationships, effective deadlines, events, timing, and outcomes; references to the matching build’s static sites Source spans are half-open UTF-8 byte ranges in the original file. Newline normalization during parsing must retain a mapping to those original positions. Static IDs are deterministic within a build; operation IDs are interpreted within one run.
Before enabling debugging or trace overlays, match the manifest to the executable and source hashes. Reject mixed-build or mixed-run observations. Runtime operation IDs and deadlines cannot be emitted as completed facts at build time.
Storage schemas, event ordering/timestamps, and whether source bytes are embedded or loaded by hash still need concrete definitions.
See build identity and source value interpretation .
Previous: Execution traces and overlays · Next: Generated Go source mapping Implemented static inspection# ms inspect <module-or-project> emits format-1 JSON with a source-derived build identity, original source hashes, deterministic entity IDs, generated declaration and local names, type descriptions, call sites including implicit cleanup, conservative transitive effects, and statement header spans. Header spans are half-open ranges in original bytes and exclude line terminators. ms diagram emits the checked static call graph as Mermaid. Native checked builds emit a separate executable/toolchain manifest.
Generated source uses Go line directives, and source programming faults collect Manuscript function positions. --debug retains native symbols, disables optimization/inlining, and uses absolute source paths. Generated local identifiers retain source names. The VS Code Manuscript DAP adapter connects to Delve and renders checked local names, records, collections, variants, interface views, and execution/service inspection. Versioned rename and code actions validate source edits. Run-event transport and generalized structural transformations remain additional tooling contracts.

title: Generated Go source mapping
content:
Generated Go source mapping# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index Generated Go includes line directives that point back to Manuscript statements. A debug build keeps symbols and disables optimization and inlining so the debugger has enough information to follow the source.
Go line directives Source positions and build mode# Line directives provide native source position mapping. Retaining symbols and disabling optimization and inlining in a debug build preserve information needed by the debugger, while build metadata supplies the type and local-variable descriptions.
Mapping a source line does not by itself explain a generated cleanup frame or a source alternative value. See the Manuscript debugger layer .
Previous: Build, source, and task metadata · Next: Debugger transport and source interpretation

title: Debugger transport and source interpretation
content:
Debugger transport and source interpretation# Guide index · Chapter index · Design index The debugger design has two parts: Go tools control execution, while a Manuscript layer explains source values, concurrent operations, and generated frames. A native line number alone cannot explain a source alternative or a cleanup frame.
Delve DAP provides native debugger transport; a Manuscript debugger layer renders source values and marks generated cleanup and runtime frames. Native line mapping alone does not provide that interpretation.
Delve DAP Inspecting parallel, Background, and with# The required debug conformance program steps through API admission, concurrent operations, joining, and cleanup. It must demonstrate source stepping, value rendering, and operation and service inspection together; native line mapping alone cannot establish that behavior.
See complete-program evidence , metadata , and Go line mapping .
Previous: Generated Go source mapping
